en.title: は vs が
en.subtitle: The eternal puzzle
en.intro: The two most important particles in Japanese — and yes, the difference is confusing at first. Even advanced learners still trip over it now and then. But don't worry: with a few core ideas, the whole thing becomes surprisingly logical. The secret is not to see は and が as opponents, but as two tools with different jobs. Both can appear in the same sentence, and that's exactly when their true nature shows best.
sections[].heading: は — "As for me..."
が — The spotlight
Together in one sentence
は for contrast
Rules of thumb
sections[].text: は (pronounced "wa") is the topic marker. It doesn't say who does something — it says what we're talking about right now. Imagine holding up a sign: "Attention, now we're talking about X!" The topic is something both speakers already know or that's currently on the table. It's the frame in which the rest of the sentence takes place. English has no direct equivalent — the closest are "As for X..." or "Speaking of X...".

が is the subject marker. It points at someone or something and says: "THAT's the one!" が comes into play whenever new information is delivered — an identity is revealed, a surprise is expressed or existence is stated. While は sets up the background, が lights up the foreground. If someone asks "Who did that?", the answer is a が-sentence, because the identity is new.

は and が often appear in the same sentence — and that's exactly where the difference is clearest. The topic (は) sets the outer frame: "What are we talking about?" The subject (が) points at something specific within that frame. A good image: は is the stage, が is the spotlight on the lead actor.

An important extra function of は: it can express contrast. When you attach は to two things, it implicitly says: "This one yes, but that one no." This even works within a single sentence. This contrastive は is extremely common and easily overlooked.

Here are the most important guidelines at a glance. These rules cover an estimated 90% of all cases:
  • New information? → が (answer to "Who? What?")
  • Known topic? → は (What are we talking about?)
  • Contrast? → は (Coffee I like, but tea I DON'T)
  • Existence / natural phenomena? → が (There is... / It's raining...)
  • Feelings & abilities? → が for the object (猫が好き, 日本語がわかる)
  • In subordinate clauses? → が (は is almost never allowed there)
sections[].tip: When in doubt: if you're answering the question "Who/What exactly?", use が. If you're talking about something both sides already know, use は. And don't overthink it — even if you get it wrong now and then, you'll still be understood!
sections[].examples[].de: I'm a student. (Literally: As for me — student.)
Tokyo is big. (As for Tokyo — big.)
It's hot today, isn't it? (As for today...)
Who came? (We're looking for the identity.)
Tanaka came! (New info: it's Tanaka!)
It's raining. (The rain is falling — natural event.)
I like cats. (As for me: cats are what I like.)
In Japan, the food is delicious. (As for Japan: food = delicious.)
I have a headache. (As for me: head = hurts.)
Coffee I drink, but tea I don't.
Meat I eat, but fish I don't.
Kanji I can read, but I can't write them.
Who opened the window? (Identity wanted → が)
Tanaka opened it. (New info → が)

en.title: たら, ば, と, なら
en.subtitle: Four ways to say "if"
en.intro: In English you mostly get by with "if" and "when" — Japanese has four different conditional forms. That sounds intimidating at first, but each form has its own character and its own "personality". Some are flexible, some are specialized. Here you'll learn the basic rules for when each form fits — and at the end you get a comparison that works as a cheat sheet.
sections[].heading: たら — The all-rounder
ば — The general condition
と — The automatic consequence
なら — "If we're talking about X..."
Quick comparison
sections[].text: たら is the most flexible and most used conditional form. It means "if/when X happens (or has happened), then...". The formation is simple: た-form + ら. That's all. たら can be used for past, future, hypothetical and real situations. When in doubt, たら is almost always an acceptable choice.

ば expresses a general, hypothetical condition — "on the condition that...". It sounds somewhat more formal and abstract than たら. Formation: with う-verbs the last syllable shifts to the え-row + ば (行く→行けば, 飲む→飲めば). With る-verbs: る → れば. With i-adjectives: い → ければ. ば is often used for proverbs and general wisdom.

と expresses a natural, automatic, inevitable consequence — "whenever X, then Y necessarily follows". It is used for laws of nature, mechanical processes, directions and habits. と is always preceded by the plain non-past form. Important: the result clause must contain no intention, no request, no suggestion — the consequence has to happen automatically.

なら picks up a topic or an assumption that someone has just mentioned and responds to it. It means something like "if that's the case", "as for X" or "assuming that...". なら has a special property: the order of condition and result can be reversed — the result can happen BEFORE the condition in time.

FormNuanceGood for
たらIf/when X happens / has happened...Everything — the safest choice, usable everywhere
ばOn the condition that...General / hypothetical conditions, proverbs
とWhenever... (automatically)Laws of nature, instructions, habits (no intention in the result!)
ならAs for X... / If that's the case...Reacting to what you've heard, recommendations, advice
sections[].tip: たら is the safest way to say "if". If you're unsure which form to use — take たら. That way you'll get it right in 95% of cases.

と does NOT work for requests, suggestions or wishes. "If it rains, take an umbrella" doesn't work with と (taking an umbrella is a deliberate action). For that you need たら. Remember: と = automatic, no control by will in the result.

In practice the boundaries sometimes blur, and often several forms are possible. But the basic rule is clear: たら for everyday situations, ば for general conditions, と for automatic consequences, なら for reacting to what has been said.
sections[].examples[].de: If it rains, I'll stay at home.
If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
When I go to Japan, I want to eat sushi.
if you eat (る → れば)
if you go (く → けば)
If it's cheap, I'll buy it. (い → ければ)
If you don't go, you'll regret it. (ない → なければ)
When you press this button, the door opens. (mechanism)
When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom. (law of nature)
If you turn right, there's a station. (directions)
If you're going to Japan, I recommend Kyoto.
If you're free — could you help me?
If that's the case, then it's fine.

en.title: ～ことにする・～ことになる
en.subtitle: Decision and outcome — choosing yourself vs. having it decided
en.intro: These two patterns look almost the same but express different perspectives. ～ことにする describes a conscious decision, ～ことになる an outcome or an arrangement that has been settled. This very shift in perspective is central for N4.
sections[].heading: ～ことにする — I decide to do it
～ことになる — it gets decided / it turns out that way
sections[].text: With verb in the dictionary form / ない-form + ことにする you express your own decision. The focus is on the speaker's active choice.

With verb + ことになる you say that something has been decided or comes about as a result. The decision doesn't come across as the speaker's active personal resolution, but as a rule, a decision made by others, or a consequence.
sections[].tip: ～ことにしている often describes a self-imposed habit or rule.
Quick formula: ～ことにする = I decide. ～ことになる = it's decided / it turns out that way.
sections[].examples[].de: I've decided to study Japanese every day.
I've decided to go by taxi today.
I make a point of not eating many sweets.
It's been decided that I'm going on a business trip to Osaka next month.
The meeting is scheduled to start at three o'clock.
Because of the rain, it was decided that the game would be canceled.

en.title: ～ようにする・～ようになる
en.subtitle: Effort and change — working at it, coming to do it
en.intro: With ～ようにする you talk about conscious effort or building habits. With ～ようになる you describe a change: something becomes possible, usual or a reality. Both structures are very important for talking about learning progress, health goals and everyday habits.
sections[].heading: ～ようにする — making an effort to do something
～ようになる — it becomes possible / things change
sections[].text: The structure verb in the dictionary form / ない-form + ようにする means that you make a conscious effort to do or not do something. It's not about a one-off decision, but about repeated effort.
With verb in the dictionary form / ない-form + ようになる you describe a change after which something becomes possible or usual. The form is especially common with potential verbs.
sections[].tip: ～ようにする is often softer than ～ことにする, because the emphasis is on effort and habit, not on a single decision.
～ようになる describes the result of a change. It's not an intention but a new state or a new ability.
sections[].examples[].de: I try to write kanji every day.
I make sure not to drink coffee in the evening.
The teacher makes an effort to speak slowly.
I can now read Japanese newspapers.
I've started getting up early.
Lately I've been eating vegetables more often.

en.title: ～し・～まま・～間に・～までに
en.subtitle: More core N4 patterns — reasons, state, time span, deadline
en.intro: Some of the most common N4 patterns are small but functionally very important. ～し links reasons loosely, ～まま describes an unchanged state, ～間に marks a window of time and ～までに a deadline. These forms come up very often in texts and listening comprehension.
sections[].heading: ～し — reasons and listing
～まま — staying in this state
～間に and ～までに — time window vs. deadline
sections[].text: With ～し you link several reasons or qualities in a loose way. It sounds more spoken and more open than a strictly logical connection with から or ので.
～まま describes that something stays unchanged. Common structures are verb in the た-form / ない-form + まま and noun + のまま.
～間に means "while / during the time that ...", ～までに means "by ... at the latest". The difference is central for N4: 間に describes an open window of time, までに a deadline.
sections[].tip: ～し often lists only some of the reasons. It sounds like: "among other things, also because ..."
～まま often marks a state that really should have been changed but stayed as it was.
Rule of thumb: 間に = at some point within the time span. までに = at this point at the latest.
sections[].examples[].de: This shop is cheap, and the food is good too.
I'm busy today, and on top of that it's raining.
I fell asleep with the light on.
Please don't come in with your shoes on.
While I'm in Japan, I want to go to Kyoto.
It rained while I was sleeping.
Please hand in the report by five o'clock.

en.title: へ・と・も・や
en.subtitle: Key N5 particles — direction, accompaniment, also, incomplete lists
en.intro: These four particles look small but carry a lot of meaning. At N5 you need to recognize them quickly and confidently, because they appear in almost every text. Precisely because they're so short, they often get mixed up in exercises.
sections[].heading: へ — Direction
と・も・や — with, also, and so on
sections[].text: へ marks the direction of a movement. It often means "to" or "toward" in the sense of heading somewhere. Important: it emphasizes the direction more than actually reaching the place.
と connects complete lists of nouns or marks accompaniment. も means "also". や lists examples and signals that the list is not complete.
sections[].tip: At N5, へ is often compared with に. へ emphasizes the direction, に the destination or point of arrival.
と in lists feels complete: AとB = A and B. や in lists feels open: AやB = A, B and other things.
sections[].examples[].de: I go to school.
I came to Japan.
I'm watching a movie with a friend.
I'm going too.
On the desk there are books, notebooks and so on.

en.title: の・ね・よ
en.subtitle: Possession, explanatory tone and conversational particles for beginners
en.intro: These forms are elementary too. の links things together, ね seeks agreement or gentle confirmation, and よ passes on new information with emphasis. If you don't internalize these differences early, you'll quickly sound unnatural or misunderstand listening texts.
sections[].heading: の — Possession, belonging, description
ね and よ — Conversational nuances
sections[].text: の connects nouns and shows possession, belonging or a descriptive relationship. It's much broader than the English possessive 's and is therefore a core building block of almost all simple noun phrases.

ね seeks agreement or shares a feeling with the listener. よ delivers information the speaker wants to emphasize or present as new. Both particles often come at the end of the sentence and noticeably change the tone.
sections[].tip: の isn't only about possession. It can also link category, place, material or topic: 日本の会社, 木の机, 音楽の本.
Rule of thumb: ね = we share this, よ = I'm telling you this. This difference in tone is exactly what matters in dialogues.
sections[].examples[].de: This is my book.
He/She is a Japanese teacher.
There's a bank in front of the station.
It's cold today, isn't it?
That shop is cheap, I'm telling you.
It's pretty, isn't it?

en.title: ～ずつ・～など・～とか
en.subtitle: Distributing, giving examples, casual lists
en.intro: These smaller forms are typical N4: ～ずつ distributes amounts evenly, ～など gives examples in rather written or neutral language, and ～とか is the casual spoken variant for examples or vague quotes.
sections[].heading: ～ずつ — each, bit by bit
～など and ～とか — giving examples
sections[].text: ～ずつ means "each" or "little by little". It is often attached to numbers or quantities and describes an even distribution or a gradual change.
～など means "for example, and so on" and sounds rather neutral or somewhat more formal. ～とか feels more spoken and casual. Both show that the list is not complete.
sections[].tip: ～ずつ often attaches directly to numbers or quantities: 一つずつ, 三人ずつ, 少しずつ.
など feels a bit more orderly, とか more spontaneous. For dialogues and listening comprehension, とか is especially important.
sections[].examples[].de: Please hand out two sheets to each person.
I study a little bit every day.
On weekends I do things like read books, watch movies and go for walks.
Among fruits, I like apples, bananas and so on.
On my days off I do stuff like watching movies or playing games.

en.title: ～みたいだ・～そうだ
en.subtitle: Appearance and hearsay — two similar but different patterns
en.intro: Learners often confuse these two forms because both express something that isn't stated as fact. Still, they have different sources: ～みたいだ is an impression or comparison, while at N4 ～そうだ comes up especially as hearsay.
sections[].heading: ～みたいだ — "seems like", "looks like"
～そうだ — hearsay
sections[].text: ～みたいだ expresses an impression, a comparison or a subjective guess. It sounds more spoken than ようだ and is very common in everyday life. It can be based on observation or on a feeling.
The 伝聞-そうだ (hearsay そうだ) means "I heard that ...". So it is based on information from others, not on your own observation. For N4 it's important to keep this そうだ apart from the appearance そう.
sections[].tip: ～みたいだ is often subjective and colloquial. It's useful when you don't want to make a hard claim.
Important for the exam: with hearsay そう, the sentence form before そう usually stays unchanged. Appearance そう is formed differently, for example おいしそう.
sections[].examples[].de: That person seems to be a teacher.
It looks like it's raining outside.
This bread is as sweet as cake.
According to the weather forecast, it's supposed to be hot tomorrow.
I heard that Tanaka is getting married next month.
I heard that the ramen at this shop is good.

en.title: ～たがる・～ようとする
en.subtitle: Other people's wishes and trying to do something
en.intro: With ～たい you express your own wish. As soon as it's about someone else's wish, ～たがる usually becomes important at N4. ～ようとする, in turn, describes an attempt or the imminent start of an action.
sections[].heading: ～たがる — another person's wish
～ようとする — trying / about to
sections[].text: Since you can't look directly into other people's heads, you often use verb stem + たがる for a third person's wish. The form describes observable behavior or a recognizable tendency.

With verb in the volitional form + とする you describe someone trying to do something or being just about to do it. The structure is common in narratives and in situations where an action is just about to begin.
sections[].tip: For yourself you normally use ～たい, not ～たがる.
Typical N4 effect: "being just about to". ～ようとしたとき appears especially often.
sections[].examples[].de: My little brother really wants a new game.
The children want to play outside.
He doesn't want to go alone.
I tried to open the door, but it wouldn't open.
Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.
The cat is trying to eat the fish.

en.title: ～はずがない・～せいで・～おかげで
en.subtitle: Strong conclusions and causes — negative or positive
en.intro: These three patterns help you express conclusions and causes with nuance. ～はずがない strongly denies an expectation, ～せいで names a negative cause, ～おかげで a positive one. These very nuances are important at N4.
sections[].heading: ～はずがない — "there's no way that's true"
～せいで and ～おかげで — negative and positive cause
sections[].text: With sentence + はずがない the speaker says that something is, in their conviction, impossible. The form is stronger than a mere negation and builds on expectation or logic.
～せいで marks a negative cause: "because of ..., unfortunately". ～おかげで marks a positive cause: "thanks to ...". In meaning they are opposites and are often learned together.
sections[].tip: The form is based on a clear expectation. It sounds stronger than でしょう or と思います.
If the outcome is good, せいで almost never fits. If the outcome is bad, おかげで almost never fits. This evaluation is the core.
sections[].examples[].de: There's no way that serious person would lie.
Today is Sunday, so there's no way the bank is open.
Because of the rain, the game was called off.
Because of lack of sleep, I have a headache.
Thanks to my teacher, I came to like Japanese.

en.title: ようだ・らしい・みたいだ・そうだ
en.subtitle: N3 contrast — impression, hearsay, typical trait
en.intro: These four forms come up earlier, but only at N3 do you need to be able to tell them apart cleanly. All of them express uncertainty or indirect information, but they do so from different sources and with different nuances.
sections[].heading: ようだ and みたいだ — impression and comparison
らしい — hearsay or typical trait
そうだ — hearsay vs. appearance
sections[].text: ようだ sounds more neutral and a bit more written, みたいだ more spoken and subjective. Both express an impression, a comparison or a guess based on observation. In meaning they are often close, but stylistically they are not identical.
らしい has two main functions: it can express hearsay ("apparently") or mark a typical trait ("typical of"). It's exactly this double function that makes らしい a classic N3 case.

そうだ remains a classic source of confusion. As hearsay it means "I heard". As 様態-そう it describes the visible impression: "looks ...". Both forms sound the same but are formed differently and rest on different grounds.
sections[].tip: ようだ fits better in explanatory or more written sentences, みたいだ better in casual conversation.
When らしい means "typical", it isn't just a guess but a characterization.
What matters for N3 is not just the individual meaning but reliably distinguishing between the source of the information and the perceived appearance.
sections[].examples[].de: It seems to be raining outside.
He really seems like a teacher.
This town seems quieter than it used to be.
Apparently Tanaka isn't coming today.
That person is really childlike / such a typical kid.
The weather has become really spring-like.
According to the news, a typhoon is coming.
This cake looks delicious.
He looks very tired.

en.title: Passive: ～られる
en.subtitle: When something happens to you
en.intro: In Japanese the passive is used much more often than in English — and it often expresses that something was done to someone. While in English the passive is often considered stylistically weak and teachers like to mark it in red, in Japanese it is a completely normal, everyday and even elegant way of expressing things. The so-called "suffering passive" (迷惑の受身, meiwaku no ukemi) is a specialty that doesn't exist in this form in English — it lets the speaker present themselves as someone affected by an action. This lesson shows you all three kinds of passive and how to use them confidently.
sections[].heading: Formation
The normal passive (直接受身)
The suffering passive — a Japanese specialty (迷惑の受身)
The passive in practice
The passive as a respectful form (尊敬語)
sections[].text: The passive is formed by taking the ない-form and replacing ない with れる. With る-verbs, る becomes られる. The result is always a る-verb that can be conjugated completely normally (られます, られない, られた etc.). Remember: forming the passive follows exactly the same stem change as the ない-form — once you've mastered that, the passive is child's play.

The normal passive works like in English: the action is described from the perspective of the one receiving it, and the doer is marked with に. It is used especially often in written language, in the news and in formal texts. In Japanese the passive often sounds more natural than the active form when the doer is unimportant or unknown.

In Japanese you can also use the passive to express that something was done to you — even with verbs that have no passive in English. There is always a feeling of annoyance, nuisance or inconvenience in it. What's special: even intransitive verbs (raining, crying, dying) can appear in the suffering passive. The "sufferer" becomes the grammatical subject, even though they aren't directly involved in the action at all.

You'll come across the passive constantly in everyday life — in the news, on signs, in formal announcements and in polite language. Many set expressions use the passive without people perceiving it as such. In spoken language, too, the passive is used to phrase things indirectly and politely instead of naming someone directly as the doer.

The passive form ～られる has a completely different function in Japanese as well: it can express respect toward the person doing the action and thus belongs to polite language (敬語, keigo). The form is identical to the passive — so 来られる can be a passive (someone comes, and you're affected by it) OR mean "to come" (respectful). The context decides: if the subject is a person you show respect to (boss, teacher, customer) and the action has no element of suffering, it's the respectful form. This use is everywhere, especially in business Japanese.
sections[].tip: With る-verbs, the passive form looks identical to the potential form (食べられる = "to be eaten" OR "to be able to eat"). The context always makes clear which is meant. In everyday speech the ら is often dropped in the potential form (食べれる), which reduces the risk of confusion.

The suffering passive is one of the reasons why Japanese sentences sometimes seem strange when translated literally. It gives the speaker the role of the "affected party" — and in Japanese that's completely normal. Pay attention to the emotional undertone: when someone says 降られた instead of just 降った, there's always an "and that was annoying for me!" behind it.
In the news (ニュース) you'll hear the passive extremely often: 逮捕された (was arrested), 発表された (was announced), 開催される (will be held). If you want to understand the news, the passive is indispensable.

How do you tell the passive from the respectful form? Look at the subject: if a higher-ranking person (先生, 社長, お客様) actively does something, it's the respectful form. If someone suffers something or is affected, it's the passive. In doubtful cases the context helps — 先生が来られた is almost always meant respectfully, because a teacher can hardly be on the receiving end of "coming".
sections[].examples[].de: to be eaten (る-verb)
to be read (む → まれる)
to be said / to be told (う → われる)
I was praised by the teacher.
This book is read by many people.
This song is loved all over the world.
I got rained on. (= I got caught in the rain — annoying!)
Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
The guy next to me smoked. (And I had to put up with it!)
This building was built in 1960. (typical of travel guides)
The meeting was postponed to next week.
Japanese is studied all over the world.
What time will the company president come? (respectful)
The teacher has already gone home. (respectful)
The customer ordered the food. (respectful)

en.title: わけだ・わけではない・ということだ
en.subtitle: Inference and rephrasing — putting things in logical context
en.intro: At N3, language becomes more abstract. You no longer just say what happens; you explain what logically follows from it, what is meant by it, or what you specifically don't want to claim across the board. That's exactly where わけだ, わけではない and ということだ become essential.
sections[].heading: わけだ — "so that means", "no wonder"
わけではない — not necessarily / not across the board
ということだ — hearsay or summary
sections[].text: わけだ expresses a logical conclusion or realization. The speaker puts a piece of information in context and makes clear: if that's true, the result is understandable or logical.
With ～わけではない you qualify a statement: "it's not that ..." or "not necessarily". This structure is typical when you take back a sweeping conclusion.
ということだ can relay information ("I hear that ...") or rephrase a statement as a summary ("so that means ..."). At N3 you need to recognize both readings from context.
sections[].tip: わけだ isn't just "so"; it's a well-founded logical conclusion.
わけではない often doesn't negate the whole content, only an overly broad generalization.
If ということだ works like reported speech, it's hearsay. If it derives something from what came before, it's a summary or conclusion.
sections[].examples[].de: If you study three hours every day, no wonder you're getting good.
Today is a public holiday. That's why the bank is closed.
It's not that everything expensive is good.
Just because people are Japanese doesn't mean they all like sushi.
According to the weather forecast, it's supposed to snow tomorrow.
The train has stopped. So that means I'll be late for work today.

en.title: うちに・間に・たびに
en.subtitle: N3 time patterns — while, as long as, every time
en.intro: These three forms all relate to recurring or limited periods of time, but they don't work the same way. At N3 the point is to distinguish carefully whether something changes within a time window, whether something happens during a state, or whether every repetition of an event is meant.
sections[].heading: うちに — while still, before something changes
間に — during a period
たびに — every time
sections[].text: うちに describes a window of time in which you should do something before the situation changes. It often carries the idea of "while still ..." or "before it's too late".
間に marks an event or action that takes place within an ongoing period. The focus is more on the period itself than with うちに.
たびに expresses repetition: whenever X happens, Y follows. It's more regular and general than a one-off connection in time.
sections[].tip: うちに often implies a change: later the opportunity is gone or the conditions change.
When a specific event happens in the middle of a period, 間に is often the natural choice.
たびに doesn't describe a one-off situation but a repeated pattern.
sections[].examples[].de: While you're young, you should have all kinds of experiences.
Please eat it while it's still hot.
While I was out, a package arrived.
While I was living in Japan, I made a lot of friends.
Every time I hear this song, I remember my student days.
Every time we meet, he's in better spirits.

en.title: こと・の の使い分け
en.subtitle: Nominalization at N3 — abstract, concrete, subjective
en.intro: Both こと and の can turn part of a sentence into a noun. At N5/N4 a rough feel is often enough, but at N3 you need to be more precise: when does こと sound more natural, when does の, and what changes in tone and perspective?
sections[].heading: こと — abstract, general, more formal
の — more concrete, more perceptible, more personal
Borderline cases and a feel for style
sections[].text: こと feels more abstract and is often used for rules, facts, concepts or more formal statements. It fits well when the action is treated as an idea or a state of affairs.
の feels more concrete and closer to an observable event. It's often used for direct perception, personal experience or emotionally closer situations.

In some sentences both are possible, but not with exactly the same tone. こと often sounds more matter-of-fact or formal, の more personal or immediate. This feel for style is exactly what becomes important from N3 on.
sections[].tip: In rules, regulations and general statements, こと is often more natural than の.
With verbs of perception such as 見る, 聞く, 感じる, の is very common.
Grammatical possibility alone isn't enough. At N3 what counts is which form sounds more natural in the situation.
sections[].examples[].de: It's important to learn foreign languages.
It's necessary to keep your promises.
I saw children playing in the park.
I like it when he laughs.
Studying Japanese is fun. (somewhat more matter-of-fact)
Studying Japanese is fun. (somewhat more personal)

en.title: 受け身・使役・使役受け身
en.subtitle: N3 system — undergoing, causing, being made to
en.intro: You already know the passive and the causative from N4. At N3, though, that's no longer enough. Now it's about seeing the three related systems together: passive, causative and causative passive. If you understand how they relate, you'll make fewer mistakes in form and meaning.
sections[].heading: 受け身 — experiencing something or being affected
使役 — making/letting someone do something
使役受け身 — being made to do something
sections[].text: The passive form doesn't just describe "something is done"; in Japanese it often also expresses that someone is affected by an action. This sense of being affected is central to the Japanese passive.
With the causative form, you make or let someone do something. Whether "let" or "make" is meant depends heavily on context.
The causative passive form combines both ideas: someone is made or forced to do something. It's more complex in form, but very relevant in N3 reading passages and listening comprehension.
sections[].tip: The "suffering" (adversative) passive in particular is a classic N3 point: the speaker is affected even if the action isn't aimed at them directly.
In causative sentences, the distribution of roles matters: who causes the action, and who actually carries it out?
The N3 goal isn't just forming them, but reliably recognizing the relationship between the three forms and their respective perspectives.
sections[].examples[].de: I was praised by my teacher.
My little brother went and ate my cake.
The teacher had the students read a book.
The mother made the child go to bed early.
My father made me eat vegetables.
The students are made to write kanji every day.

en.title: ものの・にもかかわらず・くせに
en.subtitle: Concessive N3 patterns — although, despite, and "even though" with an attitude
en.intro: All three forms connect two pieces of content that don't fit well together: something is true, but the expected result doesn't happen. At N3, though, you need to be able to do more than just translate "although". What matters is style, strength and the speaker's attitude.
sections[].heading: ものの — formal and restrained
にもかかわらず — despite, contrary to expectation
くせに — even though ...! with criticism or annoyance
sections[].text: ものの means "admittedly ... but" or "although", but it sounds rather written and restrained. It suits factual texts, explanations and more formal statements where the speaker stays sober.
にもかかわらず is stronger and more formal. It marks a clear contradiction between fact and result. The expression fits especially well in written language, reports and argumentative texts.

くせに also means "although", but it almost always carries a negative attitude on the speaker's part: reproach, annoyance, criticism or mockery. It's exactly this emotional coloring that makes くせに relevant for the exam.
sections[].tip: ものの sounds more observational than emotional. It's almost never the best choice for reproaches.
にもかかわらず is strong and factual, and rather written. It sounds weightier than のに.
くせに is subjective and often sharp. Be careful with it in polite situations.
sections[].examples[].de: I'm studying Japanese, but I still can't speak it well enough.
Spring has come, but we're still having cold days.
Despite the rain, many people came.
Even though he was sick, he kept working.
He doesn't know, yet he pretends he does.
He's a student, yet he eats at expensive restaurants every day.

en.title: ところだ・ところで・ところを
en.subtitle: N3 timing and situations — just, at that moment, even though right then
en.intro: The ところ group is one of the classic N3 stumbling blocks. The forms look similar but express different moments, transitions and situational contexts. This is exactly where rote memorization stops being enough.
sections[].heading: ～ところだ — about to, in the middle of, just finished
～ところで — even if / by the way / right then
～ところを — even though right then / at the moment when
sections[].text: ところだ marks the point in time of an action very precisely. Dictionary form + ところだ means "to be about to", ているところだ "to be in the middle of", たところだ "to have just finished".

ところで has several functions that you have to recognize from context. As a sentence connector it often means "by the way". In patterns like ～たところで it means "even if ...", often with the nuance that the result won't achieve much.
ところを describes a situation in which someone is busy or in a certain state at that moment, and then something else happens. There's often a hint of apology or consideration.
sections[].tip: At N3 it's important to know that each verb form before ところ marks a different point in time.
The "by the way" function is very common in conversation; the conditional meaning is more typical of N3 grammar questions.
ところを is often found in polite set phrases and describes an intrusion into an ongoing situation.
sections[].examples[].de: I'm just about to go out.
I'm in the middle of eating lunch.
I've just got home.
Even if we hurry now, we won't make it in time.
By the way, what time is next week's meeting?
Thank you for your time, even though you're busy.
I'm sorry for waking you up while you were sleeping.

en.title: べきだ・わけにはいかない・ざるをえない
en.subtitle: Obligation, impossibility, outside pressure — three kinds of "must"
en.intro: At N3, a simple ～なければならない is no longer enough. Now you need to distinguish whether something is morally required, whether you can't do something for social or situational reasons, or whether you practically have no choice. These three patterns cover exactly these differences.
sections[].heading: べきだ — you should, it would be right
わけにはいかない — you can't just ...
ざるをえない — you're forced to
sections[].text: べきだ expresses a normative judgment: something is the right thing morally, logically or socially. It sounds stronger and more judgmental than ほうがいい.
～わけにはいかない means that you can't do something for social, moral or situational reasons. Not because it would be physically impossible, but because the circumstances don't allow it.
～ざるをえない is a more formal structure for "can't help but, have no choice but to". It expresses that outside circumstances leave practically no other option.
sections[].tip: べきだ is often more general and normative than a simple piece of advice. It can quickly sound strong or critical.
The core is social or inner pressure, not pure impossibility.
ざるをえない feels more formal than なければならない and emphasizes pressure from circumstances rather than a rule.
sections[].examples[].de: You should keep your promises.
I should have asked for advice sooner.
I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't just skip it.
Everyone is still working, so I can't be the only one to go home.
The train stopped, so I had no choice but to take a taxi.
In this situation, we have no choice but to change the plan.

en.title: あまり～ない・ばかりか・どころか
en.subtitle: Degree and contrast — not very, not only, quite the opposite
en.intro: These three patterns all work with expectation and deviation, but in very different ways. あまり～ない tones a statement down, ばかりか surprisingly extends it, and どころか often turns the expectation completely upside down. That's exactly why they're typical N3 contrast structures.
sections[].heading: あまり～ない — not very, not much
ばかりか — not only ..., but even
どころか — quite the opposite
sections[].text: あまり + negative form means "not very" or "not much". It usually sounds softer than a blunt negation and describes a low degree rather than an absolute no.
ばかりか means "not only ..., but also / even". It adds surprising extra information and sounds a little more elevated than だけでなく; the nuance is also stronger.
どころか marks that the expectation is completely off. Rather than "not only", it often means something like "far from it" or "quite the opposite". The pattern is strongly contrastive.
sections[].tip: あまり classically goes with a negation. This exact combination is often tested directly.
ばかりか often carries a stronger note of surprise or criticism than a plain "also".
どころか corrects a wrong assumption much more strongly than でも or しかし.
sections[].examples[].de: I don't watch much TV these days.
I don't really like this dish.
It's not very cold today, is it?
He speaks not only Japanese but also Chinese.
That shop is not only expensive, its service is bad too.
Busy? Far from it, I'm free all day today.
He's lived in Japan for ten years, so far from being bad, his Japanese is very good.

en.title: に違いない・はずだ・はずがない
en.subtitle: Inference at N3 — certain, expected, impossible
en.intro: These three patterns form a clear scale of inference. はずだ expresses expectation, に違いない near-certain conviction, and はずがない firmly rejects an expectation. At N3 the fine gradation matters more than the rough translation.
sections[].heading: はずだ — it should be so
に違いない — it's certainly so
はずがない — that can't possibly be true
sections[].text: はずだ means that, based on knowledge or logic, the speaker expects something to be true. It's strong but not absolute. The statement remains an inference.
に違いない means "it must be so" or "there's hardly any doubt". It feels stronger and more subjectively convinced than はずだ.
はずがない is the negative counterpart of an expectation. Based on knowledge or logic, the speaker considers something impossible.
sections[].tip: はずだ is an expectation based on what you know, not just a vague feeling.
に違いない often sounds more decisive and personal than はずだ.
It's best to learn the three forms as a system: expected, very certain, impossible.
sections[].examples[].de: Tanaka should be home by now.
Today is Sunday, so the bank should be closed.
There are lots of people lining up in front of that shop. It must be good.
If he said something like that, there must be a reason.
There's no way that person would forget a promise.
It's only nine o'clock, so the shop can't possibly be closed already.

en.title: ことは～が・ないことはない・なくはない
en.subtitle: Softened concession — sort of yes, but not quite
en.intro: These structures are typical of N3 because they no longer just express facts, but attitude, restraint and fine gradations. The speaker doesn't simply say yes or no; they concede something and immediately qualify it again.
sections[].heading: ことは～が — admittedly ..., but
ないことはない — not completely impossible
なくはない — more compact and colloquial
sections[].text: Verb/adjective + ことは～が concedes a fact but signals right away that a reservation is coming. It often sounds cautious, diplomatic or somewhat reserved.
ないことはない means that something isn't completely ruled out. The nuance is usually: "it can be done somehow, but it's not ideal". It's a softened positive concession.
なくはない is a shorter, somewhat more spoken variant of ないことはない. The meaning is similar: "not entirely impossible" or "you could say that ...".
sections[].tip: Repeating the same expression isn't a mistake; it's part of the structure.
ないことはない often signals reserved agreement, but rarely enthusiasm.
なくはない sounds more natural in casual speech, ないことはない a bit more complete and explanatory.
sections[].examples[].de: I do understand Japanese, but I can't speak it fast.
I'd like to go, I really would, but I don't have time.
It's not that I can't do it alone, but it's a bit tough.
That proposal isn't entirely bad either.
This shop is a bit expensive, but going there isn't out of the question.
It's not that I can't eat it, but I wouldn't want to buy it again.

en.title: Causative: ～させる
en.subtitle: Making or letting someone do something
en.intro: "My boss makes me work overtime." "The mother makes the child eat vegetables." The causative expresses that someone causes or allows an action — it's the linguistic tool for power structures, permissions and hierarchies. Depending on the context, it can sound friendly or authoritarian, and exactly this ambiguity is what makes the causative so interesting. Hierarchy plays a big role in Japanese, and the causative reflects that directly: who makes whom do what? This lesson shows you the formation, the meaning and the important combinations.
sections[].heading: Formation
Forcing vs. allowing
させてください — politely asking for permission
Causative passive: ～させられる
sections[].text: Just like with the passive: take the ない-form and replace ない with せる. With る-verbs, る becomes させる. The result is again a る-verb that is conjugated normally (させます, させない, させた). The parallel with the passive is no coincidence — both forms share the same stem change, which makes learning easier.

The causative has two faces: forcing (making someone do something, in the sense of "ordering, compelling") and allowing (letting someone do something, in the sense of "permitting, letting them go ahead"). The context decides which meaning is intended. With transitive verbs, the person made to act is marked with に; with intransitive verbs, with を — this is an important distinction.

The combination causative + てください is a very polite way of asking for permission. Literally: "Please let me..." This form shows modesty because you leave the power to decide to the other person. It is extremely widespread in business and formal situations and is part of every Japanese learner's standard repertoire.

Combining the causative and the passive gives the causative passive: "to be made to do something". The formation is logical: causative form (させる) → its passive (させられる). The causative passive expresses that someone was made to do something against their will or under pressure — it's the perspective of the "victim" of an order.
sections[].tip: In colloquial speech, the causative is often shortened: 行かせる → 行かす, 食べさせる → 食べさす. You'll hear these short forms very often, especially in Kansai (Osaka/Kyoto).

Rules of thumb for the particle: transitive verb → person made to act marked with に (先生が学生に書かせる). Intransitive verb → person made to act marked with を (母が子供を遊ばせる). Why? With transitive verbs the object already has を — two を in the same sentence sounds unnatural.

させていただく is the even more polite variant, and you'll come across it constantly in formal e-mails and business Japanese. 説明させていただきます = "Allow me to explain" (超 polite). Some Japanese people overdo させていただく — it's a favorite target of parody in comedy shows.

The causative passive has a shortened form for う-verbs: 行かせられる → 行かされる, 飲ませられる → 飲まされる, 待たせられる → 待たされた. The short form is much more common in everyday life. る-verbs have no short form: 食べさせられる stays as it is.
sections[].examples[].de: make/let eat (る-verb)
make/let drink (む → ませる)
make/let go (く → かせる)
do → make/let do (irregular)
come → make/let come (irregular)
The teacher made the students write a report. (forcing)
The mother let the child play in the park. (allowing)
The department manager made the employees work overtime. (forcing)
Please let me think about it.
Please allow me to introduce myself.
Please let me rest for a moment.
I was made to eat vegetables. (as a kid, typical!)
I'm made to work overtime every day.
I was made to wait for a long time. (short form: 待たせられた → 待たされた)

en.title: ～に行く
en.subtitle: Purpose of a movement — going somewhere to do something
en.intro: With ～に行く you connect movement with a purpose. This form is extremely common in everyday life: going to eat, going shopping, going to meet friends. For beginners it's an important step from simple verb forms toward small sentence patterns.
sections[].heading: Basic structure
Movement plus destination
sections[].text: The standard form is verb stem + に行く. So the stem comes before に, not the dictionary form. The meaning is: "go to do ...". Instead of 行く, 来る or 帰る can also be used.
Before the verb of movement there's often a place marked with へ or に. That's how you combine destination and purpose in one sentence. This structure is especially productive for everyday sentences.
sections[].tip: The verb stem is what matters: 食べに行く, 見に行く, 買いに行く, 勉強しに行く.
Many textbooks cover ～に行く early because it brings together several basics: verb stem, particles and verbs of movement.
sections[].examples[].de: I'm going to see a movie with a friend.
I went to buy bread.
I came to the library to study.
On the weekend, I'm going to a restaurant to eat.
I'm going to the station to pick up a friend.

en.title: ～なくてもいい・～なければならない
en.subtitle: Not having to and having to – expressing obligation clearly
en.intro: If you want to talk about rules, homework, appointments or everyday obligations, at N5 you need two opposites: ～なくてもいい for "don't have to" and ～なければならない for "have to". Precisely because both forms look long and are easily confused with "must not", real understanding of the system pays off here more than plain memorization.
sections[].heading: ～なくてもいい — don't have to
～なければならない — have to
How to keep the two forms apart in your head
Typical short and everyday variants
sections[].text: ない-form without い + くてもいい means that something isn't necessary. The crucial point is: the action is allowed, but not required. That's why the form doesn't mean "you must not" but "you don't have to". This exact difference is a classic trap in English: "you must not" is a prohibition, "you don't have to" is not.

ない-form without い + ければならない expresses obligation or necessity. Literally, the logic behind it is "if you don't do it, it won't do". That sounds roundabout at first, but it helps when learning: the Japanese form builds a negative condition that effectively amounts to an obligation.

Always ask yourself: Is the action required? If yes, you need ～なければならない. If no, but it would be okay, ～なくてもいい fits. That way you avoid the most common beginner mistake, namely reading ～なくてもいい as a prohibition.

In real usage, alongside ～なければならない you often find shorter forms like ～なきゃ, ～なくちゃ or ～ないと. At N5 you don't need to use them all actively yet, but you should know that they express the same basic idea: "I have to".
sections[].tip: Don't mix them up: ～なくてもいい = don't have to, ～てはいけない = must not.
The structure is quite long. Many learners find it easier to understand if they first learn it as a fixed block.
If you'd say "don't have to" in English, it's almost never a prohibition.
For the exam, the long standard form is safer. For dialogues and listening comprehension, though, the short forms are worth their weight in gold.
sections[].examples[].de: You don't have to come today.
You don't have to eat it all.
You don't have to answer yet.
I have to study kanji every day.
I have to get up early tomorrow.
You must write your name on this sheet.
You don't have to wear a uniform tomorrow.
You have to wear a uniform tomorrow.
I have to go now.
I have to do my homework.

en.title: か・どんな・でしょう
en.subtitle: Questions and cautious guesses at N5
en.intro: These three building blocks are extremely common, but they're often only half understood. With か you form questions, with どんな you ask about kind or type, and with でしょう you soften statements or look for agreement. What they have in common isn't their form but their function in conversation: asking, narrowing down, cautiously estimating.
sections[].heading: か — the neutral question particle
どんな — asking about kind, type or impression
でしょう — cautious guesses
When do I use which?
sections[].text: か typically comes at the end of a sentence and turns a statement into a question. Unlike English, where "He is ..." becomes "Is he ...?", Japanese doesn't need to change the word order for this. So you say almost the same sentence as for a statement, just with か at the end.

どんな + noun doesn't ask about identity but about nature: "what kind of ...?". This sets it apart from 何, which asks more about the thing itself. So どんな is ideal when the category is already clear but you want more details.

でしょう means "probably", "right?" or a politely softened guess, depending on context. It makes a statement softer than a bare です. That's exactly why it often sounds more mature and socially skillful than a blunt claim.

These three forms do different jobs in a conversation. か turns a sentence into a direct question. どんな specifies what you're asking about in the first place. でしょう isn't a normal question for information, but rather a cautious estimate or a request for confirmation.
sections[].tip: This is liberating, especially for beginners: in Japanese the sentence structure usually stays put, and the question sits at the end.
どんな comes directly before the noun: どんな本, どんな先生, どんな料理.
でしょう sounds softer than a blunt claim. That's exactly why it's so common in polite everyday Japanese.
If you want genuinely new information, か is usually the safe choice. でしょう often assumes that you already have a guess.
sections[].examples[].de: What is this?
Is Tanaka a student?
Have you eaten already?
What kind of music do you like?
What kind of person is Tanaka?
What kind of movie do you want to see?
It will probably rain tomorrow.
This book is expensive, right?
It's surely finished by now, right?
Is this a book?
What kind of book is this?
This is expensive, right?

en.title: ～てしまう・～ちゃう
en.subtitle: Completely done, or unfortunately happened
en.intro: This form matters so much because it combines two very everyday meanings: something is completely finished, or something unfortunately happened. If you only learn the form, you miss the real point: you have to decide from context whether the focus is on completeness or on regret.
sections[].heading: Basic formation and everyday form
Meaning 1: completely finished / done
Meaning 2: happened unfortunately / by accident
How to tell the two readings apart
sections[].text: て-form + しまう is the standard form. In casual speech it often becomes ～ちゃう / ～じゃう. Both forms belong together; the short form isn't different grammar, just the same function in colloquial packaging.

Often the form simply means that something is completely finished. Then there's no regret, just the feeling: it's done, finished, seen through to the end. This reading is very common especially with tasks, eating, reading or tidying up.

Very often ～てしまう carries a tinge of regret, bad luck or something that happened unintentionally. In those cases you don't just translate it neutrally but rather with "unfortunately", "accidentally" or "ended up ...". This emotional coloring matters more in actual use than the bare form.

Always ask yourself: does the sentence sound like neutral finishing or like an unwanted result? With 食べてしまった, either can be meant depending on context: "I ate it all up" or "oops, now it's all gone". It's exactly this double function that makes the form so lively.
sections[].tip: When you hear ～ちゃった in dialogues, it's often simply ～てしまった behind it.
If "completely" or "all (up)" fits well in English, this reading is often the one meant.
The grammar alone doesn't carry the regret. The situation and tone of voice often help you find the right reading.
If you can mentally add "unfortunately", you're usually dealing with the regret reading.
sections[].examples[].de: I finished my homework completely.
I already ate it all.
I want to finish reading this book today.
I've finished writing the whole report.
Unfortunately, I forgot my wallet.
I accidentally deleted an important email.
I ate the whole cake.
Unfortunately, I ended up eating the cake all by myself.

en.title: ～ても・～でも・～かどうか
en.subtitle: Concessions, examples and open yes/no questions
en.intro: This lesson bundles three common patterns that can quickly seem alike in translation but do different jobs in a conversation: making concessions, leaving examples open, and leaving it open between yes and no. The real value here lies in separating the functions, not in the form alone.
sections[].heading: ～ても — "even if" with verbs and adjectives
～でも — also with nouns, and as an open example
～かどうか — whether or not
When do I use which?
sections[].text: て-form + も means "even if" or "even though". You accept a condition but say: the main result still stands. The pattern is especially common with small objections, permissions or statements like "even if it rains".

Noun + でも can also mean "even if", but very often it serves as an open example in the sense of "for example". In that case the important point is that the thing mentioned is just one possible option and not the only one.

普通形 + かどうか turns a yes/no question into an embedded clause: "whether ...". This lets you talk about uncertainty without putting the question directly to the other person. That's exactly why the form often appears with 分かる, 知る, 決める, 確かめる.

～ても accepts a condition. ～でも often gives an example or adds emphasis as "even". ～かどうか describes uncertainty between yes and no. Once you keep these three jobs clearly apart, you'll hardly ever mix up the forms in everyday use.
sections[].tip: ～ても is not a "because" but a "nevertheless".
In offers, ～でも often sounds soft and non-committal: just a suggestion, not a fixed plan.
If "whether" fits well in English, ～かどうか is almost always a good candidate.
The most common mix-up is reading ～でも as "whether". That is almost never right.
sections[].examples[].de: I'll go even if it rains.
I want to buy it even if it's expensive.
Shall we have some tea or something?
I sometimes work even on Sundays.
I haven't decided yet whether I'll go.
Do you know whether that shop is open?
I study even when I'm tired.
Let's have a coffee or something.
I don't know whether he's coming.

en.title: ～たばかり・～ところだ
en.subtitle: Reading closeness in time correctly
en.intro: At first glance the two patterns seem similar, because both describe something very close in time. But what really matters for learning them is the perspective: ～たばかり looks back on something that has only just happened, while ～ところだ marks the exact point of an action — just before it, right in the middle of it, or right after it.
sections[].heading: ～たばかり — have only just done
～ところだ — right before, during or after the action
The core difference
Typical learner mistakes
sections[].text: た-form + ばかり means that an action was completed only a short time ago. The "short time" is subjective. So it's not about seconds on the clock, but about the feeling: this is still fresh.
辞書形 / ている / た + ところだ marks the exact point in the process: just before, right in the middle, or just finished. That's why the pattern is more precise and technical than ～たばかり.

With ～たばかり you're saying: it wasn't long ago. With ～たところだ you're saying: the action has been completed just now. That's why ～たところだ is often more pinpointed, while ～たばかり feels more subjective and colloquial.

Many learners treat the two forms as perfect synonyms. That leads to unnatural sentences. Also, ～ところだ is often used too broadly, even though all that's meant is a fresh memory. Not every "only just" statement needs the exactly marked point in time.
sections[].tip: With ～たばかり it's often about the feeling of "only recently", not about a precisely measurable moment.
～ところだ is more tightly bound to the time of the action than ～たばかり.
If you want to stress "just this very moment", ～ところだ often fits better.
Perspective first, form second: a fresh memory or an exact point in time?
sections[].examples[].de: But I only just ate.
I only recently came to Japan, so I don't know my way around yet.
I'm just about to head out.
I'm on the phone right now.
I've just this moment finished.
I've only just had lunch.
I've just this moment finished lunch.
I only recently got married.
The meeting has just ended.

en.title: ～始める・～続ける・～終わる
en.subtitle: Phases of an action – starting, continuing, finishing
en.intro: These three verb combinations are typical N4 building blocks, because they don't just describe an action as a fact but as a process: something begins, keeps going, or is completely finished. That alone makes your Japanese sound more narrative and more precise right away.
sections[].heading: Formation: verb stem + auxiliary verb
～始める — the start kicks in
～続ける and ～終わる — process vs. completion
Typical mistakes and limits
sections[].text: The formation is always verb stem + 始める / 続ける / 終わる. The first verb supplies the actual action, the second shows its phase. Because everything is formed so regularly, these patterns are especially productive.

～始める marks the point at which an action sets in. It is especially common with weather, emotions, habits or physical reactions. It often sounds more dynamic than simply saying that something "begins", because it shows the action getting going immediately.

～続ける describes that something lasts or is deliberately carried on. ～終わる, on the other hand, shows that an action is completely finished. This contrast is important in texts: one puts the focus on duration, the other on the end point.

Not every verb sounds equally natural with all three forms. Process-like activities such as 読む, 書く, 話す, 働く fit especially well. With punctual or static verbs you need to look more closely. Also, don't confuse these forms with separate full verbs: 話し続ける is tighter and more idiomatic than ずっと話す.
sections[].tip: These three auxiliary verbs are very productive. Once you have the verb stem down, you can form lots of new expressions right away.
～始める describes the start of the action itself, not just the decision to do it.
～終わる is stronger than just the past tense: it doesn't only say that something happened, but that it is really finished.
If you're unsure, ask yourself: can this action really be thought of as a process with a beginning, a duration or an end?
sections[].examples[].de: It has started to rain.
He kept talking for three hours.
When I finish reading the book, I'll go to bed.
The child suddenly started crying.
Since I started studying Japanese, I've been busy every day.
She kept running even in the rain.
I've finished writing the report, so I'll take a short break.
A typical, natural case: a process is continued.
Also possible, but less clearly marked as a fixed process form.

en.title: ～てほしい・～させてください・～させてもらう
en.subtitle: Wishes, asking permission and getting permission
en.intro: These three forms are close to each other in communication, because they all have to do with other people and their actions. That's exactly why they need to be kept cleanly apart: ～てほしい is about a wish directed at others, ～させてください is about asking for permission, and ～させてもらう is about actually getting the permission or opportunity.
sections[].heading: ～てほしい — I want someone to do something
～させてください — please let me
～させてもらう — I may / was able to, thanks to permission
Which pattern when?
sections[].text: て-form + ほしい doesn't say "I want something" but "I want someone to do something". So the form is about a relationship. It sounds more natural when the wish isn't phrased too harshly or like an order.

使役形 + ください is a request for permission to do something yourself. The speaker doesn't just state their wish but actively asks for consent. That's exactly why you often hear the form in more formal situations.

使役形 + もらう shows that you receive permission, an opportunity or a favor. The focus is no longer on the request but on the relationship: someone lets me do something. The form often carries a tone of gratitude or politeness.
～てほしい focuses on the other person's action. ～させてください asks permission for your own action. ～させてもらう describes that this permission or opportunity exists or has been granted.
sections[].tip: For direct requests, ～てください is often clearer. ～てほしい rather describes your own wish.
The form doesn't sound like an order but like a request for some leeway or permission.
～させてもらう often sounds humbler than a plain "I'm doing this now".
The most common mistake is mixing up wishes and permission.
sections[].examples[].de: I'd like you to speak a little more slowly.
I want my parents to stay healthy.
Please let me go home before you.
Please let me think about it a little.
I was allowed to go home early today.
I'll take the opportunity to share my opinion at the meeting.
I'd like the teacher to explain it once more.
Please let me explain it once more.
I was allowed to explain it once more.

en.title: ～ばよかった・～たらどう
en.subtitle: Advice in hindsight and suggestions
en.intro: Both of these structures express advice, but from two different perspectives: once looking back with regret, once as a current suggestion. This very difference is what matters for learning them.
sections[].heading: ～ばよかった — should have
～たらどう — how about
sections[].text: Verb in the ば-form + よかった means that something would have been better in hindsight. It expresses regret or advice in hindsight.
Verb in the たら-form + どう is a suggestion: "How about you ...?" The form usually sounds direct, but it's fine for everyday use.
sections[].tip: The form looks back. It is not a current suggestion but a judgment after the fact.
～たらどう is about the present, ～ばよかった looks back. This time perspective is exactly what separates the two forms.
sections[].examples[].de: I should have gone to bed earlier.
I should have brought an umbrella.
How about resting a little?
Why don't you ask the teacher?

en.title: Giving & Receiving
en.subtitle: あげる, もらう, くれる
en.intro: In English you simply say "give". In Japanese it depends on WHO gives to WHOM and from WHOSE perspective you're speaking — and that applies not only to physical gifts but also to favors, help and kindnesses of all kinds. That sounds complicated, but it follows a clear logic that is deeply rooted in Japanese culture: who gives and who receives defines the social relationship. This system is one of the keys to natural-sounding Japanese, and once you've internalized it, you'll recognize it everywhere.
sections[].heading: あげる — I give (to someone)
くれる — Someone gives to me
もらう — I receive (from someone)
As a favor: てあげる / てくれる / てもらう
The polite forms: さしあげる / くださる / いただく
sections[].text: You use あげる when I (or my side) give something to someone. The movement goes away from me. Important: あげる implies that giver and receiver are roughly equal in status or that the receiver is lower. Toward people of higher status あげる sounds rude — for that there is the special form さしあげる.

You use くれる when someone gives something to me (or my side). The movement goes toward me. It automatically expresses gratitude and appreciation — just by choosing this verb, the speaker shows that they see the gift as kind. くれる can also cover the speaker's family members and close friends (my "in-group").

もらう describes the same event as くれる, but from the receiver's perspective. Literally: "I receive." The giver is marked with に or から. もらう emphasizes that the receiver actively got something — it sounds less like "I was given" and more like "I got / obtained / asked for it".

Combined with the て-form, these verbs express that someone does something as a favor. This construction is extremely common in Japanese and makes the difference between a neutral sentence and one that expresses social relationships. てくれる is especially important here — it's the most natural way to express gratitude for an action.

For formal situations there is a polite level (敬語, keigo) of the giving and receiving verbs. They follow exactly the same logic but sound more respectful and are used in business, toward older people and toward customers. さしあげる replaces あげる, くださる replaces くれる, and いただく replaces もらう. You'll come across いただく and くださる in particular all the time in everyday life.
sections[].tip: Careful: "I give YOU (the person you're talking to)" with あげる can sound condescending. It's often better to switch perspective and choose a different verb.
くれる always expresses gratitude as well — the giver acted voluntarily or out of kindness. It is used only from the perspective of the speaker (or their in-group): someone gives something to ME/US.

The subtle difference from くれる: もらう implies that the receiver took the initiative or asked for the favor. With くれる the giver acted on their own. 教えてくれた = he explained it to me (on his own). 教えてもらった = I had it explained to me (I asked for it).

Rule of thumb: あげる = away from me, くれる = toward me, もらう = I receive. Think of arrows: あげる → (away), くれる ← (toward), もらう ← (receiving). In everyday life てくれる is the most common form — Japanese people use it to express gratitude all the time.

The famous phrase ください (please give me / please do) is actually the て-form + くださる → くださって → ください. So you're already using keigo without knowing it! And いただきます before eating? It comes from いただく = "I humbly receive" — you're humbly giving thanks for the food.
sections[].examples[].de: I gave my friend a present.
I gave my little sister chocolate.
I give the dog food.
My friend gave me a book. (How nice!)
My mother made me a bento. (Gratitude!)
My senpai treated me to a coffee.
I got a book from my friend.
I had the teacher teach me Japanese.
I got a letter from him.
I carried the luggage (for him/her). (I do the favor)
He/she showed me the way. (Someone does ME the favor)
I had a friend help me. (I receive the favor)
I gave the teacher a souvenir. (humble-polite)
The teacher gave me a book. (respectful)
I had the privilege of being taught by the teacher. (humble-polite)

en.title: ～だけでなく・～ばかり・～ほど～ない
en.subtitle: Expanding, narrowing and comparing
en.intro: These three patterns belong together because they don't just make statements, they control their scope. You expand a statement beyond a first point, you narrow it down sharply, or you make a negative comparison. This direction of view is worth learning along with the forms.
sections[].heading: ～だけでなく — not only ... but also
～ばかり — almost only / constantly / nothing but
～ほど～ない — not as ... as
How the three functions differ
sections[].text: Noun / verb + だけでなく expands a statement: it doesn't stop at one point, something else is added. In English, "not only ..., but also ..." often sounds natural.

With ～ばかり you say that something occurs predominantly or strikingly often. Depending on the context, the form can sound neutral, critical or slightly complaining. This nuance matters more than a rigid one-word translation.
A は B ほど ... ない is a negative comparison: A is not as ... as B. Japanese has no comparative ending like English "-er" here; instead it uses a comparison with ほど plus negation.

～だけでなく opens the statement outward. ～ばかり narrows it down to a strong concentration. ～ほど～ない places two things side by side in comparison. Once you understand this direction of movement, the forms are much easier to remember.
sections[].tip: The pattern expands. It doesn't just list two things, it breaks an expectation.
～ばかり often feels more emotional than a neutral "mainly".
The pattern doesn't work without the negation. The negation is part of the comparison logic.
A good learning trick: expand, narrow, compare.
sections[].examples[].de: He speaks not only Japanese but also Chinese.
This shop is not only cheap but also tasty.
I'm eating nothing but sweets.
That person does nothing but complain.
This year it isn't as cold as last year.
The train isn't as slow as the bus.
He not only studies but also does sports.
He does nothing but study.
He isn't as tall as his younger brother.

en.title: ～によると・～について
en.subtitle: Naming a source and setting a topic
en.intro: These two forms take your language a step away from plain everyday sentences toward reporting and explanatory language. That's exactly why you often meet them in the news, in talks, in class and in factual conversations. What matters for learning is the distinction: source versus topic.
sections[].heading: ～によると — according to
～について — about / regarding
Source vs. topic
Natural situations of use
sections[].text: Noun + によると names the source of information. So the speaker isn't saying "this is true" themselves, but refers to what holds according to a person, a news report or a source.

Noun + について sets a topic in the sense of "about". So you talk, write, think, learn or ask in relation to this topic. The form is matter-of-fact and very common at school, at work and in explanatory texts.
～によると answers the question: where does the information come from? ～について answers: what is it about? Keep these two questions separate in your mind, and the forms will immediately make sense.

～によると sounds especially natural with weather forecasts, news, teachers, studies, newspapers or official information. ～について very often appears with 話す, 書く, 考える, 調べる, 勉強する. Learning these partner verbs along with it is more useful than drilling the form in isolation.
sections[].tip: ～によると doesn't introduce an opinion, it marks a source.
If "about" or "regarding" fits naturally in English, ～について is often right.
The most common mix-up is not distinguishing between the source and the topic of conversation.
Don't just learn the particle group, learn the typical verbs that go with it too.
sections[].examples[].de: According to the weather forecast, it will snow tomorrow.
According to the teacher, there's going to be a test next week.
I'm studying Japanese history.
Let's talk about that problem.
According to the news, a typhoon is approaching.
I read about the typhoon in the news.
According to the teacher, this expression is a little old-fashioned.
I'm writing a report on environmental problems.

en.title: ～方
en.subtitle: How to do something – explaining the way it's done
en.intro: ～方 is a small but very useful N4 pattern. It turns an action into a noun meaning "the way you do something". That's exactly why it shows up everywhere: in explanations, user manuals, lessons, apps, recipes and follow-up questions like "How do you use this?"
sections[].heading: Basic formation
What ～方 is used for in everyday life
～方 vs. どうやって
Typical stumbling points
sections[].text: The form is verb stem + 方. It means "the way to do ..." or "how to do ...". Typical examples are 使い方, 読み方, 書き方. With する-verbs, the noun usually comes with の before 仕方 (しかた): 勉強の仕方, 説明の仕方.

With ～方 you're not just asking about an action, but about a method. That's the difference from a direct question-word sentence. ～方 is especially handy when you're talking about reusable knowledge: how to use something, how to read it, how to prepare it, how to pronounce it.

Both can be translated as "how?", but they work differently. どうやって asks directly about the procedure within a sentence. ～方 turns the procedure itself into a noun. That lets you talk about "the way to ...", explain it, judge it or learn it.

Learners often try to put whole clauses in front of 方. That's wrong. What comes before 方 is normally the verb stem or a fixed nominalized verb form. Also, don't confuse ～方 with the polite word 方 (かた, person): they are written and read the same way but mean different things.
sections[].tip: ～方 isn't a complete sentence but a noun. That's why it can be used with を, が, は and other particles.
～方 is ideal when you treat "how do you do X?" as a topic, not just in one specific situation.
When you want to say "explain", "learn", "know", "understand" or "show", ～方 often fits especially well.
With grammar involving ～方, always ask first: is it about a method or about a person?
sections[].examples[].de: Please tell me how to read this kanji.
I don't know how to use this app.
I'm practicing how to hold chopsticks.
Do you know how to make this dish?
How to use keigo is still difficult for me.
How do you get there?
Please tell me the way / how to get there.
reading / way of reading
this person (a different word, a different pattern)

en.title: ～ずに・～ないで
en.subtitle: Without doing something
en.intro: Both forms often mean "without ...ing", but they aren't interchangeable in tone and style. That's exactly what makes this lesson valuable: not just knowing the form, but understanding when the colloquial option is more natural and when the somewhat more written variant fits.
sections[].heading: ～ないで — colloquial and very common
～ずに — somewhat more formal or written
Same meaning, different register
Don't confuse it with a prohibition
sections[].text: ない-form + で is the most common form for "without ...ing". It sounds direct and natural and is very widespread in spoken Japanese. In simple everyday sentences it's almost always the safe choice.
ない-form without ない + ずに also means "without ...ing", but feels somewhat more written, formal or set. You come across this form a lot in explanatory texts, written exercises or a more elevated style.

In many situations the difference in meaning is small. The real difference often lies in the register. ～ないで sounds neutral and more spoken, ～ずに somewhat more compact and written. So you shouldn't only ask "is it grammatically correct?" but also "which tone fits here?".

Because ～ないで also appears in requests like "～ないでください", learners sometimes confuse the form with a prohibition. This lesson, however, is about the connection "without ...ing". So the sentence usually describes two actions, one of which doesn't happen.
sections[].tip: When you're speaking spontaneously, ～ないで is usually the most natural default.
する is an important exception: しないで, but せずに.
For JLPT reading, ～ずに is important, even if in everyday life you'll say ～ないで more often yourself.
Ask yourself: is it a prohibition, or does the sentence describe a step that was left out?
sections[].examples[].de: I went out without eating breakfast.
He went home without saying anything.
He left without giving a reason.
I've been working since this morning without eating anything.
Please answer without looking at your notes.
He went into the real performance without any preparation.
I went into the room without taking off my shoes.
He just went home without apologizing.

en.title: ～さえ・～こそ
en.subtitle: Even, and precisely this one
en.intro: These two particles don't make a statement longer, but they make it much sharper. ～さえ often marks a surprising lower limit or an "even", while ～こそ highlights something on purpose: precisely this, right here, now of all times. Their value for learners lies in the emphasis, not in the basic information.
sections[].heading: ～さえ — even, not even
～こそ — precisely, exactly, of all things
How the two differ
Typical learner traps
sections[].text: Noun + さえ highlights something that is already at the limit: even X, or in a negative sentence, not even X. This often gives the sentence a nuance of surprise, a minimum threshold or a strong restriction.

Noun + こそ puts a strong focus on exactly this element. The statement often sounds more committed, more emotional or more contrastive than with は or が. You don't just highlight something, you present it as the real core.
～さえ draws a line downward or outward: even this unexpected thing. ～こそ points to a key point: exactly this element is what matters. Both add emphasis, but not in the same direction.

Learners often confuse ～さえ with a neutral "also", even though the particle is stronger and marks a limit. For ～こそ, people often learn only "especially", even though it often expresses a deliberate contrast or emphasis. So both need a feel for context, not just dictionary knowledge.
sections[].tip: In negative sentences especially, ～さえ is very strong: "not even X".
～こそ often sounds convinced or emotional. It's more than just a neutral topic.
A good contrast: ～さえ = even / at least, ～こそ = exactly that.
Don't ask "how do I translate this word?" but "what kind of emphasis does it bring to this sentence?"
sections[].examples[].de: Even children know that.
I'm so busy that I haven't even drunk any water.
Now is exactly the time to study.
It's you who is truly kind.
As long as we know the name, it'll be fine.
Effort is exactly what matters.
If only I had time, I could go.
Now is exactly when we should change.

en.title: 命令形・～なさい
en.subtitle: Direct commands and authoritative instructions
en.intro: At N4 you should above all recognize these forms reliably and be able to place them pragmatically. They are much stronger than polite requests and quickly come across as harsh or hierarchical. That's exactly why learning the forms alone isn't enough here; you need to know when the form is natural, rude or typical of certain roles.
sections[].heading: 命令形 — the direct command
～なさい — softer, but still from above
How it differs from ～てください
Typical natural contexts
sections[].text: The 命令形 (imperative) is a direct command form. It often appears in warnings, emotional outbursts, a military or sports tone, manga, films or very rough conversations. In normal polite everyday life you should rarely use it actively yourself.

Verb stem + なさい is milder than the bare imperative, but it remains a clear instruction. It is typically used by parents, teachers or people with formal authority. Toward equals or strangers it can quickly come across as patronizing.
～てください is a polite request. ～なさい is an instruction. 命令形 is a real command. This social gradation is the core of the lesson and more important for natural Japanese than the conjugation alone.

On warning signs, in sports, anime, a military tone, parents' instructions or classrooms, these forms often sound natural. In normal friendly everyday conversations, on the other hand, they are usually too strong. That's why you always have to read the context and the relationship along with them.
sections[].tip: For learners, understanding is more important than active use. The form quickly sounds harsh.
～なさい is not neutral-polite. It presupposes a hierarchy or a parenting role.
Once you can hear how much social tension there is, you've understood the lesson.
This lesson is very pragmatic: the same form can come across as fitting, strict or rude, depending on the scene.
sections[].examples[].de: Come quickly!
Stop it!
Hurry up!
Go to bed early.
Open your textbooks.
Please have a seat.
Sit down.
Sit!
Keep out.
Behave yourself.

en.title: ～くする・～にする
en.subtitle: Actively bringing something into a new state
en.intro: These forms build on adjectives and say: someone actively changes a state. That's exactly what sets them apart from ～くなる and ～になる, which rather describe the result or the change that has taken place. This is the central axis of this lesson.
sections[].heading: い-adjectives + ～くする
な-adjectives and nouns + ～にする
～くする / ～にする vs. ～くなる / ～になる
Typical situations of use
sections[].text: With い-adjectives, the い becomes く and then する follows. This is how you say that someone actively "makes" something "...". It is very common with volume, length, brightness, price or size.
With な-adjectives and nouns you use に + する. Here too, it's about someone actively deciding or bringing about that something becomes that way. ～にする is extremely common especially for decisions.

The most important contrast here is actively changing versus becoming a state. With する there is usually an agent or a conscious decision. With なる the focus is on the result or the change that has taken place.
