These forms don't only show up in adjective drills. In everyday life you say things like turn it down, make it shorter, clean it up, warm it up, go with tea, or set a meeting for a certain time. These concrete situations are exactly what bring the grammar to life.
sections[].tip: With い-adjectives, always remember the change い → く.
～にする very often doesn't just mean "make" but also "decide on something".
If you can ask who is doing it, you're usually dealing with する.
Learn the form together with typical everyday actions, not just with abstract adjective tables.
sections[].examples[].de: Please turn the sound down.
I made the text bigger.
I cleaned up the room.
I'll have tea to drink.
I made the room quiet.
The room became quiet.
We'll set the meeting for three o'clock.
Please make the soup a little hotter.

en.title: ～ていただけませんか・～てくださいませんか
en.subtitle: Asking very politely without sounding harsh
en.intro: These two patterns matter because they make requests noticeably more polite and more careful than a simple ～てください. The key teaching point here is not the literal translation but the social effect: respectful, reserved, and often a good fit for more formal or more distant situations.
sections[].heading: ～ていただけませんか — may I ask you to ...?
～てくださいませんか — would you please ...?
The difference from ～てください
When these forms sound natural
sections[].text: て-form + いただけませんか is a very polite request. It sounds reserved because, literally, it leans toward "could I receive (this) from you". In practice it often corresponds to "Would you be so kind as to ...?"

て-form + くださいませんか is also very polite, but the tone can feel a little more direct or more classic than いただけませんか. The two are close; what matters most is that both are much softer than a simple ～てください.

～てください is polite but relatively direct. ～ていただけませんか / ～てくださいませんか make the same request more careful and socially softer. Especially in situations involving distance, hierarchy or a formal tone, this is a noticeable difference.

These requests fit especially well in customer service, at reception desks, in emails, in class, or anywhere you respectfully leave the other person some room. Among close friends, on the other hand, they quickly sound too heavy or too distant.
sections[].tip: This form is especially useful in service jobs, at work and in official situations.
If いただけませんか feels too heavy to you, くださいませんか is often a good second polite option.
It's not just the grammar that changes, but the relationship between speaker and listener.
A polite pattern is only good if it fits the situation. Too much politeness can also create distance.
sections[].examples[].de: Could you please explain it once more?
Could you please write your name here?
Would you please wait a moment?
Would you please open the window?
Please write down the address.
Could you please write down the address?
Could you please send me the documents?
Would you please speak a little more slowly?

en.title: Potential form
en.subtitle: All the things you can do
en.intro: In lesson 31 you got to know できる — the general way to express "can". But for "can" there's a more elegant solution that's much more common in everyday life: the potential form. It turns any verb directly into a "can" verb — short, snappy and everywhere in daily life. Instead of the long-winded 泳ぐことができる you simply say 泳げる. The potential form is one of the most important tools for natural-sounding Japanese and comes up in practically every conversation.
sections[].heading: Formation: る-verbs
Formation: う-verbs
Irregular verbs
が instead of を — the particle shift
In practice
sections[].text: For る-verbs: cut off る and attach られる. (Yes, that looks like the passive — context clears it up.) The potential form of る-verbs can always be clearly identified from the situation: if it's about ability, it's the potential; if it's about something being done to someone, it's the passive.
For う-verbs: the last syllable shifts to the え-row and る is attached. The pattern is consistent: く→ける, む→める, す→せる, ぐ→げる, ぶ→べる, つ→てる, う→える, ぬ→ねる, る→れる. The result is always a る-verb: 泳げる → 泳げない, 泳げます.

The two usual suspects go their own way, as always. する doesn't become "される" (that would be the passive!) but a completely different word: できる. For 来る the potential form is identical to the passive form — here, too, context decides.

In the potential form the object is often marked with が instead of を. That's because the potential form describes a state ("something is possible for me"), not an active action. It's not a strict law — in colloquial speech you also hear を — but が is the traditional and safer choice, especially in exams and formal texts.

The potential form conjugates like a normal る-verb: 読める (can read), 読めます (can read, polite), 読めない (can't read), 読めた (could read), 読めなかった (couldn't read). It comes up constantly in everyday conversation — when shopping, at restaurants, when traveling, when making plans. Whenever you ask "Can I...?" or "Can you ... here?", you need the potential form.
sections[].tip: In colloquial speech many Japanese people drop the ら: 食べれる instead of 食べられる, 見れる instead of 見られる. This is called "ら抜き言葉" (ra-nuki kotoba) and isn't quite grammatically correct, but it's extremely widespread — especially among younger speakers. In formal situations and exams, though, you should keep the ら.
する → できる is the only potential form that is a completely different word. All the others are predictable. Remember this exception and you're safe.

Comparison: ことができる vs. the potential form — both mean "can", but the potential form is shorter and more natural in spoken Japanese. 泳ぐことができる (formal, written) vs. 泳げる (short, everyday). For the JLPT you should master both.
sections[].examples[].de: to be able to eat
to be able to see
to be able to get up
to be able to read (む → める)
to be able to write (く → ける)
to be able to speak (す → せる)
to do → to be able to do (a completely different word!)
to be able to come
I can read kanji. (が = traditionally correct)
I can read kanji. (を = also OK in casual speech)
I can speak Japanese.
Can you read kanji?
You can't take photos here.
I can speak a little Japanese.

en.title: ～くなる・～になる
en.subtitle: Changing – something becomes different
en.intro: With ～くなる and ～になる you describe changes. The structure matters early on because it ties in directly with adjectives, nouns and everyday topics like weather, language, age or health. The most important teaching point here isn't the form but the perspective: something becomes different, without necessarily saying who actively changed it.
sections[].heading: い-adjectives + ～くなる
な-adjectives and nouns + ～になる
～になる vs. ～にする
Typical everyday situations
sections[].text: With い-adjectives, the い becomes く and then なる follows. That's how you describe that something "becomes ...". The change can happen naturally or simply be observed; the sentence doesn't need to name anyone doing it.
With な-adjectives and nouns, you use に + なる. This too describes a change of state. The form is especially common with roles, professions, clock times, habits and characteristics.

These two forms belong together. ～になる describes the result or the change that has occurred. ～にする describes a conscious decision or an active change made by someone. In English, both are easily blurred — "get" can cover either ("the room got clean" / "I got the room clean") — so the perspective needs to be practiced consciously.

The form is used far more widely in everyday life than just in adjective drills. With ～になる you talk about changes in the weather, physical development, progress in a language, habits, social roles and even clock times. That's exactly why the structure is so central: it connects grammar directly with real communication.
sections[].tip: With い-adjectives, always remember い → く: 高い → 高くなる.
～にする means "to consciously make something so", ～になる means "it becomes so".
If you're asking about who did it, you're usually closer to ～にする. If you're only describing the new state, you're closer to ～になる.
With preferences, ～好きになる is especially common: not just "to like" but "to come to like".
sections[].examples[].de: It's gotten cold.
My Japanese has gotten a little better.
Let's go home before it gets dark.
The room has become quiet.
I want to become a teacher.
It's already ten o'clock.
The room has become clean.
I cleaned the room.
When spring comes, this park becomes beautiful.
Since coming to Japan, I've come to like fish.

en.title: ～のは～です
en.subtitle: Nominalizing actions and highlighting them deliberately
en.intro: With ～のは～です you turn an action into a topic or deliberately highlight what something is about. The pattern is very useful for definitions, focus and small contrasts. Its value isn't that it's "complicated", but that it can structure a conversation: What exactly is difficult, what exactly do you like, what is this actually about?
sections[].heading: Basic pattern
Contrast and focus
～のは～です vs. ～のが好き / 上手 / 下手
Typical beginner mistakes
sections[].text: Verb / clause + のは + noun / adjective + です roughly means: "The thing that ... is ..." or "What ... is ...". It turns the whole action before の into a topic block. So you're no longer talking about just one word, but about the activity or the whole situation as the topic.

You very often use ～のは～です to single out or contrast exactly one thing among several possibilities. That makes the structure ideal for explanations like "What's hard is X" or "What I do every day is Y". It steers the conversation very deliberately toward one particular aspect.

These structures look similar but have different functions. ～のが好き evaluates an action as something you like. ～のは～です makes the action itself the topic and then says something about it. That's a functional difference, not just a detail of form.

Learners often use the structure in places where a simpler sentence would be more natural. ～のは～です is strongly focusing. If nothing is being contrasted or defined, a normal sentence often sounds lighter. So the form isn't a replacement for every sentence with verb + です, but a tool for setting emphasis.
sections[].tip: The pattern resembles ～のが好き, but here it's not about preferences, it's about naming or highlighting something.
In JLPT questions it often matters which part comes before のは and which part comes after it.
When you're talking about a preference, ～のが is often more natural. When you're defining or highlighting, ～のは～です fits.
If you can mentally add "as for X" or "the difficult thing is ...", the structure often fits well.
sections[].examples[].de: Reading books is fun.
What's difficult is the kanji.
The most important thing is to keep at it every day.
What I like is music, but what I'm good at is drawing.
What I do every day is review.
What's difficult in Japanese is the particles.
I like reading books.
Reading books is fun.
Studying Japanese is hard work.
Japanese is hard work. (more general, less focused)

en.title: 意向形 ～よう・～おう
en.subtitle: Let's … / I'll …
en.intro: The volitional form is the short form for intention, urging yourself on and shared plans. It's important at N4 because it's used both in direct communication and in patterns like ～と思う or ～とする.
sections[].heading: Formation
Typical use
sections[].text: With う-verbs the last syllable shifts to the お-row + う; with る-verbs, る becomes よう. する becomes しよう, 来る becomes こよう.
The form expresses a shared plan or your own intention. It's very common in casual conversation.
sections[].tip: The volitional form isn't the same as ～ましょう. ～ましょう is more polite, ～よう is more direct and shorter.
For the JLPT it's important to recognize the volitional form even when it doesn't sound like a suggestion but like an inner decision.
sections[].examples[].de: to go → let's go / I'll go
to eat → let's eat / I'll eat
to study → let's study
I'll go to bed early today.
Let's go out together this weekend.

en.title: ～ことがある
en.subtitle: Something sometimes happens
en.intro: This N4 structure must not be confused with ～たことがある for experience. Here, ～ことがある means that something happens occasionally or is sometimes the case. So the core idea is not "an experience in the past" but "something is the case every now and then".
sections[].heading: Expressing occasional events
Experience vs. habit vs. occasional case
When the form sounds natural
sections[].text: 普通形 + ことがある means "it happens that ..." or "sometimes ...". Very often an adverb like ときどき or たまに goes with it.

These three areas are close to each other, but they are not the same. ～たことがある asks about an experience in your life. よく～ます / いつも～ます describes a habit. ～ことがある sits in between: not regularly, but sometimes.

～ことがある sounds especially natural when you want to express a certain distance or a generalization. The form feels less direct than a bare "sometimes". That's why it fits well in explanations, reports about daily habits, or careful statements about exceptions.
sections[].tip: ～たことがある = have experienced it before. ～ことがある = happens sometimes. The tenses are the key.
Ask yourself: am I talking about an experience, a regular habit or an occasional case?
The form is often a bit more explanatory and distanced than a bare ときどき.
sections[].examples[].de: When I'm busy, I sometimes don't eat breakfast.
Now and then you see famous people at this station.
Sometimes I go to work even on Sundays.
I have been to Japan before.
I drink coffee every morning.
On busy days, I sometimes don't eat breakfast.
In this area it sometimes snows in winter.
He sometimes suddenly gets angry.

en.title: ～っぽい・～かける・～出す
en.subtitle: Seems like it, half started, suddenly set in
en.intro: These three patterns are compact but very lively. They help you express subtle transitions in everyday language: something seems kind of like that, something is half started, or something suddenly sets in. Their great learning value lies in typical scenes, not in abstract definitions.
sections[].heading: ～っぽい — seems kind of like
～かける — half started / not yet finished
～出す — suddenly starting
Typical everyday scenes and contrasts
sections[].text: Noun / verb stem + っぽい expresses a loose, often subjective assessment: something seems like that, has something of it, or tends toward it. The form is colloquial and often more emotional than a sober description.

Verb stem + かける shows that an action has been started but is not yet finished. There's often a feeling of "half open" or "still up in the air" in it. The form is especially common with eating, reading, saying, building or tidying up.
Verb stem + 出す often marks a sudden beginning. The form is more dynamic than a neutral ～始める and comes up especially often with movements, noises, laughing, crying or weather.

～っぽい describes an impression. ～かける describes an unfinished stage. ～出す describes a sudden start. So these three patterns aren't the same in theme, but they all mark an in-between status rather than a plain fact.
sections[].tip: ～っぽい sounds more subjective and casual than a matter-of-fact adjective.
～かける doesn't just describe the start, but especially the unfinished part.
When something suddenly gets going, ～出す often sounds more natural than ～始める.
Learn the forms as types of scenes: impression, half-finished, suddenly off.
sections[].examples[].de: This color looks kind of childish, doesn't it?
He's forgetful.
There's a half-eaten piece of bread on the desk.
I started to say something and then stopped.
The child suddenly burst into tears.
It started to rain.
He gets angry easily.
I have a half-read book with me.
Everyone suddenly burst out laughing.

en.title: ～直す・～合う・～てすむ／～ずにすむ
en.subtitle: Redoing, doing things mutually and getting off lightly
en.intro: This lesson is important for learning because it brings together several very productive verb add-on patterns that easily get explained too briefly. Yet there's a lot of real language value in them: doing something again to correct it, doing something mutually, carrying something through to the very end, or getting out of a situation with little damage.
sections[].heading: ～直す — doing again and correcting in the process
～合う — mutually or together
～切る — doing completely to the end
～てすむ / ～ずにすむ — getting off lightly
Which pattern when?
Typical learner traps
sections[].text: Verb stem + 直す doesn't simply mean "do again", but often "redo in order to make it better or right". So the form often carries an idea of correction or repair.
Verb stem + 合う describes a mutual or shared action. The people involved do something with each other or for each other. Very common examples are 助け合う, 話し合う, 分け合う.

Verb stem + 切る means that you carry an action through completely to the end. There's often a feeling of determination, completion or perseverance in it. With things like reading, eating up, using up or holding out, the pattern is especially natural.
てすむ and ずにすむ mean that one thing is enough, or that you get by without something more difficult. Often the idea is: luckily that's enough, or you don't have to do something unpleasant.

～直す tackles the same process once more. ～合う connects several people in a mutual action. ～切る takes something all the way to the end. ～てすむ / ～ずにすむ describes an outcome where a simpler solution is enough or something unpleasant is avoided.

Many learners read ～直す too mechanically as "repeat", even though improvement is often meant. With ～合う people sometimes forget that mutuality has to make sense in meaning. ～切る is easily confused with a simple past tense, even though the completion is what counts. And ～ずにすむ is easily analyzed too literally, even though the real meaning is often "luckily not having to".
sections[].tip: ～直す is stronger than just もう一度. Often there's improvement or correction in it.
Not every verb goes naturally with ～合う. It works best when mutuality really makes sense.
～切る emphasizes the completion itself. It is often stronger and more determined than a neutral "finish".
In English, "luckily ... was enough" or "I didn't have to ..." often works well.
The patterns don't share a meaning. They only share that they turn simple verbs into very productive new nuances.
With ～ずにすむ it's almost always worth asking yourself: what was it that didn't have to happen in the end?
sections[].examples[].de: Please rewrite this essay.
I'll rethink the plan.
When you're in trouble, it's important to help each other.
Let's all talk it over properly.
I read this book all the way through in one day.
I've used up all the water.
I ran all the way to the end.
I went to the hospital, but taking medicine was all it took.
Since I had a reservation, I didn't have to wait long.
I looked over my answer once more and rewrote it.
In our family, we all chip in for living expenses.
I ate up my whole bento during the lunch break.
Because I took a taxi, luckily I wasn't late.
After thinking it over again, I decided not to go.
Eating it all up was hard.
If we had talked it over a little, we might have avoided a fight.

en.title: ～ふりをする
en.subtitle: Pretending
en.intro: With ～ふりをする you describe behavior that is only acted or faked. The form is very useful for dialogues, reading texts and everyday situations, because it doesn't simply describe a lie but the visible act of pretending. That's exactly where its character lies.
sections[].heading: Basic pattern
Typical forms in front of it
～ふりをする vs. simply lying
Pragmatic nuance
sections[].text: 普通形 + ふりをする means "to pretend that ..." or "to act as if ...". Very often a verb form comes before it, but adjectives and states are also possible. The important thing is: it's not about what is really true, but about the behavior shown to the outside.

Especially often, ふりをする is preceded by a state that someone fakes: knowing, not hearing, staying calm, looking well, being surprised. This often gives the structure a psychological or social coloring in everyday life: someone wants to control the impression they make or hide something.

～ふりをする does not simply mean the same as "lying". With 嘘をつく someone says something false. With ～ふりをする someone creates a false impression through their behavior. That can also happen without words. That's exactly why the form is so common in scenes and narrative texts.

The form often has a slightly critical undertone. Someone who "pretends" is hiding something, protecting themselves, avoiding responsibility or trying to control a situation. In stories, though, the form can also express sympathy, for example when someone seems brave even though they're suffering.
sections[].tip: ～ふりをする describes acted behavior, not reality.
The form fits especially well when the inner state and the outward behavior don't match.
When the deception works through body language, reactions or attitude, ～ふりをする is often exactly right.
Pay attention to the context: the form can sound reproachful, sad, brave or ironic.
sections[].examples[].de: Please don't pretend you know.
He pretended he couldn't hear.
I'm pretending to be fine, but actually I'm tired.
Pretending not to understand is rude.
She pretended everything was fine.
He pretended to be busy and didn't listen.
I pretended I hadn't seen anything.
Even though my mother was worried, she pretended nothing was wrong.
In front of everyone, he pretended he wasn't crying.

en.title: ている — More than the progressive
en.subtitle: What's happening right now (and what has already happened)
en.intro: You may know ている as the equivalent of English "-ing": 食べている = "I'm eating (right now)". But ている can do much more — it describes ongoing actions, resulting states, habits, occupations and even experiences. This versatility makes ている one of the most frequently used constructions in all of Japanese. If you want to sound natural, you need to be able to tell its different meanings apart reliably. This lesson shows you all the important uses with lots of examples.
sections[].heading: Ongoing action (進行)
Resulting state (結果の状態)
Habit & repetition (習慣)
Occupation & affiliation
Experience & knowledge (経験)
sections[].text: The best-known meaning: something is happening right now. Like English "-ing" or "right now". This use is intuitive and the starting point for most learners. Note: in colloquial speech ている is often shortened to てる (食べている → 食べてる).

With verbs that describe a change of state (opening, marrying, arriving, dying, putting on clothes...), ている expresses the resulting state — not the action itself. This is the most important difference from English "-ing" and the most common stumbling block for learners. The action is already completed, and ている describes what comes after it.

ている can also express a regular habit or a recurring action. In this case it's not about what's happening right now but about what you do regularly. Time expressions like 毎日 (every day), いつも (always) or 最近 (lately) often signal this meaning.

You also use ている for occupations, where you live and long-term affiliations. Here ている describes an ongoing life circumstance — something that applies not just right now but over a longer period. This is one of the most natural uses of ている in Japanese.

Combined with certain verbs, ている can also express that you know something because you've experienced or learned it. The best-known example is 知っている (to know [a fact or a person]). Here ている describes the state of "being in possession of knowledge". Note: the negative is 知らない (not 知っていない!) — one of the best-known exceptions in Japanese.
sections[].tip: The shortened てる instead of ている is standard in colloquial speech. 食べている → 食べてる, 読んでいる → 読んでる, している → してる. In the ます-form: 食べています → 食べてます. Use the full form in formal situations and exams.

This is the most common stumbling block: 死んでいる means "is dead" (state), not "is dying". 座っている means "is seated" (state), not "is in the middle of sitting down". Whether ている describes an action or a state depends on the type of verb: action verbs (eating, reading, running) → ongoing action. Change-of-state verbs (arriving, dying, marrying) → resulting state.

Tell ている for habits apart from the simple present: 毎日走っている (I run every day — stresses the ongoing habit) vs. 毎日走る (I run every day — a general statement or intention). ている makes the habit more vivid and stresses that you actually do it regularly.

The negative of 知っている is 知らない — never 知っていない. This is one of the few fixed exceptions and is tested in every JLPT exam. 持っている (to have/own) also behaves like a state: 車を持っている = "I have a car" (the lasting state of owning it).
sections[].examples[].de: I'm reading a book right now.
It's raining (right now).
I'm on the phone.
The window is open. (not: is opening right now)
I'm married. (not: I'm getting married right now)
It has already arrived. (state: it's here)
I jog every morning. (habit)
I always shop at that store.
Lately I've been studying Japanese.
I teach at a university. (= that's my job)
I live in Tokyo. (lasting state)
I work at a Japanese company.
I know that story.
Do you know Mr. Tanaka?
No, I don't know him. (NOT: 知っていません)

en.title: こと vs の
en.subtitle: Two ways to nominalize
en.intro: A great many N5 and N4 patterns use こと or の, but nobody explains systematically early on why one is used here and the other there. That's exactly why this lesson matters: こと usually feels more abstract and general, の often more concrete, more immediate or more closely tied to an action you observe.
sections[].heading: The basic idea
When こと is especially natural
When の is especially natural
Typical pairs to learn
sections[].text: こと and の turn an action or a whole clause into something noun-like. That lets you talk about "doing something", "the fact that ..." or "the event". The difference isn't absolute, but as an N5/N4 rule of thumb: こと sounds more abstract, の more concrete and closer to a real scene.

こと often fits when something sounds general, abstract or rule-like. That's why you meet it so often in patterns like ことができる, ことにする, ことになる or たことがある. These are less about a concretely observed scene and more about ability, experience, decisions or rules.

の often sounds more natural when an action is evaluated, observed or commented on emotionally as something concrete and perceptible. That's why it appears so often with 好き, 上手, 下手, 見る, 聞く or in focus patterns like のは～です.

Learners often trip over pairs that look similar but don't work the same way. ～のが好き is a very common pattern. ～ことが好き sounds heavier or less natural in many standard situations. Conversely, with ことができる you can almost always expect こと.
sections[].tip: A phrase to remember for starters: こと = more like "the matter / the doing", の = more like "the concrete event before your eyes".
If the form is learned as a fixed grammar pattern, it usually comes with こと automatically.
If you're mentally picturing "the scene" or "what I see/hear", の is often the better choice.
The question often isn't "which word means what?" but "what kind of content is being nominalized: an ability/rule or a concrete action?"
sections[].examples[].de: Studying Japanese is important.
I like watching children play outside.
I can read kanji.
I've been to Japan before.
I make it a rule to run every morning.
I like listening to music.
I saw him running.
What's difficult is the pronunciation.
I like reading books.
I can read books.
I can explain it, but speaking it well is difficult.

en.title: ～がる
en.subtitle: Recognizing other people's feelings from their behavior
en.intro: With ～がる you don't describe your own inner state, but how someone else visibly reacts or seems to feel something. That's exactly why the form matters at N4: you learn to cleanly distinguish between describing yourself directly and the observable behavior of others.
sections[].heading: The basic idea
Typical forms: 怖がる, 嫌がる, 欲しがる
The contrast with ～たい, ～ほしい and ～たがる
Typical learner traps
sections[].text: ～がる typically attaches to adjectives or words for states and shows that someone outwardly displays a feeling or reaction. So the speaker isn't simply claiming that the other person "is like that inside", but rather: they are showing this behavior.
Some words appear with ～がる especially often. These include 怖がる, 嫌がる and 欲しがる. 欲しがる in particular is important, because you shouldn't simply use ほしい for other people.

～たい and ～ほしい are used primarily for your own wishes or very direct questions. For other people this is often too direct. For that there are visible wish forms like ～たがる and the broader reaction form ～がる. So ～たがる functionally belongs to the same family, but specifically for verbs expressing wishes.

Many learners use ～たい or ～ほしい directly about other people, even though Japanese is more reserved here. A second source of errors is using ～がる when there is no observable behavior at all. The form lives on visible signs, reactions or habits.
sections[].tip: ～がる is especially useful when you don't want to look inside the other person's head but describe their behavior instead.
For other people, 欲しがる is often the more natural choice than plain ほしい.
Your own wish and an observed wish must not be mixed up. That's exactly what this family of forms is for.
A good check question is: "How can I tell?" If there are visible signs, ～がる often fits well.
sections[].examples[].de: My little brother is afraid of dogs / shows fear of dogs.
The child shows that it doesn't like that sound.
My daughter is visibly afraid of injections.
He's showing that he wants a new smartphone.
That cat doesn't like being picked up.
I want to go home.
He's showing that he wants to go home.
He seems to want a new book.
Children are afraid of dark rooms.
He's showing that he doesn't like speaking in front of people.

en.title: そう, よう, らしい
en.subtitle: How things seem
en.intro: "It looks as if...", "Apparently...", "It seems that..." — Japanese has several ways to express guesses and impressions, and each has its own subtle nuance. While English often gets by with a simple "seems", Japanese distinguishes very precisely where your impression comes from: Are you seeing it with your own eyes? Are you drawing a logical conclusion? Or did you hear it from someone? This distinction may seem pedantic at first, but it makes the language incredibly precise — and once you've understood the system, it becomes second nature.
sections[].heading: ～そう — "looks like" (your own observation)
Forming ～そう in detail
～ようだ / ～みたい — "it seems" (inference)
～らしい — "apparently" (hearsay)
らしい as "typical of"
Quick comparison
Easy to confuse: そうだ (hearsay)
sections[].text: そう attaches to the stem of verbs and i-adjectives (that is, the form without い or without ます). It expresses what you see with your own eyes or expect to happen right away — you're right there in the situation and making a judgment based on the visual impression. With na-adjectives the な drops and そう is attached directly. Important: そう describes the impression in the moment, not a considered analysis.

Fortunately, the rules for attaching そう are quite systematic. For verbs you take the ます-stem: 降ります → 降り → 降りそう. For i-adjectives you drop the い: おいしい → おいし → おいしそう. For na-adjectives you drop the な: 元気な → 元気 → 元気そう. そう itself then behaves like a na-adjective: you can say そうな + noun (おいしそうなケーキ) or そうに + verb (楽しそうに笑う).

ようだ (formal) and みたい (casual) express an inference based on observation, reasoning or gathered clues. The difference from そう is important: with そう you react spontaneously to a visual impression; with ようだ/みたい you've gathered information and are drawing a conclusion from it. ようだ follows the plain form of verbs and adjectives; nouns take の before it (雨のようだ), na-adjectives take な (静かなようだ). みたい is the colloquial variant and also follows the plain form, but it comes directly after nouns and na-adjectives (雨みたい, 静かみたい) — just more casually.

らしい expresses that you heard something from someone, know it from a source, or that it's commonly known information — not something you observed yourself. It follows the plain form of verbs and adjectives directly; with nouns there's no だ before it (so directly: 雨らしい, not 雨だらしい). When someone says "Xらしい", they're clearly signaling: "I wasn't there, but that's what I heard." This creates a certain distance from the information and makes it clear that you're not personally vouching for it.

There's a second meaning of らしい you should know: attached to nouns, it means "typical of" or "just as you'd expect". In this case it isn't hearsay but an evaluation of whether something matches the ideal or the expectation. The context always makes clear which meaning is intended.

FormBasisMeaningExample situation
～そうWhat I seeLooks like... / is about to...You see the dark sky
～ようだ / みたいWhat I inferIt seems that...You notice wet ground, closed umbrellas
～らしいWhat I've heardApparently... / I heard...A colleague told you it rained

Careful, there's a second そうだ that works completely differently! When そうだ is attached to the plain form (not the stem), it means "I heard that..." — in other words hearsay, similar to らしい. The difference: 降りそう (looks like it's going to rain — stem + そう) vs. 降るそうだ (I heard it's going to rain — plain form + そうだ). Mixing up these two forms is one of the most common mistakes at N4 level.
sections[].tip: Watch out for the special forms: いい becomes よさそう (not いさそう!), and ない becomes なさそう. These two exceptions are a favorite on the JLPT.
ようだ can also be used for comparisons: 雪のように白い (white as snow). In this case it means "like" rather than "it seems" — the context makes the difference clear.
"彼は男らしい" (He is manly/masculine) vs. "彼は男だらしい" (Apparently he's a man) — here the だ makes all the difference!
Memory aid: stem + そう = "looks like" (eyes). Plain form + そうだ = "I heard" (ears). Eyes need less information (just the stem), ears need the whole sentence (plain form).
sections[].examples[].de: It looks like rain. (I can see the dark clouds.)
This cake looks delicious!
You look sleepy.
I found some delicious-looking ramen. (そうな + noun)
The children are playing and look like they're having fun. (そうに + verb)
He looks like he has nothing to do.
He seems to be busy. (I'm inferring this from various clues.)
It seems like nobody's here.
The train seems to be delayed.
Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.
I hear that restaurant is good.
Apparently Tanaka is getting married next month.
She is a typically feminine person. (= fits the image)
Today is typical spring weather, isn't it?
That's a typically childlike idea.
I heard that it's going to rain tomorrow. (hearsay そう)
It looks like it's going to rain tomorrow. (appearance そう)
I heard that movie is interesting. (plain form + そうだ)

en.title: Relative clauses
en.subtitle: Sentences that describe nouns
en.intro: In English you say "the book that I bought yesterday". Japanese has no relative pronoun — no "that", no "which", no "who". Instead, you simply put the describing clause BEFORE the noun, directly and without any fuss. That sounds radical at first, but it's surprisingly elegant and logical once you've internalized it. Relative clauses are one of the most important building blocks for more complex sentences, and once you master them, you can suddenly express yourself in Japanese with far more nuance.
sections[].heading: The basic principle
In full sentences
Different roles of the noun
Important rules
Common everyday patterns
sections[].text: In Japanese, a whole sentence can describe a noun by being placed directly in front of it. No "that/which/who", no comma, no relative pronoun — just clause + noun. The verb in the clause is always in the plain form (so 買った rather than 買いました). Think of the clause as one long adjective: just as 大きい犬 (big dog) works, so does 昨日買った本 (yesterday-bought book).

The relative clause + noun is then used as a perfectly normal part of the main sentence — as subject, object or in any other role a noun can take. The particles (は、が、を、に etc.) come after the noun, just as with any other noun. The nice thing is: once you recognize the clause as a block, even a long sentence breaks down into manageable parts.

A special feature of Japanese relative clauses: the noun being described can play any role at all in the clause — subject, object, place, time, companion and so on. In English you need different words for this (who, whom, which, where, with whom...), but in Japanese the construction doesn't change. That makes it both easier and more confusing: easier because the form is always the same; confusing because you have to work out from context which role the noun plays.

• Plain form before the noun: The clause always uses the plain form (食べた, not 食べました). This is non-negotiable — even when the main sentence is in the ます-form.
  • は becomes が: The subject in the clause is marked with が, not は. The topic particle は belongs in the main sentence, not in the clause.
  • Nesting is possible: You can stack several clauses — but be careful, it quickly becomes hard to follow. In everyday language people usually stick to one or two levels.
  • こと and の: With ～たこと and ～ること you can turn whole sentences into nouns: 日本に行ったこと = "the fact that I went to Japan".

Certain combinations of clause + noun come up so often that they work almost like fixed expressions. It's worth internalizing these patterns, because they appear constantly in conversations and texts. ～たことがある (experience), ～ているところ (being in the middle of something) and ～たばかり (having just done something) are especially essential.
sections[].tip: Remember: in Japanese the description ALWAYS comes before the noun. That applies to single adjectives (大きい猫) just as much as to whole clauses (昨日見つけた猫). It's the same principle!

Tip for reading long sentences: first find the main noun — everything before it is the clause that describes it. Then find the main verb at the end of the sentence. The core of the sentence lies between the described noun and the main verb.
sections[].examples[].de: the book that I bought yesterday
a person who speaks Japanese
the cake that my mother made
The book that I bought yesterday was interesting.
Let's eat at the shop that's in front of the station.
The town where I live is small.
the food that Tanaka made (noun = object in the clause)
the person who made the food (noun = subject in the clause)
the restaurant I went to with friends (noun = place)
The flowers my friend gave me are pretty.
I forgot the name of the movie I saw last week.
Have you ever been to Japan? (lit.: Is there the fact that you went to Japan?)
I'm in the middle of reading it right now.
a student who has just come to Japan
Even though I just ate, I'm already hungry again.

en.title: ように & ために
en.subtitle: Goals and intentions
en.intro: "In order to ..." — a simple concept in English that Japanese expresses quite differently depending on the situation. The key question is: do you have direct control over the goal, or are you aiming for a state that can only be reached indirectly? ために stands for conscious, deliberate intentions — you act purposefully. ように stands for states, abilities and results that you aim for but can't directly force. This concept is not only relevant to grammar, it also reveals something about the Japanese way of thinking: there is a clear distinction between what you do yourself and what comes about.
sections[].heading: ために — "in order to" (conscious intention)
ように — "so that" (target state)
ために vs. ように — the difference in a nutshell
ようになる — "it has come about that..."
ようにする — "making sure that..."
sections[].text: ために is used with the dictionary form (plain non-past, affirmative) and expresses a conscious, deliberate goal. The subject of both parts of the sentence is typically the same: I do X to achieve Y. The verb before ために always describes a controllable action — something you can actively do or not do. ために can also be used with nouns, in which case の comes before it (家族のために).

ように is used when the goal is a state or an ability — something you don't directly control or that is meant to come about as a result. That's why ように is often preceded by the potential form (話せる, 読める) or the negative form (忘れない, 遅刻しない). With ように the speaker has less direct control over the result — they do something in the hope that a certain state will come about. That makes ように softer and more indirect than ために.

The key question is always: Do you control the result directly? If yes → ために. If you're only creating the conditions for it → ように. A concrete example: "in order to study Japanese" = 日本語を勉強するために (studying is a conscious action). "so that I can speak Japanese" = 日本語が話せるように (being able to speak is a state that comes about). This difference may seem subtle, but it's absolutely central to natural-sounding Japanese.

ようになる describes a gradual change — a transition from one state to another. Something you couldn't do before, you can do now; something you didn't do before, you now do regularly. It's not a sudden switch but a process that has taken place over time. Its counterpart is ようにする, which describes a conscious effort: "I make sure that...".

While ようになる describes a change that has taken place, ようにする expresses a conscious effort or habit. It means: "I make sure / I try to...". This form is extremely useful in everyday life for expressing good resolutions or habits. In the ている-form (ようにしている) it describes an ongoing habit.
sections[].tip: ために sounds very purposeful and determined. When you use it, you signal: "I have a concrete goal and I'm working deliberately toward it."
Rule of thumb: is the goal construction preceded by a potential form or ない? Then it's almost always ように. Is it preceded by an ordinary volitional verb in the dictionary form? Then ために.
ようになった = "it has turned out that..." (result). ようにしている = "I make sure that..." (conscious effort). Both are similar, but the perspective is completely different!
sections[].examples[].de: I came to Japan to study Japanese.
I study every day to pass the exam.
I work for my family. (noun + のために)
I practice every day so that I can speak Japanese.
I got up early so that I wouldn't be late.
I made a note so that I wouldn't forget.
I exercise to lose weight. (active goal)
I eat vegetables so that I don't gain weight. (avoiding a state)
I can read kanji now. (I couldn't before.)
I've started exercising every day.
These days I often eat Japanese food.
I make sure to eat vegetables every day.
I make sure not to be late.
I try to use Japanese as much as possible.

en.title: という & って
en.subtitle: Quoting, explaining, naming
en.intro: "They say that...", "That means...", "I heard that..." — these constructions show up literally everywhere in Japanese, from formal business letters to relaxed chats among friends. The particle と is the link that connects quotes, thoughts, names and explanations to the rest of the sentence. Combined with 言う (to say), 思う (to think) and other verbs, it creates an incredibly flexible system. And then there's って — the casual short form that's everywhere in spoken language and that you're guaranteed to hear in every anime, every TV series and every everyday conversation.
sections[].heading: と言う — direct and indirect quotation
という — "that is" / "named" / "so-called"
って — the all-purpose short form
と思う — "I think that..."
More と constructions
sections[].text: と言う (to iu) is the basic construction for reporting what someone said. For direct quotes you put the words in Japanese quotation marks 「」; for indirect quotes you leave them out. In both cases the plain form comes before と. Note: in indirect quotes you adjust the perspective (as in English: "I'm coming" → He said he was coming). This construction is the basis for many extended expressions that we'll see shortly.

という (to iu) in its attributive use serves to name, define or explain something. It links a name, term or description to the noun it specifies. The combinations ということ (the fact that...) and というのは (as for X / X means...) are especially useful. You'll come across these forms constantly in texts and conversations, especially when things are being explained or new concepts introduced.

って (tte) is the spoken short form of と and という. It's incredibly versatile: depending on context, it replaces と言う (quotation), という (naming), は (topic) and even というのは (explanation). In colloquial speech って is so ubiquitous that you hardly hear a sentence without it. It makes speech more natural, faster and more relaxed. At first it may be confusing because って can mean so many things, but the context almost always makes the meaning clear.

と思う (to omou) expresses your own opinion or assessment. The plain form always comes before と. An important cultural point: と思います is used very often in Japanese, even for statements that would be phrased as facts in English. It makes a statement softer and less absolute — an important social function in a culture that avoids direct confrontation. The ている-form (と思っている) describes an ongoing belief, while と思う tends to express a spontaneous thought.

The particle と in its quoting function isn't limited to 言う and 思う. There's a whole range of verbs that combine with と, each expressing a different nuance. These constructions are absolutely essential from N4/N3 on and make the way you express yourself much richer and more natural.
sections[].tip: ということ is one of the most useful expressions of all. It turns a whole sentence into a noun: "the fact/thing that...". Absolutely indispensable from N4 level on.
って is extremely common in colloquial speech. If you read Japanese subtitles or watch anime, you'll hear it in almost every dialogue. Get used to seeing it as a "flexible all-purpose tool"!
"I don't think that..." = ～ないと思う (the negation comes BEFORE と思う, not after it). ～と思わない (I don't think so), by contrast, sounds much stronger and more dismissive.
sections[].examples[].de: He/she said, "It's hot." (direct quote)
He/she said that he/she would come tomorrow. (indirect quote)
My mother said, "Go to bed early!"
Do you know the flower called "Sakura"?
a food called ramen
I didn't know that he wasn't coming. (ということ = the fact that)
Apparently there's a test tomorrow. (hearsay = と言っていた)
What's ramen? (= ラーメンというのは何?)
Tanaka is really kind, right? (って as a topic marker)
I think it'll rain tomorrow.
I think this movie is interesting.
I'm thinking of going to Japan. (ongoing thought/wish)
I heard that there's a test tomorrow. (と聞く = to hear that)
I decided to become a doctor in the future. (と決める = to decide)
I asked him to help me. (と頼む = to ask)

en.title: を, に, で
en.subtitle: The three musketeers of particles
en.intro: Three little particles that show up in almost every Japanese sentence. Together with は and が they form the backbone of Japanese sentence structure. Each of the three has its own job — and once you get them, sentences almost assemble themselves. The key is not to ask "What does this mean in English?" but "What role does this word play in the sentence?".
sections[].heading: を — What you do (the direct object)
に — Where something IS, where you GO
で — Where you DO something, what you do it with
に vs で — The classic
sections[].text: を (pronounced "o") marks the direct object — the thing affected by the action. You eat something, you read something, you buy something. In English, the direct object is the answer to "what?" or "whom?" after the verb (I eat what? — an apple). In Japanese, を takes on this job — reliably and without exceptions. Every transitive verb needs a を object.

に is the particle for destination, location, point in time and recipient. It answers the questions "Where to?", "Where?" (for existence), "When?" (for specific points in time) and "To whom?". Of all the particles, に is probably the most versatile — it shows up in a wide range of contexts, but it always has to do with some kind of "target point".

で marks the place of an active action, the means or tool, the cause and sometimes the scope (e.g. "the two of us", "in total"). The crucial difference from に: with で, something actively happens. It's the stage on which an action takes place — not the quiet spot where something exists.

The difference between に and で is one of the most common stumbling blocks for learners. The rule of thumb: に = existence / state / target point (something IS there or something moves TO there), で = action / means (something HAPPENS there or is done with it). For locations, this question helps: Is something actively happening there? → で. Is something simply there (present, living, attached)? → に.
sections[].tip: を also marks places you pass through or leave. This special meaning often surprises learners: 公園を歩く (walk through the park), 家を出る (leave the house), 橋を渡る (cross a bridge). Here the place is basically the "object" of the movement.

Time expressions with に: specific points in time (clock times, days of the week, dates) need に. Relative time expressions like 今日, 明日, 来週 do NOT take に, because they already express a time relationship to "now".

で can also express cause and extent: 病気で休む (be absent because of illness), 三人で食べた (ate as a group of three). These meanings all come from the basic idea: で describes the circumstances under which something happens.
Memory aid: に is like a pin on a map — a fixed point where something exists or arrives. で is like a stage — a place where something is performed. Remember that and you'll almost always be right.
sections[].examples[].de: I read a book.
I drank water.
Let's watch a movie!
I go to school. (destination of a movement)
I live in Tokyo. (place of living/existing)
I get up at seven. (specific point in time)
I study at the library. (place of the action)
I eat with chopsticks. (tool)
Please speak in Japanese. (means/language)
There's a cat in the park. (に = it exists there, quietly)
I play in the park. (で = I'm actively doing something there)
I arrived at the station. (に = target point)

en.title: Respectful language: the basics
en.subtitle: Keigo without panic
en.intro: Keigo — the word alone makes Japanese learners shudder. It's the linguistic system that reflects social hierarchy, politeness and respect in the Japanese language. But don't panic: the basics aren't nearly as wild as their reputation suggests. At heart it's about a single principle — linguistically "raising" the person you're talking to and "lowering" yourself. Once you've internalized this concept, the rest makes logical sense. Here you'll get a relaxed introduction to the three levels of politeness, with the most important verbs and patterns you'll actually need in everyday life.
sections[].heading: The three levels
丁寧語 — the basis you already know
尊敬語 — raising the other person
謙譲語 — lowering yourself
The most important keigo pairs
Keigo in everyday life — where you'll hear it
Common beginner mistakes
sections[].text:
Japanese has three politeness registers that together make up the keigo system. You already know the first level — the です/ます-form you've been using since the first lessons. The other two levels are more specialized and are used mainly at work, with customers and in formal situations. The good part is: you don't have to master all three at once. Most Japanese people find keigo difficult themselves and make mistakes with it!
  • 丁寧語 (teineigo) — polite language: です/ます-forms. The basic level of politeness that you already know. It gets you through everyday life without any problems.
  • 尊敬語 (sonkeigo) — respectful language: linguistically "raises" the actions of the person you're talking to or of a third person. Used toward superiors, customers and older people.
  • 謙譲語 (kenjōgo) — humble language: linguistically "lowers" your own actions. You make yourself small so that the other person appears relatively bigger.

The good news first: you already master the most important level of politeness! です and ます are 丁寧語 (teineigo), "polite language". It's the standard form you use in shops, with strangers and in most everyday situations. Everything beyond that (尊敬語 and 謙譲語) is an extension for especially formal contexts.

You use respectful language when talking about the actions of others — customers, superiors, older people, people you show respect to. There are two ways to do this: first, special respectful verbs that are completely different words (いらっしゃる instead of いる). Second, the general pattern お + ます-stem + になる, which works with almost any verb. In addition, the passive form can be used as a mild respectful form — that's the simplest level and a good place to start.

You use humble language for your own actions toward people of higher status. By making yourself linguistically "smaller", you indirectly express respect for the other person. Here too there are special humble verbs (伺う instead of 行く/聞く) and a general pattern: お + ます-stem + する. Important: 謙譲語 is used only for your own actions or those of your own group (e.g. "My boss is coming" — when you're talking to a customer, you use 謙譲語 for your boss because he belongs to your group).

This table shows the most common verbs at all three levels. It's worth learning these pairs as fixed units, because they come up constantly in everyday life — at work, in shops, in formal emails and even on the train. The special keigo verbs developed historically and follow no recognizable pattern — you simply have to memorize them.
Normal尊敬語 (respectful)謙譲語 (humble)
行く / 来るいらっしゃる参る / 伺う
いるいらっしゃるおる
食べる / 飲む召し上がるいただく
言うおっしゃる申す
見るご覧になる拝見する
するなさるいたす
知っているご存じだ存じている
くれるくださる—
あげる—差し上げる
もらう—いただく

Even if you don't have to use keigo actively, you'll hear it all the time. You'll come across keigo forms in shops, restaurants, train stations and hotels. So it's worth being able to recognize the most common set phrases. Many of these sentences are so standardized that they work almost like fixed expressions — staff use them automatically without thinking about the grammatical structure.

Keigo has some typical pitfalls that even Japanese people sometimes get wrong. The following mistakes are especially common — if you avoid them, you're already ahead of many learners. The basic principle is: 尊敬語 for the actions of others, 謙譲語 for your own actions. Mix them up and you achieve the opposite of the respect you intended.
sections[].tip: Imagine a stage: 尊敬語 puts the other person on a pedestal. 謙譲語 has you step down a level yourself. Either way, the difference in height grows — and that's exactly what respect is.

The pattern お + ます-stem + になる is your wild card! It works with almost any verb: お読みになる (to read), お使いになる (to use), お待ちになる (to wait)... It lets you make verbs respectful even when there's no special respectful verb for them.
Important trap: never use 謙譲語 for other people's actions! Saying "the customer 参ります" would be a serious mistake — you'd be "lowering" the customer instead of showing respect.

For now it's perfectly enough to be confident with the です/ます-form and to recognize the most common keigo words when you hear them. You only need to use keigo actively once you work at a Japanese company or want to handle very formal situations. Most Japanese people will really appreciate it if you use the ます-form correctly at all!
sections[].examples[].de: There's a meeting tomorrow. (ます-form = polite)
That's a good idea. (です = polite)
Excuse me, where is the station? (polite everyday language)
The teacher has already gone home. (passive form as respect)
The company president is here. (いらっしゃる = to be/go/come, respectful)
What would you like to eat/drink? (召し上がる = to eat/drink, respectful)
I will visit you tomorrow. (伺う = to go/ask, humble)
I have looked at the documents. (拝見する = to see, humble)
I will come/go. (参る = to go/come, humble)
Welcome! (You'll hear this in every shop and restaurant.)
Please wait a moment.
Would this be all right for you? (よろしい = polite いい)
Wrong! 申す is humble — you'd be lowering the teacher.
Right! おっしゃる is respectful — the teacher is raised.
Wrong! いらっしゃる is respectful language — you'd be raising yourself.

en.title: ～ようにする & ～ようになる
en.subtitle: Habits and changes
en.intro: Japanese has two elegant constructions for talking about change: ようにする expresses a conscious effort to change something — "I make sure that..." — while ようになる describes a change that has come about naturally — "It has come to the point that...". The two make a perfect pair: ようにする is the intention, ようになる is the result. Once you understand the difference, you can talk about personal growth, habits and life changes in Japanese with surprising nuance.
sections[].heading: ようにする — conscious effort
ようになる — natural change
The pair compared
Negation: ～ないようにする / ～なくなる
sections[].text: ようにする expresses that you make a conscious effort to keep up or change a certain behavior. It's not about doing something once, but about a lasting effort or a new habit. In English it's best translated as "I make sure that..." or "I try to ...".

ようになる describes a change that has come about naturally — an ability you've acquired or a state that has developed. In English: "It has come about that..." or "I can now...". Unlike with ようにする, active effort isn't in the foreground here — the change simply happened.
At its core the difference is simple: ようにする = intention (I make an effort), ようになる = result (it came about). Often both are told in one story: first the effort, then the result.

To express that you no longer do something or that you make sure not to do something, there are two important forms. ～ないようにする = "I make sure NOT to do it." ～なくなる = "It has come about that I no longer do it." The negation follows the same intention-vs-result logic.
sections[].tip: ようにしている (progressive form) = an ongoing habit. ようにした (past) = you decided to do something from now on.
～なくなる is often surprisingly emotional: 笑わなくなった (he doesn't laugh anymore), 話さなくなった (she doesn't talk to me anymore) — sentences like these can tell a whole story.
sections[].examples[].de: I make sure to eat vegetables every day.
I try to go to bed as early as possible.
Please make sure not to be late.
I can speak a little Japanese now. (It developed over time.)
My child eats green peppers now. (Didn't before, does now.)
Lately I've been able to sleep well. (Couldn't before.)
I decided to practice every day. (intention)
Thanks to that, I can now play well. (result)
I make sure not to eat sweets. (intention)
I make sure not to drink alcohol.
Lately I've stopped drinking coffee. (It just happened that way.)

en.title: ～てしまう (ちゃう)
en.subtitle: Oops — that wasn't on purpose
en.intro: ～てしまう is one of the most versatile and emotional forms in Japanese. Depending on context, it expresses regret, completion or unintended actions. In colloquial speech it's shortened to ～ちゃう (after て) or ～じゃう (after で) — a form you'll hear constantly in manga, anime and everyday life. Once you understand ～てしまう, a whole world of Japanese nuance opens up.
sections[].heading: Regret & unintentional actions
Completion — "totally done"
Colloquial: ～ちゃう / ～じゃう
sections[].text: The most common use of ～てしまう: something happened that you didn't want or regret. In English: "Unfortunately I...", "I ended up...", "I stupidly...". The speaker signals that the result was unwanted.

～てしまう can also express that an action is completely finished — often faster or more thoroughly than expected. There's no regret here, but rather surprise or emphasis. In English: "ate it all up", "already finished reading", "used it all up".

In spoken language ～てしまう is almost always shortened to ～ちゃう. After the で-form it becomes ～じゃう. The conjugation follows the godan verb (u-verb) pattern: ちゃう → ちゃった (past), ちゃって (て-form). These forms are extremely common and important to recognize!
sections[].tip: Whether regret or completion is meant depends on context. ケーキを食べてしまった can mean either: "I ate the whole cake" OR "Unfortunately I ate it (even though I shouldn't have)."
In formal situations: ～てしまう. In everyday life with friends: ～ちゃう. In manga and anime: almost always ～ちゃう.
sections[].examples[].de: I stupidly forgot my wallet.
I accidentally deleted an important file.
I dropped the cake (and it was a special one, too).
I read this whole book in one day.
I've already finished all my homework.
I ate the whole cake.
Forgot it. (= 忘れてしまった)
Ate it all. (= 食べてしまった)
It broke. (= 壊れてしまった)
Drank it all. (飲んでしまった → 飲んじゃった, で→じゃ)

en.title: ～ばかり の使い方
en.subtitle: Only just, always, nothing but
en.intro: ばかり is a small word with a big effect. Depending on context and verb form, it means "only just" (time), "always" (habit) or "nothing but" (exclusivity). It's one of those words that turn up all the time and whose nuances become clear naturally over time. Here you get a clear overview of the three main meanings.
sections[].heading: ～たばかり — Only just
～てばかり / ～ばかり + verb — Nothing but
～ばかりか / ～ばかりでなく — Not only
～ばかりに — Just because
sections[].text: Verb た-form + ばかり expresses that an action has only just happened: the memory is still fresh, the situation still new. In English: "I've only just...", "It hasn't been long since...". Important: "only just" is subjective; it can be minutes or weeks, as long as it still feels fresh to the speaker.

～てばかりいる (verb て + ばかり + いる) expresses that someone does nothing but one thing, often with a slight reproach. Noun + ばかり + verb means "nothing but" that noun. In English: "All you ever do is...", "He eats nothing but...".
～ばかりか or ～ばかりでなく means "not only ... but also". It stresses that something goes beyond what was expected: an escalation in a list. More formal and emphatic than ～だけでなく.
～ばかりに means "just because..." / "simply because...": it expresses that a single reason led to a (usually negative) result. In English: "Just because I..." or "All because...".
sections[].tip: This usage almost always has a slightly reproachful or annoyed tone.
ばかりに almost always has a note of regret: "If only that one thing had been different..."
sections[].examples[].de: I've only just come to Japan.
I only just ate, but I'm already hungry again.
She's only just moved here.
Stop playing games all the time and study!
He eats nothing but sweets.
Stop complaining all the time.
He can speak not only English but also Chinese.
Not only is it raining, but the wind has picked up too.
I got scolded just because I said one word too many.
I lost out just because I didn't know.

en.title: ～ことにする & ～ことになる
en.subtitle: Decisions and fate
en.intro: Who made the decision? That question is at the heart of the difference between ことにする and ことになる. One expresses a personal, active decision — "I've decided...". The other describes an outcome that came about, often without an identifiable decision-maker — "It was decided that..." or "It turned out that...". Together they're a powerful pair for talking about decisions, fate and turning points in life.
sections[].heading: ことにする — I decide
ことになる — it comes about
ことにしている — a fixed habit
ことにする vs ようにする — decision vs habit
Comparison: する vs なる
sections[].text: Verb (dictionary form/ない-form) + ことにする expresses a personal, conscious decision. The speaker has decided to do or not to do something. In English: "I've decided to ...", "I'm choosing to ...".

Verb (dictionary form/ない-form) + ことになる describes an outcome or decision that has come about — without the speaker as the active decision-maker. Typical for company decisions, strokes of fate, or situations where "it was decided" rather than "I decided".
ことにしている (progressive form) expresses a fixed habit or rule that you've set for yourself and follow consistently. It's stronger than ようにしている, because it's a conscious rule and not just an effort.

Both forms sound similar but express something fundamentally different:
  • ことにする → the moment of decision: "I've decided!" — a clean break.
  • ようにする → the ongoing effort: "I make sure..." — a continuous process.
ことにする marks the point at which you commit. ようにする describes the daily discipline of sticking with something. In real life a ことにする is often followed by a ようにしている — first the decision, then putting it into practice.

The key question is always: Who made the decision?
  • ことにする → I decided (active, personal)
  • ことになる → IT came about (passive, from outside)
  • ことにしている → I stick to this rule (fixed habit)
  • ことになっている → It's the rule/regulation that... (general norm)
sections[].tip: ことになる is also the Japanese way of softening unpleasant news: instead of "I've been transferred" you say "It has turned out that I'm being transferred" — the responsibility gets blurred.
ことにする sounds more resolute — like drawing a line under a discussion. ようにする sounds like a process that takes discipline. In everyday life the two are often combined: 「甘いものを食べないことにして、毎日野菜を食べるようにしている。」
sections[].examples[].de: I've decided to go running every morning starting next month.
I'm deciding not to drink any alcohol today.
I've decided to study abroad.
It's been decided that I'll be transferred to Osaka next month.
It was decided to postpone the meeting until next week.
In the end, it came to a divorce.
I make it a rule to always eat breakfast.
I make it a rule not to work on Sundays.
I've decided to exercise every day. (the moment of decision)
I make sure to exercise every day. (the ongoing effort)
I've decided not to eat sweets anymore. (a clean break — from now on!)
In Japan it's customary to take off your shoes.
At the company, the rule is not to work overtime.
Since it's been decided that I'll be transferred, I'm moving.

en.title: ～わけ
en.subtitle: The logical conclusion
en.intro: わけ is one of the most nuanced words in Japanese. Literally it means "reason" or "logical conclusion", but in practice it takes on quite different meanings depending on the construction. ～わけだ, ～わけがない and ～わけにはいかない are three core patterns that are tested on the JLPT from N3 up and come up constantly in everyday life. Once you understand わけ, you can express logical connections, impossibilities and social constraints elegantly.
sections[].heading: わけだ — That explains everything!
わけがない — No way!
わけにはいかない — I can't (allow myself to)
わけではない — Not necessarily
sections[].text: わけだ expresses that something is a logical consequence: "No wonder...", "That explains why...", "So that means...". The speaker draws a conclusion from known facts.
わけがない expresses that something is logically impossible or simply cannot be true. Stronger than ～はずがない. In English: "There's no way that...", "Absolutely not!" The speaker firmly rejects something.

わけにはいかない expresses that you can't do something for social, moral or practical reasons, even if you might want to. It's about outside circumstances, responsibility or social expectations. In English: "I can't afford to ...".
わけではない is a partial negation: "It's not that...", "That doesn't mean...". You use it to correct a wrong assumption without contradicting completely. Softer than わけがない.
sections[].tip: In casual speech it's often shortened to わけない (without が). "そんなの無理に決まってる！" has a similar meaning, but わけがない sounds more logical and less emotional.
わけではない = "not necessarily" (partial negation). わけがない = "no way" (total negation). The difference is crucial!
sections[].examples[].de: He lived in Japan for 10 years? No wonder his Japanese is so good!
The trains aren't running? Then it makes sense that we'll be late.
You walked all day? No wonder you're tired.
There's no way it could be that easy!
There's no way he's the culprit.
There's no way you didn't know that!
I have an exam, so I can't afford to goof around.
Since I promised, I can't just quit.
I can't possibly say something like that to my boss.
It's not that I dislike it, but today is a bit...
I'm not especially good at Japanese, but I can hold everyday conversations.

en.title: ～として・～にとって・～によって
en.subtitle: Roles, perspectives, and "depending on" or means
en.intro: Japanese can express very precisely from which perspective or in which role someone does or experiences something. ～として means "as" (in a particular capacity), ～にとって "for" (from the point of view of), and ～によって marks, depending on context, a means, a cause or differences. At first glance these expressions sound similarly matter-of-fact, but they highlight different aspects of a situation.
sections[].heading: として — "As" (in a role)
にとって — "For" (from the point of view of)
によって — "Depending on", "through", "by"
The difference in practice
sections[].text: として is attached to a noun and means "as" or "in the capacity of". It defines the role, function or capacity in which someone acts or something is viewed.
にとって is attached to a noun (usually a person or group) and means "for" or "from the point of view of". It expresses a subjective evaluation from that person's perspective.

によって is more versatile than the other two patterns. It can mark differences depending on the case, a means or cause, and, in the passive, the agent. For everyday use, the meaning "depending on ..." is especially important.

The core: として = objective role (what am I?), にとって = subjective perspective (how do I see it?), によって = condition, means or agent (through what / depending on what / by whom?). You can describe the same situation from different angles, but the patterns answer different questions.
sections[].tip: にとって always comes before an evaluation (good/bad/important/difficult...). It introduces: "From THIS perspective, it's LIKE THIS."
Remember these as safe starting points: 人によって = depending on the person, ～によって作られた = made by ..., ～によって変わる = changes through/depending on ...
sections[].examples[].de: As your friend, I'm warning you.
Tokyo has developed as the capital.
I came to Japan as an exchange student.
For me, family is the most important thing.
This movie is too scary for children.
Things that are obvious to Japanese people can seem strange to foreigners.
The way people think differs from person to person.
This song is loved by many people.
The trains were stopped by the typhoon.
As a teacher, I guide my students. (My role)
For a teacher, the students' growth is the greatest joy. (My perspective)
Teaching styles differ depending on the teacher. (The difference depends on who it is)
He's famous as an actor. (In that role)

en.title: ～一方で & ～反面
en.subtitle: Two sides of the same coin
en.intro: Life is full of contradictions, and Japanese has elegant tools to express them. ～一方で (ippō de) and ～反面 (hanmen) both show a contrast ("on the one hand... on the other hand..."), but with different nuances. ～一方で presents facts that exist side by side, while ～反面 highlights the unexpected flip side of a characteristic. Both are typical N2 structures that are everywhere in newspaper articles, reports and formal language.
sections[].heading: 一方で — On the other hand, at the same time
一方だ — Further and further in one direction
反面 — The flip side
sections[].text: 一方(で) connects two contrasting or parallel facts. It can mean "on the other hand", "meanwhile" or "at the same time". The contrast doesn't have to be negative; two different aspects can simply be placed side by side.

一方だ (ippō da) at the end of a sentence has a completely different meaning: a development keeps going further in one direction without stopping. Often negative or worried. In English: "It keeps getting worse", "There's no end to it".

反面 highlights the unexpected or opposite side of a characteristic of the same thing or person. It's always a contrast within one subject, not between two different things. In English: "On the other hand..." or "But at the same time...".
sections[].tip: 一方で comes after: verb dictionary form, い-adjective, な-adjective + な/である, noun + の/である.
一方で = can compare different subjects. 反面 = always the same subject with two opposite characteristics.
sections[].examples[].de: While the population of urban areas keeps growing, rural areas are becoming depopulated.
He's strict, but at the same time he takes very good care of people.
Social media is convenient, but on the other hand there are privacy issues.
Prices just keep rising.
Environmental problems keep getting worse.
My debts just keep growing, and there's nothing I can do about it.
She's kind, but on the other hand she has a stubborn side.
The countryside is quiet, but shopping is inconvenient.
This job pays well, but on the flip side it's also very stressful.

en.title: ～に対して & ～について
en.subtitle: Toward and about
en.intro: When you talk about someone or something, perspective matters: are you directing your action toward someone (に対して), or are you talking about a topic (について)? These two expressions are often confused, but the difference is fundamental. に対して is directed at a target or sets up a contrast. について marks a topic that is being talked or thought about.
sections[].heading: に対して — Toward, in contrast to
について — About, regarding
The key difference
sections[].text: に対して has two main meanings: 1) "toward": an action or attitude directed at someone/something. 2) "in contrast to": a direct contrast between two things. In factual language, the reading "with regard to / in response to" also comes up often.
について marks a topic that you talk, think, write or give information about. In English: "about", "regarding", "concerning". More neutral and topic-oriented than に対して.
について = topic (what are we talking about?). に対して = target/counterpart (who or what is something directed at?). A simple test: if you'd say "about" in English → について. If you'd say "toward" → に対して.
sections[].tip: Related forms: に関して (more formal than について), に対する + noun (used attributively: "the attitude toward...").
sections[].examples[].de: The teacher is strict toward the students.
There were objections to his way of doing things.
While the average life expectancy for men is 81, for women it's 87.
He answered that question immediately.
I'm doing research on Japanese culture.
Let's talk about this problem.
I don't know anything about her.
To think about environmental problems. (Topic)
To take action against environmental problems. (Target of an action)
I have a question about Japanese. (Topic of the question)

en.title: ～ものだ & ～ものではない
en.subtitle: That's just how it is
en.intro: もの (often shortened to もん) is one of the most versatile words in Japanese grammar. Depending on the construction, it expresses nostalgia, general truths, social expectations or emotional exclamations. The different uses feel unrelated at first, but they share a core: ものだ links personal experience with universal truths or norms.
sections[].heading: ものだ — Nostalgia: "It used to be like this..."
ものだ — General truth: "That's just how it is"
ものではない — That's not done
ものだから — Excuse: "Because, you see..."
sections[].text: Verb た-form + ものだ expresses nostalgic memories: things you used to do regularly. In English: "I often used to...", "Back then we would always...".
Verb dictionary form / adjective + ものだ expresses a general truth or law of nature. In English: "That's just the way it is", "It's in the nature of things that...".
ものではない expresses a social norm or expectation: something you shouldn't do. It's not a strict prohibition, more a "that's not proper" or "one doesn't do that". Typical of advice from older people.
ものだから (colloquially もんだから) is used as an excuse or explanation. It implies: "I couldn't help it, because that's how things were." In English: "It's just that...", "Because, you see...".
sections[].tip: This form has a warm, sentimental sound. You use it for fond or meaningful memories.
ものではない sounds like wise advice, not like an order. Typical context: grandparents to grandchildren, teachers to students, mentor to mentee.
sections[].examples[].de: As a child, I often used to play in this park.
I used to study until late at night.
Grandma used to sing this song a lot.
Everyone makes mistakes — that's just human nature.
Time really flies!
Parents just worry — that's how it is.
You shouldn't speak ill of others.
You shouldn't waste food.
You shouldn't lie.
I was late because, you see, the train was delayed.
It suddenly started raining, you see, so I bought an umbrella.

en.title: です & ます
en.subtitle: Polite from the start
en.intro: Japanese has politeness levels built right in — and the good news is that the basic level isn't hard at all. With です and ます you're well equipped for the vast majority of situations. Whether in a shop, at the train station, at the doctor's or with new acquaintances: so-called "teineigo" (丁寧語, polite language) is the standard every learner of Japanese should master first. Everything else builds on it.
sections[].heading: です — The polite "is"
ます — The polite verb ending
The four basic forms
です in every tense
When does Japan go casual?
sections[].text: です (desu) comes at the end of the sentence after nouns and な-adjectives. It makes the sentence polite and means roughly "is/am/are". In casual speech, だ (da) is used instead — but as a learner you're always on the safe side with です. Think of it as the necktie of the Japanese sentence: you can leave it off when the situation is relaxed, but with it you're always appropriately dressed.

ます (masu) is attached to the verb stem (also called the "ます-stem") and makes any verb polite. Almost all textbooks start with the ます-form because it works everywhere. Finding the verb stem is easy: with る-verbs you drop る (食べる → 食べ); with う-verbs you change the ending to the い-row (行く → 行き, 話す → 話し, 飲む → 飲み).
The ます-form can easily be turned into four forms. The system is refreshingly regular — no exceptions, no irregular forms. Once you have the verb stem, everything works like a building kit:
Just like ます, です has its four forms too. They follow the same pattern and apply equally to nouns and な-adjectives:

The so-called plain form (also called the "short form" or "dictionary form") is used among close friends, in the family, in diaries and — very importantly — in subordinate clauses. So the plain form is by no means rude; it's simply intimate. But as a beginner, the ます/です-form is your safe harbor. With it, you can't go wrong anywhere. Better too polite than too casual — Japanese people appreciate that.
sections[].tip: With い-adjectives, です is optional and purely for politeness — it doesn't change the grammar. 大きいです = 大きい + politeness. You do NOT say 大きいだ — that would be redundant and wrong.
The two most important irregular verbs in the ます-form: する → します and くる (来る) → きます. All する-verbs follow the same pattern: 勉強する → 勉強します, 運動する → 運動します.
Note: Japanese grammar doesn't distinguish between present and future. 食べます means both "I eat" and "I will eat" — context takes care of the rest.

Remember: you still need the plain form — it shows up constantly in subordinate clauses (と思う, から, のに...), quotations and conditionals. So you'll be learning it soon anyway, even if you stick with ます/です in the main clause!
sections[].examples[].de: I'm a student.
This is a book.
It's quiet. (な-adjective + です)
I eat.
I study Japanese.
I run every day.
eat / will eat (present/future, polite)
don't eat (negative, polite)
ate (past, polite)
I didn't eat yesterday. (past + negative)
is a student (present, polite)
is not a student (negative, polite)
was a student (past, polite)
I wasn't a student. (past + negative)
to eat (casual → polite)
expensive (casual → polite)
student (casual → polite)

en.title: ～てこそ & ～からこそ
en.subtitle: Precisely because — only then
en.intro: こそ is an emphasis particle that stresses: "THAT's exactly it!" Combined as てこそ and からこそ, it forms two powerful expressions that play a special role in Japanese. ～てこそ says: "Only when you do THIS does the result follow." ～からこそ says: "PRECISELY BECAUSE it's like this..." Both express a strong conviction and are typical of speeches, essays and emotional statements.
sections[].heading: こそ — The emphasis particle
てこそ — Only when...
からこそ — Precisely because
Comparison & nuances
sections[].text: Before we look at the combinations, a quick word about こそ on its own: it highlights a word or phrase as the decisive point. In English: "EXACTLY that", "THAT in particular". You may already know it from set phrases.
Verb て-form + こそ expresses that something gets its true meaning or full value only through a particular action. In English: "Only when you..., then..." or "Only by...".
