からこそ expresses a reason that is especially emphasized: "PRECISELY BECAUSE it's like this...". It stresses that the reason isn't trivial but the decisive factor. Often used in emotional or persuasive contexts.

Both expressions add emphasis, but in different ways:
  • てこそ → emphasizes the precondition: "Only WHEN you do X, THEN Y"
  • からこそ → emphasizes the reason: "PRECISELY BECAUSE X, Y"
てこそ looks forward (condition → result), からこそ looks back (reason → consequence).
sections[].tip: てこそ often has a philosophical or motivating tone. Typical of life lessons, speeches and inspiring texts.
こそ expressions give your Japanese depth and persuasive power. They're the linguistic equivalent of a "mic drop" moment.
sections[].examples[].de: The pleasure is all MINE.
THIS time I'm going to pass!
Are YOU all right, though? (Concern for the other person, not for yourself.)
Only by failing can you grow.
It only means something if you do it yourself.
Only once you've been through hardship do you understand true joy.
It's PRECISELY BECAUSE I like you that I'm telling you this straight.
It's PRECISELY BECAUSE it's hard that it's rewarding.
It's PRECISELY BECAUSE I have experience that I can say this.
Only THROUGH practice can you get good. (Condition)
It's PRECISELY BECAUSE I practiced every day that I got good. (Reason)

en.title: ～てもいい / ～てはいけない
en.subtitle: Permission & prohibition
en.intro: May I? You may not! Do I have to? — Three of the most common questions in everyday life, and Japanese has elegant constructions for them. ～てもいい gives the green light, ～てはいけない shows the red card, and ～なくてもいい takes the pressure off. These three forms belong to the absolute basics and turn up in practically every everyday situation — from the classroom to the office to the restaurant. If you master them, you can ask for permission, understand rules and set limits politely. Especially important: in Japanese the difference between "you must not" and "you don't have to" is crystal clear, because each has its own form.
sections[].heading: ～てもいい — Permission: "You may..."
～てはいけない / ～てはだめ — Prohibition: "You must not..."
～なくてもいい — Not necessary: "You don't have to..."
sections[].text: The て-form + もいい expresses permission: "It's okay if you...", "You may...", "You can...". As a question (～てもいいですか) it becomes a polite request for permission. The construction couldn't be simpler: take the て-form of the verb and attach もいい (or, more politely, もいいですか). In formal contexts いい can be replaced with よろしい.

The て-form + はいけない (or はだめ) expresses a prohibition: "You must not...", "You're not allowed to...". はいけない is the neutral to formal variant and is used in rules, regulations and by authority figures. はだめ is the colloquial variant — more relaxed, but just as firm. In spoken language ては is often shortened to ちゃ (after a て-sound) or じゃ (after a で-sound): 食べちゃだめ, 飲んじゃだめ.

The ない-form (without い) + くてもいい means: "You don't have to...", "It's not necessary to..." This is a crucial difference from ～てはいけない! てはいけない = prohibition (you must not), なくてもいい = no obligation (you don't have to, but you may). Don't confuse "you must not" with "you don't have to" — in Japanese the two forms are kept strictly apart. If you master the difference, you'll avoid embarrassing misunderstandings.
sections[].tip: In very formal situations you replace いい with よろしい: 質問してもよろしいでしょうか (May I ask a question?). This sounds much more respectful and is used with superiors or customers.

～てはいけない is a real prohibition (rule/regulation), while ～ないでください is a polite request. "Smoking is not allowed here" (てはいけない) vs. "Please don't smoke here" (ないでください) — the difference between law and politeness.
Compare: 食べてはいけない = "You must not eat!" (prohibition) vs. 食べなくてもいい = "You don't have to eat." (no obligation, but allowed). This difference is a popular trap on the JLPT!
sections[].examples[].de: May I sit here?
Feel free to take photos.
Is it okay if I don't come tomorrow?
Smoking is not allowed here.
You may not use a dictionary during the exam.
You mustn't run!
You don't have to come early tomorrow. (But you can if you want.)
You don't have to eat it all.
You don't have to push yourself.

en.title: ～ばかりか / ～のみならず
en.subtitle: Not only... but also
en.intro: When you want to say that something goes beyond what was expected ("Not only X, but even Y!"), you need ～ばかりか or ～のみならず. Both express an escalation, but in different registers. ～ばかりか is emphatic, often with a touch of surprise, and fits both conversation and writing, while ～のみならず is at home in newspaper articles and speeches. Together with the neutral ～だけでなく they form a team of three that you can use depending on the situation.
sections[].heading: ～ばかりか — Not only X, but even Y
～のみならず — A formal "not only..."
Comparison: ばかりか vs のみならず vs だけでなく
sections[].text: ～ばかりか stresses a surprising escalation: not only the one thing, but something even stronger on top. It's neutral to slightly elevated; in casual conversation people tend to say だけじゃなくて. Formation: verb / i-adjective / na-adjective (+ な/である) / noun + ばかりか. The second clause often contains さらに, も or even まで to underline the escalation.

～のみならず is the formal, written variant of ～ばかりか. You find it in news articles, academic texts and official speeches. Formation: noun / verb (dictionary form) + のみならず. The meaning is identical to ばかりか, but the tone is noticeably more elevated.

All three mean "not only... but also", but they differ in register and nuance:
  • だけでなく → Neutral, fits anywhere. The safe default choice.
  • ばかりか → Neutral to slightly elevated. Stresses surprise and escalation: "Not only that, but even THAT!"
  • のみならず → Formal/written. Matter-of-fact, objective; typical of news and essays.
sections[].tip: ばかりか can also express negative escalation: 「遅刻したばかりか、宿題も忘れた。」(Not only was he late, he even forgot his homework.) The escalation works in both directions.
のみならず sounds over the top and stiff in everyday conversation; use it only in written or formal contexts. In a conversation among friends, だけじゃなくて would be more natural.
Rule of thumb for the JLPT: if the question contains a formal text, のみならず is often the right answer. For a surprising or critical escalation, ばかりか fits. And when in doubt, だけでなく always works.
sections[].examples[].de: He speaks not only English but also French.
Not only is it raining, but the wind has even picked up.
This restaurant is not only cheap, the food is good too.
This issue is being debated not only in Japan but all over the world.
She excels not only in her studies but also in sports.
Environmental pollution affects not only health but also the economy.
He knows not only Japanese but also Chinese. (Neutral)
Not only are his grades bad, he even skips class. (Escalation!)
Our school enjoys a high reputation not only at home but also abroad. (Formal)

en.title: ～ばいい / ～たらいい
en.subtitle: Giving advice
en.intro: What on earth should I do? — One of the most common questions in everyday life. Japanese offers an elegant duo for it: ～ばいい and ～たらいい. At heart both mean "It would be good if you...", but they differ in nuance and warmth. One sounds a little more matter-of-fact and direct, the other softer and more like a recommendation. Once you master these two forms, you can give advice that sounds neither too pushy nor too vague — an art that is especially valued in polite Japan.
sections[].heading: ばいい — clear advice
たらいい — gentle suggestion
Negative advice: ～なければいい / ～なかったらいい
Comparison: ばいい vs たらいい vs ほうがいい
sections[].text: Verb ば-form + いい expresses direct, clear advice: "You just need to do X, and it'll be fine." It has a slightly matter-of-fact tone and tells the other person concretely what the solution is.
Verb たら-form + いい is softer advice that sounds more like a recommendation. It sounds like "How about ...?" or "It would be good if you...". Often with よ at the end for a friendly tone.
You can also advise someone not to do something: ～なければいい or ～なかったらいい. In English: "Just don't do it" or "It would be better if you didn't."

Three ways to give advice — in increasing strength:
  • たらいい → gentle suggestion: "How about...?"
  • ばいい → clear advice: "You just need to..."
  • ほうがいい → urgent advice: "You'd better..."
sections[].tip: ばいい can also be used as a question: どうすればいい？ — "What should I do?" That's one of the most common phrases in Japanese.
のに at the end adds regret: "It would be good IF you did it... (but unfortunately you don't)."
sections[].examples[].de: If you don't understand, just ask the teacher.
If you're hot, just turn on the air conditioner.
If you don't have time, just take a taxi.
If you're tired, go ahead and rest a little.
If you go to Japan, you should see Kyoto.
Why don't you try asking him directly?
If you don't want to, just don't go.
It would be good if you didn't worry so much.
You just have to stop eating too much.
You could go to the doctor. (gentle)
Just go to the doctor. (clear)
You really should go to the doctor. (urgent)

en.title: ～はずだ / ～はずがない
en.subtitle: Expectations and impossibility
en.intro: Sometimes you're pretty sure about something — not because you've seen it, but because logically it MUST be so. And sometimes you're just as sure that something absolutely CANNOT be. はず is the Japanese tool for this kind of logical conclusion. ～はずだ says: "It should really be that way." ～はずがない says: "There's no way that can be!" Between these two extremes lies はずだった — "It was supposed to be that way, but..." A trio of expectation that's indispensable in everyday life.
sections[].heading: はずだ — logical expectation
はずがない — impossible!
はずだった — disappointed expectation
sections[].text: Verb / adjective / noun + はずだ expresses a well-founded expectation: you have good reasons to assume that something is the case. In English: "It should...", "It ought to..." It's stronger than "maybe" but weaker than a fact.
はずがない expresses a strong conviction that something is impossible. In English: "That can't be!", "That's impossible!" Often in emotional contexts — surprise, indignation, disbelief.
はずだった (past) describes an expectation that didn't come true. In English: "It should have...", "It was planned that..." There's always a slight sense of disappointment.
sections[].tip: はずがない is emotionally stronger than the neutral ないはずだ (expecting that it isn't so). はずがない expresses personal conviction and indignation.
sections[].examples[].de: He should have arrived by now.
I made a reservation, so there should be seats.
This road should be the right one.
That person can't possibly be the culprit!
There's no way you can't solve such an easy problem.
He would never lie. (That can't be.)
It was supposed to arrive today, but it still hasn't come.
It was supposed to be easy, but it was really hard.
We were supposed to meet at 6, but he didn't come.

en.title: ～ように / ～ために
en.subtitle: Expressing purpose and goals
en.intro: Why are you doing that? — A fundamental question, and Japanese offers two elegant answers: ために and ように. Both express a purpose, but in fundamentally different ways. ために is direct and goal-oriented: "I do X IN ORDER TO achieve Y." ように is more indirect: "I do X SO THAT Y becomes possible." The difference lies in control — can you influence the goal directly, or are you hoping it will come about? This distinction is typically Japanese and reveals a lot about how the language thinks.
sections[].heading: ために — direct goal
ように — indirect goal / wish
When ために, when ように?
sections[].text: Verb dictionary form / noun + の + ために expresses a direct, conscious purpose. The subject has full control over the action. In English: "in order to ...", "for ...".
Verb dictionary form (often potential form or ない-form) + ように expresses an indirect purpose. The result isn't entirely in the speaker's hands. In English: "so that ...", "in such a way that ...".

The rule of thumb is surprisingly simple:
  • ために → volitional verbs (study, buy, go): you can control the goal directly
  • ように → non-volitional verbs, potential form, ない-form: the result can't be controlled directly
sections[].tip: ために is used with volitional verbs — verbs where the subject acts deliberately.
With the potential form (～できる, ～える) and negative forms (～ない) you almost always use ように, not ために.
sections[].examples[].de: I came to Japan to study Japanese.
I studied a lot to pass the exam.
I run every day for my health.
I wrote it in my planner so that I wouldn't forget.
I spoke loudly so that people could hear me.
I explained it so that even a child could understand.
I study to get into university. (direct goal)
I study so that I CAN get into university. (hope)
I keep warm so that I don't catch a cold. (not controllable)

en.title: ～にしては / ～わりに
en.subtitle: Expectations & contradictions
en.intro: People have expectations, and reality constantly departs from them. Japanese has two elegant constructions for expressing exactly this gap: ～にしては and ～わりに. At their core, both say: "I'd actually have expected X, but Y is the case." The difference lies in the degree of surprise and in the nuance. にしては stresses the unexpected more strongly; it's almost always surprising. わりに is more neutral and expresses a mismatch instead. Once you master these two forms, you can talk with nuance about expectations, disappointments and pleasant surprises, a skill that's needed on the JLPT N3 and in everyday life alike.
sections[].heading: ～にしては — "For a.../Considering that..."
～わりに(は) — "Relative to.../Although..."
Comparison: にしては vs わりに
sections[].text: Noun / verb (普通形) + にしては expresses that the result contradicts the expectation. You know what would normally be expected and notice that reality looks different. In English: "For a...", "Considering that...". Crucially, にしては always implies that the result is surprising: it clearly deviates from the norm. The surprise can be positive or negative.

Noun の / な-adj. な / い-adj. / verb (普通形) + わりに(は) expresses a mismatch: the result isn't in the expected proportion to the premise. In English: "Relative to...", "Although..., still...". Unlike with にしては, the surprise doesn't have to be as strong. わりに rather describes a proportional deviation: you expect A to lead to B, but the result is out of proportion. わりに can express both positive and negative deviations.

Both express a deviation from expectation, but with a different nuance:
  • にしては → Strong surprise: "For X, the result is unexpected!" Uses a category or characteristic as the yardstick.
  • わりに → Proportional mismatch: "Relative to X, Y doesn't add up." More matter-of-fact, less surprised.
An example makes the difference clear: "That's good for a beginner" (にしては — surprising!) vs. "Although he practices a lot, he isn't that good" (わりに — mismatch).
sections[].tip: にしては always presupposes a clear yardstick: "For X (= the yardstick), Y is surprising." Without a recognizable yardstick, the sentence sounds unnatural.
Rule of thumb: if you want to say "Wow, I didn't expect that!", use にしては. If you mean something more like "Hmm, that doesn't add up", use わりに.
sections[].examples[].de: For a child, you know an amazing amount.
For someone who's lived in Japan for 5 years, his Japanese isn't very good.
For a first try, you did well.
This restaurant is tasty for the price. (= cheap and still good)
Even though I studied hard, my grades didn't go up.
Even though he says he's busy, he goes out a lot.
For something so cheap, the quality is good. (= surprisingly good!)
Considering the low price, the quality is good. (= a matter-of-fact observation)
He looks young for his age. (= surprise at his appearance)

en.title: ～べき / ～べきではない
en.subtitle: Should / Should not
en.intro: "You should do that", but how strong is that "should"? Japanese has ～べき for it, and it's no gentle suggestion. ～べき expresses a strong moral or logical conviction: "That's the right thing." It sits between the gentle ～ほうがいい (friendly advice) and the strict ～なければならない (external obligation). When someone uses べき, they mean it: it's about principles, responsibility and what you feel is right.
sections[].heading: ～べきだ — You should...
～べきではない — You shouldn't...
Comparison: べき vs ほうがいい vs なければならない
sections[].text: Verb (dictionary form) + べきだ expresses a strong moral or logical recommendation. It's not a friendly tip but a firm conviction: "That's the right thing!" Formation: verb dictionary form + べきだ. Important exception: with する there are two forms, するべき and すべき (somewhat more formal). べき isn't used for trivial everyday decisions; it's always about something meaningful.

Verb (dictionary form) + べきではない expresses a strong negative recommendation: "You really shouldn't do that." In formal contexts べきではない is preferred; in casual speech you also hear べきじゃない. Note: the negation goes on べき, not on the verb, so it's 行くべきではない (not: 行かないべき).

All three express a kind of "should", but their strength and tone differ considerably:
  • ～ほうがいい → Gentle advice, a friendly suggestion: "It would be better if you...", no pressure.
  • ～べきだ → Strong moral/logical conviction: "You should..."; the speaker is convinced it's the right thing.
  • ～なければならない → External obligation, rule or necessity: "You must..."; there's no choice.
sections[].tip: べき comes from the classical Japanese auxiliary verb べし and therefore sounds somewhat elevated. In modern casual speech you also hear べきだよ or べきじゃない, but in essays and speeches べきだ / べきである is the standard form.
Watch the word order: it's 食べるべきではない (shouldn't eat), NOT 食べないべきだ. The negation applies to べき, not to the verb before it.
べき is inappropriate for mundane everyday things: 「傘を持っていくべきだ」 sounds exaggerated; ほうがいい fits better there. Save べき for topics with moral weight: honesty, responsibility, social duties.
sections[].examples[].de: Students should study every day. (Strong conviction)
You should keep your promises. (Moral principle)
You should decide important things for yourself.
You shouldn't reveal other people's secrets.
You shouldn't fight in front of children.
You shouldn't give up so easily.
You should eat your vegetables. (Friendly advice among friends)
Politicians should listen to the voice of the people. (Strong conviction)
You have to pay taxes. (Legal obligation — no choice)

en.title: ～きり / ～っぱなし
en.subtitle: Ever since / Left as is
en.intro: Some situations simply don't change, and some things are just left the way they are. Japanese has two expressive constructions for exactly these situations: ～きり (also ～っきり) describes that nothing more has happened since a certain moment: "Since then... nothing." ～っぱなし describes that something was left in a certain state, often carelessly or thoughtlessly. Together with the familiar ～ばかり they form a trio that covers different facets of "only that / still / left as is". These forms give Japanese an emotional depth that English often needs a whole paraphrase to express.
sections[].heading: ～きり / ～っきり — "Only.../Ever since..."
～っぱなし — "Just left as is..."
Comparison: きり vs っぱなし vs ばかり
sections[].text: Verb た-form + きり (or っきり) expresses that nothing more has happened since a certain action. The situation hasn't changed since then. In English: "Since...", "... and never again", "Only...". きり emphasizes finality or the absence of an expected change. With nouns and numbers, きり means "only": 二人きり (just the two of us), これっきり (just this once). The double-consonant variant っきり is more colloquial and emotionally stronger.

Verb ます-stem + っぱなし describes that something was left in a certain state without being corrected or finished. In English: "left standing/lying/open", "the whole time...". っぱなし comes from 放す (hanasu, to let go) and almost always carries a negative connotation: carelessness, forgetfulness or thoughtlessness. It's also used when someone stays in one state the whole time: "standing / sitting the whole time".

All three can mean "only" or "still", but with a different focus:
  • きり → "Nothing since then." Focus on the turning point after which nothing changed. Often with regret.
  • っぱなし → "Left just as it is." Focus on the unchanged state that someone didn't fix. Often with criticism.
  • ばかり → "Always just that." Focus on repetition or exclusivity. Can be neutral or annoyed.
sections[].tip: きり always emphasizes: "Nothing has changed since then." There's often a note of regret or longing: the contact that never came again, the person who never returned.
っぱなし almost always implies criticism or unease: a door left open, a light left on, water left running; there's an undertone of "That shouldn't have been left like that!"
Memory aid: きり = "Since that moment: radio silence." っぱなし = "Just left like that, typical!" ばかり = "Always just the one thing, it's getting annoying."
sections[].examples[].de: He went out and hasn't come back since.
I haven't heard from them since the day we met.
I'd like to talk with just the two of us (in private).
Don't leave the door open.
I had left the water running the whole time.
I was standing on the train for two whole hours.
No contact since we met. (Turning point → silence)
I fell asleep with the TV left on. (State → carelessness)
Lately I do nothing but work. (Repetition → exclusivity)

en.title: ～ものだ / ～ものではない
en.subtitle: General truths and memories (in depth)
en.intro: You already met ものだ in lesson 102. Now let's go deeper into the more advanced nuances, especially ～ものがある (impression), ～というものだ (true nature) and the emotional exclamation ～ものだ/もんだ. These constructions make the difference between a solid N3 level and a natural-sounding N2 speaker. ものだ is like the Swiss Army knife of Japanese grammar: the more uses you know, the more versatile you become.
sections[].heading: ものがある — A strong impression
というものだ — The true nature
ものだ — Emotional exclamation
sections[].text: ～ものがある expresses that something leaves a strong impression or has a certain quality that you acknowledge. In English: "There's something... about it", "You have to admit that...".
というものだ expresses the true nature or essence of something. It adds a philosophical or judgmental note. In English: "That's just...", "That's what you call...".
ものだ (often もんだ in casual speech) expresses amazement, admiration or deep emotion. In English: "What a...!", "How...!". It turns a statement into a heartfelt exclamation.
sections[].tip: よく + verb + ものだ can express both admiration and indignation; context decides. よく来てくれたものだ = "It's great that you came!" vs. よくもそんなことを = "How could you!"
sections[].examples[].de: There's something deeply moving about his speech.
There's something about this movie that makes you think.
There's something in her singing voice that touches your heart.
Ignoring other people's feelings — THAT is rudeness.
THAT is what true friendship is.
Succeeding without any effort — that would be too good to be true.
I can't believe you passed such a hard exam!
How big you've gotten!
How dare you say such a thing!

en.title: い-adjectives & な-adjectives
en.subtitle: Two families, two rules
en.intro: Japanese adjectives come in two kinds, and this is one of the first forks in the road you reach as a learner. The good news: you can usually tell them apart by their ending. The bad news: there are a few sneaky exceptions. But they're manageable — promise. Once you've understood the basic rules, you can describe things, compare them and talk about the past without breaking a sweat.
sections[].heading: い-adjectives — The shape-shifters
な-adjectives — The noun-like ones
Before nouns: the difference
Connecting adjectives
The famous traps
sections[].text: い-adjectives end in い and conjugate like verbs. The い at the end isn't decoration — it's the part that changes depending on whether you need present, past, negative or adverb. You can think of い-adjectives as "independent words" that carry everything they need within themselves, without help from です or だ (even though です is often added for politeness).

な-adjectives behave more like nouns. They always need a "glue" to connect to the rest of the sentence: な before nouns, だ/です at the end of the sentence, で as an adverb. You can think of them as descriptive nouns — they don't exist "on their own" like い-adjectives but always need a grammatical bridge.

Before a noun, the difference is most obvious. い-adjectives simply stand directly in front of it — the い stays and nothing is inserted in between. な-adjectives need な as a link to modify the noun. This pattern is completely reliable and one of the easiest tests for determining the adjective type.

If you want to string several adjectives together (like "big and beautiful"), you need the て-form of adjectives. With い-adjectives, い becomes くて; with な-adjectives, な becomes で. The last adjective in the chain stays in its normal form.

Some words look like い-adjectives but are actually な-adjectives. They do end in い, but that い belongs to the word stem — it's not a conjugable い. Unfortunately, you just have to memorize these words. The most common candidates are:
sections[].tip: The adverb form (い → く) is super useful: 早く起きる (get up early), 大きくなる (get big), 安く買う (buy cheaply). It turns the adjective into a "how" word.
The trickiest な-adjectives that look like い-adjectives: きれい(な) = pretty, 有名(な) = famous, 嫌い(な) = disliked. They end in い but do NOT conjugate like い-adjectives. きれくない is wrong — きれいじゃない is correct!

Rule of thumb for traps: if the い is part of a longer word block (e.g. きれい = きれ+い, but the い isn't a separate suffix), it's probably a な-adjective. Real い-adjectives have an い you can "grab and change". When in doubt: look it up!
sections[].examples[].de: big
expensive → not expensive (い → くない)
expensive → was expensive (い → かった)
It wasn't hot yesterday. (い → くなかった)
a quiet town (な before a noun)
quiet → not quiet
was quiet → was not quiet
big house (い simply stays)
pretty flower (な connects)
new car (い-adjective)
a big, new house (い → くて)
a quiet, pretty town (な → で)
This dish is cheap and delicious.
pretty / clean — NOT きれくない!
famous — looks like い, but is な
disliked — also a な-adjective!

en.title: ～に対して / ～に比べて / ～に関して
en.subtitle: Comparison and reference
en.intro: If you want to argue, compare and make connections, you need precise tools. The three expressions に対して, に比べて and に関して are exactly that: grammatical precision instruments that turn a vague text into a structured one. に対して targets a contrast or a counterpart, に比べて puts things side by side for comparison, and に関して introduces a topic. Together they're the foundation of formal Japanese, essential for JLPT texts, news and academic discussions.
sections[].heading: に対して — Toward / In contrast
に比べて — Compared to
に関して — Regarding / With regard to
Related expressions: について / にとって
sections[].text: に対して has two main meanings: (1) toward someone/something (an attitude, a behavior) and (2) in contrast to (contrasting). In English: "Toward...", "While..., on the other hand...".
に比べて puts two things directly side by side for comparison. In English: "Compared to...", "In comparison with...".
に関して formally introduces a topic. It's the more elevated equivalent of について. In English: "Regarding...", "With regard to...", "As far as ... is concerned...".

For completeness:
  • について → "About..." (more general, more common than に関して)
  • にとって → "For ... (from the point of view of)": expresses perspective
sections[].tip: に比べると is an equivalent alternative to に比べて; both are correct and interchangeable.
に関して → before verbs (に関して話す), に関する → before nouns (に関する本). This distinction is important!
sections[].examples[].de: You mustn't be rude to your teacher.
While the older brother is extroverted, the younger one is introverted.
While word order in Japanese is free, the position of the verb in German is fixed.
Compared to last year, it's warmer this year.
Compared to Tokyo, food in Osaka is cheap.
Compared to Japanese, Chinese pronunciation is difficult.
Regarding this matter, I'll contact you later.
Do you have any questions regarding Japanese culture?
A discussion regarding environmental issues was held.
I'm learning about Japanese history.
For me, family is the most important thing.
For foreigners, keigo is the most difficult part.

en.title: ～ば～ほど
en.subtitle: The more... the more
en.intro: Some things in life reinforce each other: the more you practice, the better you get. The more you know, the more questions you have. In Japanese, ～ば～ほど expresses exactly this proportional relationship, and it does so wonderfully elegantly. This construction is a favorite in essays, speeches and philosophical statements. Once you've got the hang of it, you'll find you want to use it all the time; the more you use it, the more natural it becomes. See what I did there?
sections[].heading: Basic form: verb + ば + verb + ほど
With adjectives
Two different verbs / adjectives
Short forms and variants
sections[].text: The basic construction repeats the same verb: ば-form + dictionary form + ほど. In English: "The more you X, the more Y." The repeated verb emphasizes the increasing intensity.
With い-adjectives: ～ければ～ほど. With な-adjectives: ～なら～なほど or ～であれば～であるほど.
You can also combine two different expressions to show a cause-and-effect relationship.
～ほど on its own (without the ば part) can also express "the more", but it's somewhat more informal. There's also the set phrase ～ば～だけ with a similar meaning.
sections[].tip: ～ば～ほどいい (the more, the better) is an extremely common everyday phrase!
sections[].examples[].de: The more you study, the more interesting it gets.
The more you think about it, the more confusing it gets.
The more you eat, the hungrier you get.
The cheaper, the better.
The bigger, the better.
The quieter it is, the better I can concentrate.
The older you get, the faster time seems to pass.
The more you practice, the better you get.
The more you learn Japanese, the more you come to love Japanese culture.
The more you look at it, the more beautiful it is.
The more you know, the more there is that you don't know.
The more you do, the more results you get.

en.title: ～っぽい / ～がち / ～気味
en.subtitle: Expressing tendencies
en.intro: Not everything is black or white; often you want to say that someone has a tendency, that something is "a bit" that way, or that you're prone to something. For that, Japanese offers three wonderful suffixes: っぽい (seems like, tends to), がち (unfortunately tends to) and 気味 (a touch of). Each has its own character and mood. Together they're essential for natural-sounding Japanese at the intermediate to advanced level.
sections[].heading: っぽい — "Seems like...", "Tends to..."
がち — Negative tendency
気味（ぎみ）— A touch of
Comparing the three suffixes
sections[].text: っぽい is attached to nouns, verbs (stem) or い-adjectives (without い) and expresses that something gives an impression or that someone tends to be or do something. In English: "-ish", "-like", "seems like...".
がち is attached to the verb stem or to nouns and expresses an undesirable tendency: something unfortunately happens often. In English: "tends to...", "is prone to...".
気味 is attached to the verb stem or to nouns and expresses that something is present to a small degree or leans slightly in one direction. In English: "a bit...", "slightly...", "somewhat...".

• っぽい → Outward impression / general tendency (neutral to slightly negative)
  • がち → Undesirable habit / frequent negative tendency
  • 気味 → Slight degree / early stage of something
sections[].tip: っぽい is conjugated like an い-adjective: っぽくない, っぽかった, etc. It can be neutral or slightly negative.
がち almost always has a negative connotation! You don't say 成功しがち (tends to succeed); that would sound strange.
sections[].examples[].de: He's quick-tempered / gets angry easily.
This color is whitish.
I've become forgetful lately.
He tends to be late.
In winter, people tend to catch colds.
Living alone tends to lead to an irregular lifestyle.
I feel like I'm coming down with a cold, so I'll go to bed early today.
I've put on a bit of weight lately.
Today's meeting started a bit late.
forgetful (personality) → prone to forgetting (tendency) → a bit tired (current state)
He seems childish. (Impression)
Children tend to get sick. (Tendency)

en.title: ～にしても / ～としても / ～にせよ
en.subtitle: Concessions
en.intro: Sometimes you have to concede: even IF something is true, it doesn't change the outcome. In English you say "Even if...", "Even though...", "Suppose that...". Japanese has no fewer than three elegant constructions for this, which differ in formality and nuance. にしても is the all-rounder, としても emphasizes the hypothesis, and にせよ/にしろ belong to formal language. Master these three and you can skillfully concede a point in an argument and still make your own, a key skill for debates and essays.
sections[].heading: にしても — Even if / Even though
としても — Suppose that...
にせよ / にしろ — Formal concession
Nuances compared
sections[].text: にしても is the most versatile expression and is used both in casual speech and in more formal contexts. It concedes: "Even if X is true, Y still applies."
としても puts more emphasis on the hypothetical nature: "Suppose that were the case..." It's especially suited to scenarios that may never actually happen.
にせよ and にしろ are more formal variants of にしても. にせよ is the most formal form and often appears in written texts. にしろ sits in between.

• にしても → Everyday to slightly formal, versatile
  • としても → Emphasizes a hypothetical assumption
  • にせよ → Formal, written, "be it..."
  • にしろ → Between にしても and にせよ
sections[].tip: にせよ～にせよ and にしろ～にしろ are often used in pairs: "Whether A or B, in either case..." It's an elegant way to structure an argument.
sections[].examples[].de: Even if you're busy, you should eat properly.
Even as a joke, that's going too far.
Even if it's cheap, quality matters.
Even if I won the lottery, I wouldn't quit my job.
Even if you live in Japan, that doesn't mean your Japanese will become perfect.
Even if I apologized, they probably wouldn't forgive me.
Whatever the reason, late is late.
Whether you're for it or against it, you should voice your opinion.
Whether you like it or not, you have to do it.
Even if you fail, you gain experience. (general)
Even supposing you fail, it would still be experience. (hypothetical)
Be it a failure, it is experience all the same. (formal)

en.title: ～ざるを得ない / ～ないわけにはいかない
en.subtitle: The unavoidable
en.intro: There are situations where you have no choice — you HAVE to act, even if you don't really want to. Japanese has two powerful expressions for this, both conveying a kind of reluctant necessity. ～ざるを得ない comes from the classical language and sounds formal and resolute: "I cannot help but..." ～ないわけにはいかない stresses social or moral obligations: "It won't do for me NOT to do it." Both express: the circumstances leave me no other choice.
sections[].heading: ざるを得ない — I cannot help but
ないわけにはいかない — It won't do not to do it
Comparison: ざるを得ない vs ないわけにはいかない
sections[].text: Verb ない-stem + ざるを得ない means "to have no choice but to do something" — you are forced by the circumstances. It is formal and is often used in business or official contexts. Exception: する → せざるを得ない.
Verb ない-form + わけにはいかない expresses that you HAVE to act for social, moral or situational reasons. The double negative produces a strong affirmative: "I can't afford NOT to do it."

• ざるを得ない → External circumstances force you: "The situation leaves me no choice"
  • ないわけにはいかない → Social/moral duty: "My sense of duty won't allow it"
Both express necessity, but the source of the pressure is different.
sections[].tip: ざる is the classical negative form (ず → ざる before を). する becomes せざる, not しざる. This pattern is one of the few places where classical Japanese has survived in modern usage.
ざるを得ない sounds heavier and more formal — ideal for business language. ないわけにはいかない is somewhat more everyday and personal.
sections[].examples[].de: Given the evidence, I have no choice but to admit it.
It's company policy, so I have no choice but to comply.
The trains stopped, so I had no choice but to take a taxi.
I was invited, so I can't NOT go.
I can't NOT cause my parents worry — no, what I mean is I mustn't cause them worry.
It won't do for me not to report to my boss.
Because of the typhoon, I had no choice but to stay home from work. (external pressure)
I promised, so I have to go. (moral duty)

en.title: ～かねる / ～かねない
en.subtitle: Inability and risk
en.intro: かねる is an elegant verb that is at home in formal language — in business letters, customer service and diplomatic phrasing. ～かねる means "I'm afraid I can't" and is the most polite way of saying "No, that's not possible." Its counterpart ～かねない flips the meaning: "It could unfortunately happen" — a warning about an undesirable outcome. If you know these two forms, you can both decline politely and warn diplomatically.
sections[].heading: かねる — Polite refusal
かねない — It could happen (warning)
かねる vs できない — Declining with style
sections[].text: Verb stem + かねる means "to be unfortunately unable to do something". It is much more polite than できない and is often used at work and in customer service. In English: "I regret that I'm unable to...", "I'm afraid it's not possible for me to...".

Verb stem + かねない means "it can't be ruled out that..." or "there is a danger that...". It warns of an undesirable possible outcome. In English: "Unfortunately, it could happen that...", "You run the risk of...".

The practical difference is the level of politeness:
  • できません → Neutral, matter-of-fact: "It's not possible."
  • かねます → Polite, regretful: "I'm afraid that won't be possible."
In emails, business letters and customer interactions, かねます is the preferred choice.
sections[].tip: かねる sounds like "I'd love to, but unfortunately I can't" — there's a note of regret. Perfect for polite refusals at work.
かねない is used almost exclusively for NEGATIVE outcomes. You don't say 成功しかねない — that would be like warning someone about success, which makes no sense.
sections[].examples[].de: I regret that I am unable to meet that request.
I'm afraid I cannot give out personal information.
I'm afraid I can't agree under these conditions.
With an attitude like that, you could end up getting fired.
If you leave it alone, it could turn into a big problem.
He's quite capable of doing that. (He might really do it.)
Returns are not accepted. (matter-of-fact)
We regret that we are unable to accept returns. (polite)
There may be cases where we are unfortunately unable to meet your expectations.

en.title: ～に他ならない / ～にすぎない
en.subtitle: Emphasis and limitation
en.intro: In debates and essays you need two basic rhetorical tools: asserting something forcefully and putting something into perspective. に他ならない is the hammer: "It is nothing other than X!" — an absolute assertion. にすぎない is the scalpel: "It is merely X" — an elegant qualification. Master both and you can build arguments like a pro: first make the point strongly, then qualify it — or the other way round. These forms are the rhetorical backbone of sophisticated Japanese texts.
sections[].heading: に他ならない — Nothing other than
にすぎない — Merely / Only
Rhetorical combination
sections[].text: Noun + に他（ほか）ならない expresses a strong, absolute conviction: "X is nothing other than Y." In English: "It is nothing less than...", "It is due solely to...".
Verb / Noun + にすぎない expresses that something is less important or significant than one might think. In English: "It is merely...", "It is only...", "It is just a matter of...".
The real power shows when you use both forms together in one argument — first qualify, then emphasize (or the other way round).
sections[].tip: に他ならない is always emphatic — it highlights the true nature or the true reason, whether the matter is positive or negative. It is the rhetorical equivalent of an exclamation mark.
にすぎない puts things into perspective, に他ならない emphasizes absolutely. Together they create a convincing contrast — a powerful rhetorical technique.
sections[].examples[].de: His success is nothing other than the result of hard work.
This is nothing short of a miracle.
Environmental destruction is nothing other than the result of human actions.
It's merely my opinion.
This is just a rumor.
He's still only a student.
Admittedly, he is just one employee, but what he said reflects nothing other than the thinking of the entire company.
Money is just a tool. What matters is nothing other than how you use it.

en.title: ～たりとも / ～すら / ～だに
en.subtitle: Extreme emphasis
en.intro: At N1 level, the language becomes poetic, rhetorical and powerful. The three expressions たりとも, すら and だに are tools of extreme emphasis that are at home in speeches, literary texts and formal writing. たりとも says: "Not even a single second!" すら goes even further than さえ and says: "Not even THAT!" だに is the rarest and most literary form: "The mere thought of it..." If you know these forms, you can appreciate the depth and elegance of the Japanese language at the highest level.
sections[].heading: たりとも — Not even a single...
すら — Not even (stronger than さえ)
だに — The very thought
sections[].text: Counter / quantity + たりとも + negative expresses that not even the smallest unit is allowed, present or acceptable. In English: "Not even a single...", "Not one...".
すら is a literary, more intense version of さえ. It stresses that even the bare minimum or the most obvious thing is not there. In English: "Not even...", "Even... doesn't".
だに is the rarest and most literary of these three forms. It is used almost exclusively with verbs of thinking: 想像する, 考える, 思う. In English: "The mere thought...", "Just imagining it...".
sections[].tip: たりとも almost always follows a quantity with "one" (一秒, 一歩, 一円, 一日) and is always followed by a negative.
すら sounds more literary and dramatic than さえ. In everyday speech people tend to use さえ, in writing and speeches すら.
だに is limited to a few set phrases. The most common are: 想像だにしない, 予想だにしない, 考えるだに. You mainly come across it in news and literature.
sections[].examples[].de: I don't want to waste even a single second.
Don't move a single step!
I won't lend you a single yen.
I don't even know the name.
It's a problem even a child can solve.
He didn't even say hello.
It's an outcome I never even imagined.
Just thinking about it is frightening.
It was a turn of events nobody could have foreseen.

en.title: ～をもって / ～を踏まえて / ～を余儀なくされる
en.subtitle: Formal expressions
en.intro: N1 grammar is often the grammar of the official world — business letters, news, government documents and academic texts. The three expressions をもって, を踏まえて and を余儀なくされる belong to this register. をもって is the formal way of saying "with" or "as of". を踏まえて means "based on" — you take something into account when making a decision. And を余儀なくされる describes a forced action — you are compelled to do something. If you know these forms, you can read Japanese news and write formal texts.
sections[].heading: をもって — With / As of
を踏まえて — Based on
を余儀なくされる — To be forced to
sections[].text: をもって has two main meanings: (1) means or manner: "with..., by..." and (2) the point in time of an end or beginning: "as of..., from...". It is a formal alternative to で.

を踏まえて (from 踏まえる — "to take into account, to build on") means that you take something as the basis or starting point for a decision. In English: "Based on...", "Taking into account...", "In light of...".
を余儀（よぎ）なくされる means "to be forced to do something" — the circumstances leave no other choice. It is more formal than ざるを得ない and is often found in news and official reports.
sections[].tip: 本日をもって (as of today) is a very common phrase in business announcements — closures, resignations, last working days.
を余儀なくされる is used almost exclusively in the passive and always describes an involuntary action forced by external circumstances.
sections[].examples[].de: We will be closing our doors as of today.
We hereby notify you in writing.
To respond with sincerity.
We will review the plan based on the survey results.
Taking this experience into account, I'd like to think about ways to improve.
We will make the final decision after taking all of your opinions into account.
Because of the typhoon, the event had to be canceled.
The residents were forced to evacuate.
The company is being forced into large-scale restructuring.

en.title: ～ともなると / ～ともなれば
en.subtitle: When you consider that...
en.intro: There are moments when you look at a status, a position or a situation and realize: from this point on, different rules apply. ～ともなると and ～ともなれば express exactly that: "When it gets to the point that..." or "Once you are X / have reached X..." They imply that a certain status brings certain expectations, duties or consequences with it. They are expressions of reflection and a shift in perspective — typical of reflections on careers, age, responsibility and social roles.
sections[].heading: ともなると — When it gets to the point that...
ともなれば — When you consider that...
Nuances and usage
sections[].text: Noun + ともなると expresses that from a certain point or status on, the situation changes. It implies: "Once you are X, then..." In English: "When it comes to being...", "Once you...".
ともなれば is almost synonymous with ともなると, but has a slightly stronger, more conditional tone. It stresses the expectation even more: "If you are in such a position, it goes without saying that...".

The two forms are almost interchangeable. A subtle difference:
  • ともなると → descriptive, observational tone: "When it gets to that point..."
  • ともなれば → more conditional tone: "Supposing that..."
Both are mainly used with nouns (status, point in time, position).
sections[].tip: ともなると/ともなれば express a "with status comes responsibility" philosophy — a concept that is especially important in Japanese society.
sections[].examples[].de: Once you're the company president, the responsibility is heavy.
Once you're a university student, you're expected to be able to think for yourself.
Once it's December, the whole town is filled with Christmas spirit.
Once you're a parent, your children are your biggest worry.
If you're a professional, it's only natural that you can do something like this.
When you're famous, it's hard to protect your privacy.
When summer comes, lots of people go to the beach every weekend.
Once you turn 30, you start thinking about the future.
When graduation comes, you feel a sense of sadness.

en.title: The て-form
en.subtitle: The Swiss Army knife
en.intro: If there's one verb form you absolutely need to master, it's the て-form. It's the basic building block for dozens of further constructions: requests, ongoing actions, permission, prohibitions, listing actions, causes and much more. Forming it is a bit tricky at first, because for う-verbs it follows a sound pattern — but once it's in, it sticks. And then it opens door after door to new ways of expressing yourself.
sections[].heading: Formation: る-verbs (vowel stem)
Formation: う-verbs (consonant stem)
Irregular verbs
Everything you can do with it
More て-constructions
sections[].text: With る-verbs (ichidan / group 2) it couldn't be simpler: cut off る, add て. These verbs always end in -iru or -eru (but watch out: not everything that ends in -iru/-eru is a る-verb — some are う-verbs in disguise, e.g. 帰る, 走る, 切る). When in doubt, a dictionary helps.

With う-verbs (godan / group 1) the ending changes according to a sound pattern. There are five groups, best memorized with mnemonics. The pattern depends on which consonant comes before the う — and that determines whether the て sound becomes って, んで, いて or して.
Japanese has only two truly irregular verbs — する (to do) and 来る (to come). You simply have to memorize their て-forms, but it's only two words:

This is where it gets really exciting — the て-form is the foundation for a whole range of important constructions. That's why it's called the "Swiss Army knife": one tool, many functions. Here are the most important uses you'll already encounter at N5 level:
Beyond the basic uses, there are more important patterns built on the て-form. You'll get to know all of them over the course of N5 and N4:
sections[].tip: Exception: 行く (iku) becomes 行って (itte), not 行いて. It's the only exception in this category — and it comes up so often that you'll learn it automatically.
The て-form is like the alphabet: on its own it doesn't say anything, but without it you can hardly write anything. Invest the time to internalize the formation rules — it pays off a hundredfold.
sections[].examples[].de: to eat
to see
to get up
買う→買って, 待つ→待って, 帰る→帰って
飲む→飲んで, 遊ぶ→遊んで, 死ぬ→死んで
書く→書いて, 聞く→聞いて
泳ぐ→泳いで, 急ぐ→急いで
話す→話して, 消す→消して
to do
to come
to study (する-verb → して)
Please open the window. (request: て + ください)
I'm eating right now. (progressive: て + いる)
May I take a photo? (permission: て + もいい)
I'll take an umbrella with me. (て + いく = and then head off)
My friend helped me. (て + くれる = as a favor to me)
I'd like to try eating it. (て + みる = try out)

en.title: ～んばかりに / ～まじき / ～べからず
en.subtitle: Literary and archaic forms
en.intro: At the end of our grammar journey are three expressions that come from classical Japanese and are still alive today in formal, literary and public contexts. ～んばかりに describes an action so intense that it seems something is about to happen — "as if about to..." ～まじき expresses moral condemnation: "That is inexcusable for someone who..." And ～べからず is the formal prohibition you find on signs and in regulations: "It is forbidden!" Once you recognize these forms, a new layer of the Japanese language opens up to you — the bridge between the classical and the modern.
sections[].heading: んばかりに — As if about to...
まじき — Inexcusable for a...
べからず — It is forbidden!
Classical Japanese in everyday life
sections[].text: Verb ない-stem + んばかりに (exception: する → せんばかりに) describes extreme intensity — it looks as if something is about to happen, even though it doesn't actually happen. In English: "as if about to...", "almost as if...".
Noun + にあるまじき / Noun + としてあるまじき expresses that a behavior is inexcusable for someone in a certain position. In English: "unworthy of a...", "inexcusable for a...".

Verb dictionary form + べからず is a formal, categorical prohibition. You find it on signs and in regulations and rules. In English: "It is forbidden!", "... is prohibited!" It sounds old-fashioned and authoritarian.

These three forms show how classical Japanese is still alive today. You come across them in certain contexts:
  • んばかりに → literature, news, elevated narration
  • まじき → news commentary, formal criticism
  • べからず → signs, rules, proverbs
sections[].tip: んばかり comes from the classical form ん (= む, intention/conjecture). The construction lives on today in written language and in the news.
まじき comes from classical まじ (= べきではない, "should not"). Today you mainly find it in news commentary and formal criticism.
初心忘るべからず is one of the best-known Japanese proverbs. It comes from Zeami, the founder of Nō theater, and is still often quoted today — in speeches, motivational talks and as a piece of life wisdom.
sections[].examples[].de: She begged as if she were about to burst into tears.
The hall was filled with applause so thunderous it seemed about to burst.
He listened to the story with eyes that seemed about to light up.
That is conduct unworthy of a teacher.
He made a remark unworthy of a doctor.
That is a mistake a professional athlete should never make.
No entry!
Never forget it! / Do not forget!
Never forget your beginner's spirit! (famous proverb)
His face looked as if it were about to overflow with joy. (literary)
It was criticized as a remark unworthy of a politician. (news)
Keep off the grass! (sign)

en.title: ～ながらも / ～つつも / ～ものの
en.subtitle: Concession and contradiction
en.intro: In this lesson we look at three important concessive expressions in Japanese, all of which express some form of "although" or "even so". Although their basic meaning is similar, they differ considerably in nuance, formality and context of use. ～ながらも stresses an inner contradiction between two states that exist at the same time, ～つつも expresses that you are aware of something but still act differently, and ～ものの marks an expectation that is disappointed in the second part of the sentence. Mastering these three forms is essential for N1, since they appear frequently in formal texts, newspaper articles and literary works.
sections[].heading: ～ながらも — Although / Despite (inner contradiction)
～つつも — Although you know / Although you do it (conscious contradiction)
～ものの — True..., but / Although (disappointed expectation)
Comparing the nuances: summary
sections[].text: ～ながらも attaches to the stem form of verbs, to adjectives or to nouns, and expresses that two contradictory states or qualities exist at the same time. It stresses an inherent contradiction — something is a certain way even though you would expect the opposite. With い-adjectives the dictionary form is used (小さいながらも), with な-adjectives the stem (残念ながらも), and nouns attach directly (子供ながらも). This form has a slightly literary ring and is used both in writing and in elevated speech.

～つつも attaches to the verb stem (ます-form without ます) and expresses that someone is aware of something but still acts or feels differently. It often carries a nuance of self-reproach or inner conflict — you know what would be right but do the opposite. This form is more formal than ～ながらも and appears especially in written language, essays and introspective texts. It is used only with verbs, not with adjectives or nouns.

～ものの attaches to the plain form (verbs, い-adjectives in the dictionary form, な-adjectives + な, nouns + である) and expresses that although something is the case, the expected result does not happen. It has the nuance of a disappointed expectation: the situation in the first part of the sentence would normally lead to a certain result, but the second part shows that things turned out differently. ～ものの is stylistically neutral to slightly formal and is used frequently in both speech and writing.

All three expressions mean "although", but they differ in perspective. ～ながらも states an objective contradiction between two states and can be used with verbs, adjectives and nouns. ～つつも stresses the speaker's subjective awareness of the contradiction and is used only with verbs — it often has a self-critical note. ～ものの expresses that the result falls short of expectations and is the most versatile of the three forms. All three are used frequently in formal texts, with ～つつも sounding the most literary.
sections[].tip: Remember: ～ながらも stresses that two qualities exist at the same time that actually contradict each other. The も reinforces the concessive character — without も (just ～ながら) it can also simply mean "while".
～つつも almost always implies awareness of the contradiction. If you want to say "I actually know better, but...", ～つつも is the perfect choice.
Comparison: ～ものの focuses on the disappointing result, ～ながらも on the simultaneous contradiction, and ～つつも on consciously acting against your better judgment.
sections[].examples[].de: Although he is poor, he lives happily.
Although it is small, this company is famous worldwide.
Although he is just a child, the boy has astonishing talent.
Although I know it's bad for my health, I can't quit smoking.
Although I felt bad about it, I turned down his request.
Although she sensed the danger, she kept moving forward.
Although I studied Japanese for years, I still can't speak it fluently.
I bought a new computer, but I don't really know how to use it.
I'd like to change jobs, but I just can't bring myself to act on it.
(Objective:) Although he made an effort, there were no results.
(Conscious:) Although I knew I should make an effort, I ended up slacking off.
(Disappointment:) I did make an effort, but there were no results.

en.title: ～に至る / ～に至って / ～に至っては
en.subtitle: Up to the point of... / When it came to that...
en.intro: This lesson covers three closely related expressions, all based on the verb 至る (itaru, "to reach, to arrive at"). They describe a development that reaches a certain point — whether a climax, a turning point or an extreme case. ～に至る describes the process that leads to a certain point, ～に至って marks the moment when a decisive change occurs, and ～に至っては highlights a particularly extreme or noteworthy case. These expressions are typical of formal written language, news texts and academic papers and are part of the core vocabulary of the N1 exam.
sections[].heading: ～に至る / ～に至るまで — Up to / To come to the point that
～に至って / ～に至っても — When it came to that / Even when it came to that
～に至っては — As for... / Especially in the case of
sections[].text: ～に至る describes a process or development that eventually reaches a certain point. It stresses the path or chain of events that led to this result. In the form ～に至るまで it means "right up to" and stresses the range or scope of something. The nominalized form ～に至った経緯 (ni itatta keii) means "the circumstances that led to it" and is a very common expression in formal reports.

～に至って marks a turning point: it describes the moment when a situation has progressed so far that a reaction or realization finally occurs. The nuance is often "only when it came to that" — it implies that the reaction came too late or only at the last moment. The negative variant ～に至っても means "even when it came to that" and expresses that not even in this extreme situation did the expected reaction occur.

～に至っては highlights a particularly extreme or remarkable case within a series. It is used to say: "When it comes to X, it is particularly bad / extreme / remarkable." The expression implies that there are already other cases, but this one is the most extreme. It is often used in negative contexts but can also be neutral when it simply marks an outstanding case.
sections[].tip: ～に至る has a factual, reporting tone. Use it when you describe a chain of events that led to a result.
～に至って almost always contains the nuance "only now that it has come to this". It often implies criticism: why didn't anyone act sooner?
～に至っては is often used after a generally negative situation to highlight the worst individual case. The structure is: "A is already bad, but with B it's the worst."
sections[].examples[].de: The negotiations ended in a breakdown.
The situation got worse and eventually led to a resignation.
Allow me to explain the circumstances that led to this plan.
Only when his condition became serious did he finally go to the doctor.
Only when the company went bankrupt did they realize how serious the problem was.
Now that things have come to this, there's no turning back.
The grades were bad in every subject, and in math it was actually a failing grade.
Many employees come in late, but as for Tanaka, he is late every single day.
Prices are rising, and as for housing prices, they have doubled.

en.title: ～をよそに / ～をものともせず / ～を顧みず
en.subtitle: Ignoring and defying
en.intro: In this lesson we learn three powerful N1 expressions that all describe someone ignoring something, disregarding it or not being deterred by it. Although they all express a form of "paying no attention", their nuances differ considerably: ～をよそに often has a critical note and implies indifference to other people's worries, ～をものともせず expresses admirable strength and courage, and ～を顧みず describes the determination to accept risks or consequences. These expressions give texts an elevated, often literary quality.
sections[].heading: ～をよそに — Regardless of / Without regard for (critical)
～をものともせず — Undaunted by (admiring)
～を顧みず — Without regard for / Without considering (determined)
sections[].text: ～をよそに literally means "to set something aside" and expresses that someone ignores the worries, feelings or expectations of others and does their own thing. This expression almost always has a critical or reproachful nuance — the speaker disapproves of how indifferent the person concerned is. よそ means "another place" or "elsewhere" and suggests that the person regards other people's affairs as "none of their business". The construction is: Noun + をよそに.

～をものともせず expresses that someone is not intimidated by difficulties, obstacles or adverse circumstances and bravely pushes forward. Unlike ～をよそに, this expression has a positive, admiring nuance — the person described shows strength and determination. ものともしない literally means "not to regard something as anything" (i.e. to think nothing of it). The construction is: Noun + をものともせず.

～を顧みず literally means "without looking back at" and expresses that someone knowingly accepts risks, danger to their own safety or the consequences. 顧みる (kaerimiru) means "to look back, to consider, to take into account", and the negation ず is the classical Japanese form of ない. This expression is neutral to positive — it describes determination and a willingness to make sacrifices. The construction is: Noun + を顧みず.
sections[].tip: ～をよそに is almost always used critically. It implies: "This person should have cared, but didn't." Typical nouns before it: 心配 (worry), 反対 (opposition), 批判 (criticism), 期待 (expectation).
～をものともせず is used for heroic or admirable actions. Typical nouns before it: 困難 (difficulties), 逆境 (adversity), 反対 (opposition), 痛み (pain).
Comparison: ～をよそに = critical (indifference), ～をものともせず = admiring (strength), ～を顧みず = determined (willingness to sacrifice). All three are built with Noun + を.
sections[].examples[].de: Ignoring his parents' worries, the son set off on a dangerous journey.
Despite the opposition of those around her, she went independent and started her own business.
Ignoring the public's anxiety, the government pushed ahead with the plan.
Undeterred by harsh criticism, he continued his research.
Undaunted by the heavy rain, the players fought the match through to the end.
Refusing to let her illness stop her, she completed the full marathon.
With no thought for his own safety, he rescued the child from the river.
Disregarding her family's opposition, she moved abroad.
With no regard for his health, he kept working until late at night, day after day.

en.title: ～てやまない / ～にたえない / ～にかたくない
en.subtitle: Unceasing feelings
en.intro: This lesson is devoted to three elevated expressions that describe intense, often overwhelming emotions. They are typical of formal speeches, letters and literary texts and give what is said a solemn, earnest atmosphere. ～てやまない expresses a feeling that never ends, ～にたえない describes something so intense that you can hardly bear it (positive or negative), and ～にかたくない means that something is easy to imagine because the circumstances are so obvious. Mastering these expressions lets you convey nuanced emotions in formal situations.
sections[].heading: ～てやまない — Unceasingly / With all one's heart
～にたえない — Unbearable / Hard to bear
～にかたくない — Not hard to... / Easy to imagine
sections[].text: やまない comes from the verb 止む (yamu, "to stop") in its negative form. ～てやまない therefore literally means "it does not stop..." and expresses a feeling that never fades. It is used with verbs of feeling and wishing: 願う (to wish), 望む (to hope), 祈る (to pray), 愛する (to love), 尊敬する (to respect). The construction is: Verb (て-form) + やまない. This expression is very formal and is often used in speeches, words of greeting and official addresses.

～にたえない (に堪えない) literally means "one cannot bear it" and has two different uses. First, it can describe an emotion so strong that it is hard to bear — both positive (gratitude, joy) and negative (shame, regret). Second, it can mean that something is so bad that it is "not worth" doing (e.g. 聞くにたえない = "unbearable to listen to"). The construction is: Noun + にたえない or Verb (辞書形) + にたえない.

～にかたくない (に難くない) literally means "it is not hard to..." and expresses that something is easy to imagine or easy to understand, even if you haven't experienced it yourself. It is used with a limited number of verbs: 想像する (to imagine), 推察する (to guess), 理解する (to understand), 予想する (to anticipate). The construction is: Verb stem + にかたくない. This expression is very formal and is used in written texts, commentaries and formal analyses.
sections[].tip: In the polite form, やまない becomes やみません. This expression is used almost exclusively with positive feelings — wishes, hopes, love, respect.
With emotion nouns (感謝、感慨、慚愧) it means "overwhelming emotion". With verbs like 聞く、見る、読む it means "so bad that you cannot bear it".
The most common combination is 想像にかたくない. Learn this expression as a set phrase — it appears regularly on the N1 exam.
sections[].examples[].de: I sincerely wish you all every success.
I never stop praying that world peace will become a reality.
I have the deepest respect for her talent.
I cannot thank you all enough for your support.
I am filled with deep shame that things have turned out like this.
His speech was unbearable to listen to.
The suffering of the people in the disaster area is not hard to imagine.
It is not hard to guess how frustrated he must have been.
It is easy to predict that this decision will have a major impact.

en.title: ～たが最後 / ～が早いか / ～や否や / ～なり
en.subtitle: In the same moment
en.intro: This lesson covers four expressions that all describe a second action happening immediately after the first — practically in the same instant. Although their basic meaning is similar, their nuances differ considerably. ～たが最後 means that after the first action there is no going back (negative consequence), ～が早いか stresses the lightning-fast sequence from an observer's perspective, ～や否や expresses an immediate reaction, and ～なり describes an immediate, often unexpected action. These forms belong to the elevated register and are particularly important in literature and on the N1 exam.
sections[].heading: ～たが最後 — Once you..., then... (no going back)
～が早いか — No sooner... than / The moment...
～や否や — Hardly... when...
～なり — As soon as... immediately... (unexpected)
sections[].text: ～たが最後 (た + が + 最後) literally means "if it was the last time that..." and expresses that a certain action is followed by an irreversible, negative state. It carries the nuance: "Once you do that, it's over." The first action triggers a chain reaction that can no longer be stopped. The construction is: Verb (た-form) + が最後. The second part of the sentence always describes a negative or undesirable consequence.

～が早いか literally means "whether it was quick" and describes the second action following the first so quickly that they happen practically at the same time. It is used from an observer's perspective — the speaker describes what they saw someone else do. The construction is: Verb (辞書形/た形) + が早いか. The second action is often surprising, energetic or impulsive.

～や否や (やいなや) literally means "whether it... or whether it didn't..." and expresses that the second action follows the first instantly and directly. It stresses the speed and immediacy of the reaction. The construction is: Verb (辞書形) + や否や. Compared with ～が早いか, ～や否や is somewhat more formal and is used more often in written language. It can be used both for your own actions and for actions you observe.

～なり describes someone doing something unexpected immediately after an action. It carries the nuance that the second action is surprising or unexpected — often impulsive or rude. The construction is: Verb (辞書形) + なり. An important feature: the subject of the first and the second action must be the same person (usually a third person, not the speaker). This expression is used almost exclusively in narrative contexts.
sections[].tip: ～たが最後 is always used with negative consequences. It is a warning: "Don't you dare do that, or else..." Similar to ～たら最後.
～が早いか describes observed scenes — you recount what you saw others do. It is not used for your own actions.
～や否や always uses the dictionary form of the verb. It sounds very literary and elegant.
Remember the differences: ～たが最後 = negative consequence, ～が早いか = observed quick action, ～や否や = immediate reaction, ～なり = surprising immediate action by the same person.
sections[].examples[].de: Once you lend that person money, you'll never get it back.
Once you start this game, you can't stop for hours.
Once you tell her a secret, everyone will know about it.
No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out of the classroom.
No sooner had he opened the door than he dashed into the room.
The moment the child saw its mother, it burst into tears.
The moment he woke up, he checked his phone.
The instant the final whistle blew, the spectators leapt to their feet.
As soon as the train doors opened, the passengers surged in.
The moment he entered the room, he collapsed onto the sofa.
As soon as she answered the phone, she started yelling.
As soon as he saw my face, he burst into tears.

en.title: ～ごとき / ～ごとく / ～いかんによらず / ～いかんにかかわらず
en.subtitle: Like... / Regardless of...
en.intro: In this lesson we cover two important groups of N1 grammar. The first group — ～ごとき and ～ごとく — comes from classical Japanese and is used for poetic, literary comparisons. They correspond to modern ～ような / ～ように, but sound much more elevated and solemn. The second group — ～いかんによらず and ～いかんにかかわらず — expresses that something applies regardless of the circumstances. The word いかん (如何) means "how, in what way" and is a key word in formal Japanese expressions. Both groups are ubiquitous in formal texts, literary works and official documents.
sections[].heading: ～ごとく / ～ごとき — Like / Just as (classical comparison)
～ごとき for modesty or disdain
～いかんによらず / ～いかんにかかわらず — Regardless of / Irrespective of
sections[].text: ～ごとく and ～ごとき come from the classical Japanese word 如し (gotoshi, "just like"). ～ごとく is used adverbially (it modifies a verb), while ～ごとき is used attributively (it modifies a noun). The construction is: Noun + の + ごとく/ごとき or Verb (が) + ごとく/ごとき. These forms are much more literary than ～のように/～のような and are used in poetic texts, proverbs, speeches and dramatic descriptions. They practically never occur in colloquial language.

～ごとき has a special use for expressing modesty or disdain. When you apply it to yourself, it expresses extreme modesty: "Someone like me (who is worth nothing)." When you apply it to others, it can express contempt or disdain: "Someone like you (who isn't worth it)." This use is very formal and appears especially in historical dramas, novels and formal speeches.

いかん (如何) means "how, in what way" and is the basis of several formal expressions. ～いかんによらず and ～いかんにかかわらず both mean "regardless of" or "irrespective of" and express that an outcome does not depend on the circumstances. The construction is: Noun + のいかんによらず/にかかわらず or Noun + いかんによらず/にかかわらず. These expressions are extremely formal and appear mainly in official documents, contracts, regulations and business communication. A shorter variant is ～いかんを問わず.
sections[].tip: ごとく = adverbial (before verbs), ごとき = attributive (before nouns), ごとし = at the end of a sentence (predicative). These are the three forms of the same classical word.
Applied to yourself = extreme modesty. Applied to others = disdain. The context makes the difference clear.
～いかんによらず/にかかわらず = "no matter how" (the outcome is fixed). ～いかんにかかっている/によって = "depends on how" (the outcome varies). Note this important difference in meaning!
sections[].examples[].de: Time flies like an arrow. (proverb)
He raced past like the wind.
It was a voice with a crystal clarity, like water.
It would be presumptuous for someone like me to offer an opinion.
What could someone like you possibly understand?
An amateur like you shouldn't butt in.
Whatever the reason, violence is not acceptable.
Regardless of the outcome, you should do your very best.
This applies to all citizens, regardless of nationality.

en.title: ～極まりない / ～の極み / ～の至り / ～限りだ
en.subtitle: The utmost
en.intro: In this lesson we look at four expressions that all describe the highest degree or the extreme of a quality or feeling. They all mean roughly "extremely, to the highest degree, the height of...", but differ in usage and nuance. ～極まりない is a strong expression for extreme qualities, ～の極み describes the absolute peak of a state, ～の至り expresses deep personal feelings (especially in set phrases), and ～限りだ describes a feeling that could not be any stronger. These expressions are essential for the N1 exam and give formal texts and speeches special emphasis.
sections[].heading: ～極まりない / ～極まる — Extremely / To the highest degree
～の極み — The height of / The epitome of
～の至り — Deep feeling (formal set phrases)
～限りだ — As... as can be (personal feeling)
sections[].text: ～極まりない (きわまりない) and ～極まる (きわまる) mean "extremely" or "boundlessly" and express that a quality has reached its absolute maximum. 極まる means "to reach the limit", and paradoxically the negation 極まりない means the same thing — "there is no limit, that's how extreme it is". The construction is: な-adjective (stem) + 極まりない/極まる. This expression is often used with negative adjectives (dangerous, rude, foolish), but can also be positive.

～の極み (きわみ) means "the height" or "the epitome" and describes the absolute peak of a state or quality. It is used as a set phrase with certain nouns and sounds very solemn and elevated. The construction is: Noun + の極み. Particularly common combinations are: 贅沢の極み (the height of luxury), 疲労の極み (utter exhaustion), 幸せの極み (the greatest happiness). In everyday language you also know it as part of 感極まる (to be overwhelmed with emotion).

～の至り (いたり) literally means "the utmost of" and is used in set phrases to express deep personal feelings, especially in formal situations such as speeches, letters and official occasions. 至り comes from the verb 至る (itaru, "to reach") and here means "the highest degree". The most important set combinations are: 光栄の至り (the greatest honor), 恐縮の至り (I am extremely sorry to trouble you), 若気の至り (youthful folly), 赤面の至り (enough to make one blush). The construction is: Noun + の至り.

～限りだ (かぎりだ) expresses that a feeling is so strong that it could not be any stronger. It is used to describe personal, subjective feelings — the speaker feels something to the highest degree. The construction is: い-adjective + 限りだ or な-adjective + な + 限りだ. Typical adjectives are: うらやましい (enviable), 心強い (reassuring), うれしい (happy), 残念な (regrettable), 心細い (anxious, uneasy).
sections[].tip: 極まりない and 極まる are interchangeable, though 極まりない is used somewhat more often. Note: it is only used with な-adjectives, not with い-adjectives.
～の極み sounds very poetic and solemn. It is often used in speeches, reviews and literary descriptions.
～の至り occurs almost only in set phrases. Learn them by heart as a whole — 光栄の至り and 若気の至り in particular appear frequently on the N1 exam.
Comparison: ～極まりない = objective judgment of an extreme (な-adj.), ～の極み = poetic peak, ～の至り = formal set phrases, ～限りだ = extreme personal feeling (い/な-adj.).
sections[].examples[].de: That kind of driving is extremely dangerous.
His attitude is rude in the extreme.
Remarks like that are utterly tactless.
This dish is the height of luxury.
Having reached the limit of exhaustion, he collapsed on the spot.
At the moment of victory, he was overcome with emotion and shed tears.
It is the greatest honor to have been invited.
I am terribly sorry to trouble you when you are so busy, but I have a favor to ask.
The mistakes I made back then were youthful folly.
I really envy him for being so successful abroad.
It is truly reassuring to have the support of all of you.
I am overjoyed that my son has come back safe and sound.

en.title: N1 Formal Written Japanese
en.subtitle: Official, formal, indispensable
en.intro: This final lesson covers four formal expressions that are ubiquitous in official documents, news articles, academic texts and business correspondence. They form the backbone of elevated written Japanese and are essential for understanding formal texts. ～において/における marks the framework or context of a statement, ～に即して means "in line with" reality, ～に準じて means "in accordance with" a rule or standard, and ～をもって indicates the means, the point in time or the reason. These expressions appear in almost every N1 reading text and are indispensable for passing the exam.
sections[].heading: ～において / ～における — In / At / In the field of
～に即して / ～に即した — In line with / In keeping with reality
～に準じて / ～に準ずる — In accordance with / Corresponding to (a standard)
～をもって — With / By / As of (means, point in time, reason)
sections[].text: ～において and ～における are the formal equivalents of ～で (place, field, point in time). ～において is used adverbially (it closes an adverbial phrase), while ～における is used attributively (before a noun). They mark the framework, context or field in which something takes place — whether a physical place, a field of study, a period of time or a situation. The construction is: Noun + において/における. These expressions are extremely common in news articles, academic texts and official documents.

～に即して (にそくして) means "in line with" or "adapted to" and stresses that something is based on actual reality, practice or concrete circumstances — not on theory or ideals. 即する (sokusuru) means "to conform to, to adapt to". ～に即して is used adverbially, ～に即した attributively (before a noun). The construction is: Noun + に即して/に即した. Typical nouns are: 現実 (reality), 実態 (actual state), 実情 (real circumstances), 法律 (law).

～に準じて (にじゅんじて) means "in accordance with", "corresponding to" or "analogous to" and expresses that something is handled according to a certain standard, rule or model. 準じる (junjiru) means "to follow, to correspond to". Unlike ～に即して, which refers to reality, ～に準じて refers to rules, norms and existing systems. ～に準ずる is the attributive form (before nouns). The construction is: Noun + に準じて/に準ずる. This expression is especially common in contracts, employment guidelines and legal texts.

～をもって is a versatile formal expression with three main meanings. First, it indicates the means or method: "with, by" (a formal version of ～で). Second, it marks a point in time: "as of, with" — especially for official dates and deadlines. Third, it indicates the reason or basis. The construction is: Noun + をもって. This expression is extremely widespread in business letters, official announcements and formal notices.
sections[].tip: ～において = ～で (formal). ～における = ～での (formal, before nouns). This conversion helps you understand them: 学校で → 学校において, 学校での → 学校における.
～に即して stresses the connection to reality. It is often used when criticizing something as too theoretical and calling for it to be adapted to reality.
Difference: ～に即して = adapted to reality (flexible). ～に準じて = in accordance with an existing standard (rule-based). Both are formal, but the point of reference differs.
The polite form をもちまして is used especially often at the end of events and ceremonies: 以上をもちまして... (With this, ...). Learn this phrase as a set formula.
sections[].examples[].de: This conference will be held in Tokyo.
The role of technology in modern society is immeasurable.
In the field of education, Japan maintains a high standard.
It is necessary to take measures that are grounded in reality.
Laws should be revised in keeping with the times.
There is a demand for education that fits the actual circumstances of each region.
Part-time employees also receive treatment in line with that of regular employees.
Please handle this in accordance with precedent.
Employees in positions equivalent to management are also covered.
We will contact you in writing.
As of today, this service will be discontinued.
We will respond with sincerity.

en.title: ～に伴って・につれて
en.subtitle: Correlated change — "The more X, the more Y"
en.intro: This lesson covers two important N2 grammar points that both express correlated change: when X changes, Y changes proportionally along with it. Both expressions are extremely common in everyday life and in exam texts. ～に伴って emphasizes that one change accompanies or causes another, while ～につれて describes a gradual, parallel change. The difference is subtle, but important for the N2 exam.
sections[].heading: ～に伴って / に伴い — Along with / Accompanying
～につれて / につれ — The more... the more...
Comparison and usage
sections[].text: ～に伴って (にともなって) expresses that a change or event brings about or accompanies another change. It's often used for larger social or natural changes.
