The construction is: noun + に伴って or verb (辞書形) + のに伴って. The more formal variant ～に伴い is preferred in written texts. Before nouns, ～に伴う is used.

～につれて expresses that two things change in parallel and gradually. It emphasizes the gradual nature: the more one increases, the more the other changes. The construction is: verb (辞書形) + につれて or noun + につれて. Unlike ～に伴って, ～につれて only fits gradual changes, not sudden events.

Both expressions are often translated as "with" or "the more... the more...", but they aren't always interchangeable. ～に伴って emphasizes causation or an accompanying effect: one thing brings about the other. ～につれて emphasizes parallelism: both things change simultaneously and gradually. With gradual changes both can be used, but with one-off events only ～に伴って.
sections[].tip: ～に伴って can also be used with one-off events (e.g. 引っ越しに伴って = "in connection with the move"), not just with gradual changes.
Remember: ～につれて = always a gradual, parallel change. ～に伴って = can also describe one-off events or accompanying effects.
The N2 exam likes to ask about the difference. Rule of thumb: if it's a one-off event with consequences → に伴って. If it's a slow, parallel change → につれて (or に伴って).
sections[].examples[].de: With the growth of the population, the housing problem is becoming more serious.
Along with economic development, environmental destruction also advanced.
Please be on the alert for heavy rain accompanying the typhoon.
As you get older, your physical strength declines.
As I've studied Japanese, I've also become interested in Japanese culture.
As spring approaches, the days have been getting longer.
As technology has advanced, life has become more convenient. (Gradual → both OK)
A tsunami occurred along with the earthquake. (One-off → only に伴って)
As the temperature rose, the snow began to melt.

en.title: The past with た
en.subtitle: What happened yesterday
en.intro: The past tense in Japanese is surprisingly straightforward — especially if you already know the て-form from Lesson 9. That's because the た-form follows exactly the same sound pattern. Just replace て with た (and で with だ), done. That means: if you can do the て-form, you basically get the past for free. And best of all: Japanese doesn't distinguish between the simple past and the present perfect ("I ate" vs. "I have eaten") — た covers both.
sections[].heading: た-form = て-form, just with た
Polite past: ました / ませんでした
Adjectives in the past
Nouns in the past
The た-form beyond the past
sections[].text: Forming the た-form follows the same rules as the て-form. You simply swap て for た and で for だ. All groups (る-verbs, う-verbs, irregular verbs) work identically. So if you've already mastered the て-form, you'll feel right at home here:

In polite speech, the past is even easier — you don't need the た-form here at all. You simply take the ます-form and change it. This works the same way for all verbs, without exception. There are only two forms you need:

Adjectives can be put in the past too. With い-adjectives, い becomes かった (positive) or くなかった (negative). With な-adjectives, the だ/です at the end changes to だった/でした. The adjective itself stays unchanged.
Nouns with です/だ follow the same pattern as な-adjectives. That makes sense, since な-adjectives behave like nouns anyway. So the forms are identical:
Surprisingly, the た-form isn't used only for the past. It also shows up in other contexts that have nothing to do with "yesterday":
sections[].tip: You still need the た-form (plain past): in subordinate clauses and before のに, から, と思う and many other constructions, the plain form is always used. So: ました for the main clause, た for the subordinate clause.

Once you've got the て-form down, the た-form comes free — the formation is identical, only the last sound changes. And the た-form is just as versatile as the て-form: it's the key to conditionals (たら), experiences (たことがある) and much more.
sections[].examples[].de: ate (る-verb)
bought (う→って→った)
drank (む→んで→んだ)
ate (polite)
went (polite)
didn't eat (polite, negative)
was expensive (い-adj.: い → かった)
wasn't expensive (い → くなかった)
was delicious (polite)
was a student (polite)
was a student (casual)
It wasn't a day off.
If it rains, I won't go. (た + ら = conditional, future!)
Oh, there it is! / Found it! (discovery in the present)
It was tomorrow, right? (double-checking something in the future)

en.title: ～を契機に・をきっかけに
en.subtitle: Seizing the moment — triggers and turning points
en.intro: This lesson introduces two expressions that describe the occasion or trigger for a change. ～を契機に (をけいきに) is more formal and is used for significant turning points, while ～をきっかけに is more everyday and suits personal triggers. Both answer the question "What prompted...?" and come up often in the N2 exam.
sections[].heading: ～をきっかけに / きっかけで — Prompted by / Triggered by
～を契機に / を契機として — With... as a turning point
sections[].text: きっかけ means "occasion, impetus, trigger" and describes the event that gave the initial push for a change. The construction is: Noun + をきっかけに/で or Verb (た-form) + のをきっかけに. It is used in both everyday and written language and is especially suited to personal experiences and turning points.

～を契機に (をけいきに) is the more formal variant and is used for significant social or historical turning points. 契機 means "opportunity, decisive moment, turning point". The construction is: Noun + を契機に/として. This expression sounds weightier than きっかけ and often appears in news articles, reports and formal analyses.
sections[].tip: きっかけ is also very commonly used as a standalone noun: 「日本語を勉強するきっかけは何ですか」 (What got you started learning Japanese?) — a popular conversation question!
を契機に sounds formal and weighty — use it for major events and social changes. For personal, everyday experiences, をきっかけに is more natural.
sections[].examples[].de: Studying abroad was what got me started learning Japanese.
A friend inviting me was what got me started playing tennis.
Getting sick was what made me start taking care of my health.
The Olympics prompted a major upgrade of the infrastructure.
The earthquake disaster became a turning point that raised awareness of disaster preparedness.
The change in the law prompted a major change in the way people work.

en.title: ～に基づいて
en.subtitle: On the basis of — well-founded and justified
en.intro: The expression ～に基づいて (にもとづいて) means "on the basis of" or "based on" and expresses that an action, decision or statement rests on something concrete — data, laws, experience, facts. It is everywhere in formal writing, reports, news and legal contexts and is part of the standard N2 vocabulary.
sections[].heading: ～に基づいて / に基づき — Based on / On the basis of
Comparison with similar expressions
sections[].text: 基づく (もとづく) is a verb meaning "to be based on, to rest on". In the て-form it is used adverbially: Noun + に基づいて means "on the basis of X". The more formal short form ～に基づき is preferred in official texts. Typical nouns that come before it are: データ (data), 法律 (law), 経験 (experience), 事実 (facts), 調査 (survey), 原則 (principles).

Several expressions mean "based on", but each has its own focus. ～に基づいて stresses a solid, reliable foundation (facts, laws, data). ～をもとに is less formal and means more like "using as source material" — it implies that something new is created from it. ～によると names a source ("according to") and is used for quotes and reports.
sections[].tip: The attributive form ～に基づいた/に基づく comes directly before a noun: 「データに基づいた判断」 (a data-based decision). Both forms (に基づいた and に基づく) are correct.
Rule of thumb: に基づいて = solid basis (law, data). をもとに = creative source material (story, idea). によると = source of information (news, person).
sections[].examples[].de: A new policy was decided on based on the survey results.
Appropriate measures will be taken in accordance with the law.
Allow me to offer you some advice based on my many years of experience.
The analysis was carried out based on actual data. (Solid basis)
This film was made based on a true story. (Source material)
According to the weather forecast, it's supposed to rain tomorrow. (Source)

en.title: ～を問わず・にかかわらず
en.subtitle: No matter what — regardless of conditions
en.intro: This lesson covers two expressions that both mean "regardless of" or "whether or not" and lift restrictions. ～を問わず sets aside a specific category or condition, while ～にかかわらず expresses "despite" or "irrespective of" more generally. Both are extremely common in job ads, official texts, rules and announcements and are core N2 knowledge.
sections[].heading: ～を問わず / を問わない — Regardless of / Whether or not
～にかかわらず / にかかわりなく — Regardless of / Despite
sections[].text: 問う (とう) means "to ask, to question". So ～を問わず literally means "without asking about" — that is, "regardless of, whether or not". It is used to say that a certain category or condition does not matter. The construction is: Noun + を問わず. It often goes with contrasting pairs such as 男女 (men/women) or 経験の有無 (whether or not one has experience), and with nouns covering a whole range, such as 年齢 (age) or 国籍 (nationality).

～にかかわらず means "regardless of, without regard to, despite" and is a bit more general than ～を問わず. It can be used with nouns, contrasting pairs or whole clauses. The construction is: Noun + にかかわらず or Verb (辞書形/ない形) + にかかわらず. The variant にかかわりなく has the same meaning.
sections[].tip: ～を問わず is especially popular in job ads. Memorize combinations like 年齢を問わず, 経験を問わず, 男女を問わず — they come up regularly in the N2 exam.
Difference: ～を問わず sets aside categories (age, gender, experience). ～にかかわらず can be used more broadly and can also take clauses (whether X or not).
sections[].examples[].de: Anyone can take part, regardless of age.
We are hiring regardless of experience.
We hire capable people regardless of gender.
The event will be held regardless of the weather.
Whether people agree or not, this plan will go ahead.
Regardless of the result, there is meaning in having given it your all.

en.title: ～上で・上は
en.subtitle: With regard to — context and condition
en.intro: The expression ～上で (うえで) has two different meanings depending on context: "in / with regard to" and "after / once". On top of that there is ～上は (うえは), meaning "now that..., then". All three belong to the standard N2 repertoire and are very common in formal texts, instructions and advice. Telling the meanings apart correctly is a popular exam topic.
sections[].heading: ～上で① — With regard to / In / For
～上で② — After / Only once
～上は — Now that... then...
sections[].text: In its first meaning, ～上で expresses the area or context in which something is relevant. It answers the question "In what respect?" The construction is: Noun + の + 上で or Verb (辞書形) + 上で. Typical contexts are: 仕事の上で (at work), 健康の上で (with regard to health), 生活する上で (for living). This meaning is often used for advice and important notes.

In its second meaning, ～上で expresses that one action must be completed before the next one begins. It stresses that the first action is a necessary prerequisite. The construction is: Verb (た-form) + 上で. Note: with the た-form = "after"; with 辞書形 = "in / for" (first meaning).

～上は (うえは) expresses that, because of a certain situation or decision, you accept a responsibility or consequence. It means: "Now that things are this way, you also have to..." The construction is: Verb (た-form) + 上は or Verb (辞書形) + 上は. The second half of the sentence often contains determination, obligation or a consequence.
sections[].tip: This meaning of ～上で can often be translated as "when..." or "for...". Pay attention to the context — if it's about an area or aspect, it's this meaning.
Rule of thumb for telling them apart: Verb (辞書形) + 上で = "in, for" (context). Verb (た-form) + 上で = "after" (order in time).
～上は always expresses determination or a sense of duty. It is often combined with expressions like ～なければならない, ～つもりだ, ～しかない.
sections[].examples[].de: For living in Japan, Japanese is indispensable.
There are several points to watch out for when signing a contract.
What matters most at work is the ability to communicate.
I will give you my answer after thinking it over carefully.
I'd like to talk it over with my parents first and then decide.
Please read the instructions before use.
Now that I've taken it on, I intend to see it through to the end.
Once you've made a promise, you have to keep it.
Now that things have come to this, all I can do is resign myself to it.

en.title: ～に応じて
en.subtitle: Responding flexibly — depending on the situation
en.intro: The expression ～に応じて (におうじて) means "depending on", "according to" or "in line with" and expresses that an action or state adapts flexibly to the circumstances at hand. It is used very often in professional contexts, instructions and official texts and is a core N2 grammar point.
sections[].heading: ～に応じて / に応じた — Depending on / In line with
Comparison: に応じて vs. によって vs. 次第で
sections[].text: 応じる (おうじる) means "to respond to, to correspond to, to adapt". ～に応じて expresses that something is adapted flexibly to a condition or situation. The construction is: Noun + に応じて. The attributive form ～に応じた comes before nouns. Common nouns are: 状況 (situation), ニーズ (needs), 能力 (ability), 予算 (budget), 希望 (wishes), 年齢 (age).

All three can mean "depending on", but with different nuances. ～に応じて stresses flexible adaptation to changing conditions. ～によって stresses difference — the result differs depending on who or what it is. ～次第で stresses dependence — the result depends entirely on it. In many cases they are interchangeable, but the nuances make the difference.
sections[].tip: に応じて stresses flexibility — it's always about something adapting to changing conditions. When the condition changes, the result changes too.
The N2 exam likes to ask about these differences. Remember: に応じて = adaptation, によって = difference, 次第で = dependence.
sections[].examples[].de: Salary is determined according to ability.
We provide services tailored to our customers' needs.
The plan may be changed depending on the situation.
We'll suggest a plan to suit your budget. (Flexible adaptation)
Opinions differ from person to person. (Difference)
The results change depending on your effort. (Complete dependence)

en.title: ～にわたって
en.subtitle: All the way across — extent and duration
en.intro: The expression ～にわたって (にわたって) means "over", "throughout" or "extending over" and describes something that covers a long period, a wide area or a broad scope. It stresses extent and breadth and is often used in news, reports and formal texts. An N2 classic that shows up in almost every exam.
sections[].heading: ～にわたって / にわたり / にわたる — Over / Extending over
Typical combinations and exam tips
sections[].text: In this context, わたる (渡る/亘る) means "to extend over". ～にわたって expresses that something lasts or extends over a long period, wide area or broad scope. The construction is: Noun + にわたって. The more formal variant ～にわたり is used in written texts. Before nouns, ～にわたる is used. Typical nouns are: 時間 (hours), 年 (years), 地域 (region), 分野 (field), ページ (pages).

In the N2 exam, ～にわたって appears regularly in reading passages and grammar questions. Combinations with time expressions (何年にもわたって = over many years) and expressions of scope (多岐にわたって = extending across many fields) are especially common. The attributive form ～にわたる + noun is also very common.
sections[].tip: ～にわたって always stresses that something is large, long or extensive. It would be unnatural to say "5分にわたって" — the period or scope has to be impressive.
Remember the three forms: にわたって (adverbial), にわたり (formal adverbial), にわたる (before nouns). All three have the same meaning but different grammatical functions.
sections[].examples[].de: The negotiations went on over three days.
Damage occurred over a wide area.
He has continued his research in this field for many years.
He is active in a wide range of fields.
It is a tradition that has been handed down over centuries.
The results of ten years of research have finally been published.

en.title: ～をめぐって
en.subtitle: Contested and debated — debates and conflicts
en.intro: The expression ～をめぐって means "concerning", "around" or "over" and is used specifically for topics that are the subject of debate, conflict, disagreement or discussion. It is not a neutral "concerning" — it always implies that different parties take different positions. An important N2 expression for news and social issues.
sections[].heading: ～をめぐって / をめぐり / をめぐる — Over / Around (a point of dispute)
Telling them apart: をめぐって vs. について vs. に関して
sections[].text: めぐる literally means "to go around, to revolve around", and in this grammar point: "to revolve around a topic". ～をめぐって expresses that different opinions or positions revolve around a contested issue. The construction is: Noun + をめぐって. Before nouns, ～をめぐる is used. Typical words that follow are: 議論 (discussion), 対立 (confrontation), 論争 (controversy), 問題 (problem), 争い (dispute).

All three can mean "concerning", but the tone is completely different. ～について is neutral and general: "about, concerning". ～に関して is more formal, but also neutral. ～をめぐって, on the other hand, always implies controversy and differing positions. If you have to choose in the exam, look out for keywords like 議論, 対立, 意見, 問題 — they point to ～をめぐって.
sections[].tip: ～をめぐって always implies disagreement or conflict. Don't use it for neutral topics — that's what ～について or ～に関して are for.
Memory aid: picture different people standing around the topic, arguing heatedly — that's the image of をめぐって.
sections[].examples[].de: There is fierce debate over the new bill.
The conflict over the territorial issue has gone on for many years.
The siblings are fighting over the inheritance.
We talked about Japanese culture. (Neutral)
Do you have any questions regarding this matter? (Formal, neutral)
The ruling and opposition parties are at odds over this policy. (Controversial)

en.title: ～に先立って
en.subtitle: Before it all begins — preparation and precedence
en.intro: The expression ～に先立って (にさきだって) means "before / ahead of / prior to" and is used when an action takes place as preparation or a prerequisite before an important event. It is more formal than ～前に and often implies that the earlier action is carried out deliberately and according to plan. An important N2 expression for formal announcements and reports.
sections[].heading: ～に先立って / に先立ち / に先立つ — Ahead of / Prior to
Typical contexts and exam tips
sections[].text: 先立つ (さきだつ) means "to precede, to go before". ～に先立って expresses that an action takes place ahead of an important event — often as preparation, an announcement or a necessary step. The construction is: Noun + に先立って. The more formal form ～に先立ち is used in official texts. The attributive form ～に先立つ comes before nouns.

～に先立って appears especially often in contexts such as opening ceremonies, product launches, official events, construction projects and travel. In the N2 exam it is often used in reading passages about events or official procedures. Look out for formal nouns like 開催 (holding an event), 実施 (implementation), 着工 (start of construction).
sections[].tip: ～に先立って sounds formal and planned. For a simple everyday "before", use ～前に. ～に先立って implies: "As important preparation before the big event..."
Remember the three forms: に先立って (te-form), に先立ち (formal), に先立つ (before nouns). All three can come up in the exam.
sections[].examples[].de: Ahead of the opening ceremony, a meeting of those involved was held.
Prior to the release, a prototype was unveiled to the public.
Please carry out a safety check before departure.
Ahead of the film's release, a special preview screening was held.
Before the exam was held, the examinees were briefed on the instructions.
Before the new semester starts, you need to buy your textbooks.

en.title: ～を通じて・を通して
en.subtitle: Through and through — means and time span
en.intro: The expressions ～を通じて (をつうじて) and ～を通して (をとおして) have two meanings: "through / by means of" (a means or intermediary) and "throughout" (an entire period). The two are largely interchangeable, with ～を通じて sounding a bit more formal. They are basic N2 knowledge and appear frequently in reading passages.
sections[].heading: ～を通じて① / を通して① — Through / By means of / Via
～を通じて② / を通して② — Throughout / During the entire...
sections[].text: In their first meaning, ～を通じて and ～を通して express that something serves as a means, channel or intermediary. It answers the question "In what way?" or "Through whom/what?" The construction is: Noun + を通じて/を通して. Typical nouns are: インターネット (internet), 友人 (friend), 経験 (experience), メディア (media).

In their second meaning, both expressions say that something applies throughout an entire period or area — from beginning to end, without interruption. The construction is again: Noun + を通じて/を通して. Typical nouns are: 一年 (a year), 人生 (life), 四季 (the four seasons).
sections[].tip: In the meaning "through/by means of", を通じて and を通して are almost always interchangeable. を通じて sounds a bit more formal.
The two meanings are easy to tell apart: if it's about a period of time (一年, 人生, 四季), it means "throughout". If it's about a means (internet, friend, experience), it means "through/by means of".
sections[].examples[].de: Through the internet, you can connect with people all over the world.
I got to know him through a friend.
I learned a lot through volunteer work.
This region has a mild climate all year round.
It is important to keep learning throughout your life.
This museum is open all year round.

en.title: ～に際して
en.subtitle: On this occasion — formal and solemn
en.intro: The expression ～に際して (にさいして) means "on the occasion of", "at the time of" or "when" and is used for special, important occasions. It is more formal than ～時に and implies that the occasion is significant. ～に際して often appears in speeches, official announcements and formal letters — and, of course, in the N2 exam.
sections[].heading: ～に際して / に際し / に際しての — On the occasion of / When / In the event of
Comparison: に際して vs. にあたって vs. 時に
sections[].text: 際する (さいする) means "to be at an occasion". ～に際して expresses that you are in a special situation or at an important occasion and are doing something or need to keep something in mind. The construction is: Noun + に際して or Verb (辞書形) + に際して. The more formal short form ～に際し is used in written texts. Before nouns, ～に際しての is used.

All three can mean "at, on the occasion of, when", but with different levels of formality and different nuances. ～時に is neutral and everyday: "when". ～にあたって stresses the beginning or start of an important undertaking and often carries determination. ～に際して stresses the special occasion and is the most formal. In many cases, にあたって and に際して are interchangeable.
sections[].tip: ～に際して is used almost exclusively for important, formal occasions. For everyday situations like "when shopping" or "when I get home", ～時に is more natural.
Rule of thumb: everyday life → 時に. A new start with determination → にあたって. A formal, special occasion → に際して.
sections[].examples[].de: Please submit several documents upon enrollment.
When traveling abroad, we recommend taking out insurance.
When starting the new business, we conducted market research.
When I left, I checked that I hadn't forgotten anything. (Neutral)
As the new fiscal year began, I set myself new goals. (Beginning, determination)
Many people kindly helped us in holding the ceremony. (Formal occasion)

en.title: Negation
en.subtitle: Saying no in Japanese
en.intro: In Japanese, you negate at the end of the sentence — and it works a little differently depending on whether it's a verb, an adjective or a noun. What all negatives have in common: they somehow end in ない (or its polite version ません). Once you recognize this pattern, negation will never give you a headache again. Here's the complete overview — casual and polite, present and past.
sections[].heading: Negating verbs
Negating い-adjectives
Negating な-adjectives & nouns
Not yet: まだ～ていない
Negation as a suggestion: ～ませんか
sections[].text: In the polite form, ます simply becomes ません — this applies to all verbs without exception. In the plain form (casual), the ending becomes ない, but how you form it depends on the verb type. For る-verbs: る → ない. For う-verbs: the last syllable shifts to the あ-row and then ない is added (e.g. 行く → 行かない, 飲む → 飲まない, 話す → 話さない).

With い-adjectives, い is replaced by くない. Since ない is itself an い-adjective, you can keep conjugating it: くなかった (was not), くなくて (not and...). The system is refreshingly regular — with one famous exception.

な-adjectives and nouns are negated identically — logical, since な-adjectives behave like nouns. Negation uses じゃない (casual) or じゃありません (polite). The じゃ is a contraction of では, and in very formal contexts you'll also hear ではありません.

"Not yet" is expressed with まだ + て-form + いない/いません. It's a combination of the adverb まだ (still/yet) and the ている construction (resulting state) in the negative. It expresses that an expected action hasn't happened so far.

An elegant use of the negative: ～ませんか is a polite invitation. Literally you're asking "Won't you do it?", but what you mean is "Shall we...?" or "Wouldn't you like to...?". It sounds more inviting and more polite than a direct question.
sections[].tip: Two special cases: ある (to exist) becomes ない (not あらない!) — that's the only exception among う-verbs. And する/来る: する → しない, 来る → 来ない (こない).
Special case: いい (good) becomes よくない, NOT いくない! That's because いい historically comes from よい. All conjugations of いい are based on よ-: よくない, よかった, よくなかった.
ではない is the more formal/written variant, じゃない the casual/spoken one — both mean the same thing. In essays and formal speeches: ではありません. Talking with friends: じゃない.
Don't confuse まだ～ていない (haven't done yet) with もう～ない (no longer). もう食べない = I don't eat it anymore / I won't eat any more. まだ食べていない = I haven't eaten yet.
sections[].examples[].de: don't eat (polite)
don't eat (casual, る-verb: る → ない)
don't go (casual, く → かない)
do → not do (irregular)
there is → there isn't (special case: NOT あらない!)
not expensive
not hot (polite)
wasn't delicious (past)
not quiet (casual)
not quiet (polite)
am not a student (polite)
I haven't eaten yet. (polite)
I haven't decided yet. (casual)
I haven't done my homework yet.
Won't you eat with me?
Shall we watch a movie?
Would you like some tea?

en.title: ～次第で・次第だ
en.subtitle: It depends — dependence and immediate action
en.intro: The word 次第 (しだい) is extremely versatile and has two main uses in N2 grammar: ～次第で means "depending on / it depends on", and ～次第 (after the verb stem) means "as soon as". Both uses are equally important in the exam and in everyday life. This lesson explains both meanings with clear examples.
sections[].heading: ～次第で / 次第だ — It depends on / Depending on
～次第 — As soon as / Immediately when
sections[].text: ～次第で expresses that the result depends entirely on a condition. It stresses the decisive role of this condition — if it changes, everything changes. The construction is: Noun + 次第で (adverbial) or Noun + 次第だ (predicative). It is often combined with words like 努力 (effort), やり方 (way of doing things), 考え方 (way of thinking), 天気 (weather).

After the verb stem (ます-stem), 次第 means "as soon as, right after". It expresses that you will do something immediately once an action is completed. The construction is: Verb (ます-stem) + 次第. This expression is formal and is often used in business contexts, especially in promises and announcements.
sections[].tip: ～次第で stresses complete dependence: "Everything hinges on X." It is stronger than に応じて, which expresses flexible adaptation instead.
Verb stem + 次第 is very handy in business Japanese. It expresses readiness and speed — "I'm just waiting for X, and then I'll act right away."
sections[].examples[].de: Whether you succeed or not depends on your effort.
Depending on how you go about it, the result can change a lot.
Depending on how you look at it, even a difficulty can become an opportunity.
We will contact you as soon as it arrives.
We will let you know by email as soon as it has been decided.
Let's set off as soon as we're ready.

en.title: ～たところ
en.subtitle: When I tried it — surprising results
en.intro: The expression ～たところ has different meanings depending on context, but the most important N2 meaning is: "when I did X, it turned out that..." It describes an action and its (often surprising) result. It expresses that you tried or did something and in doing so discovered a result you hadn't necessarily expected.
sections[].heading: ～たところ — When I did..., (it turned out that...)
Other uses of ところ
sections[].text: Verb (た-form) + ところ expresses that you carried out an action and in doing so came upon a result or discovery. It often implies that the result was unexpected or noteworthy. The construction is: Verb (た-form) + ところ + result. The second half of the sentence describes the result — what happened or what you found out.

ところ (place, point) is used in many grammar expressions. Verb (辞書形) + ところだ = "I'm just about to". Verb (ている) + ところだ = "I'm right in the middle of it". Verb (た) + ところだ = "I've just done it". These describe the point in time of an action and should be kept apart from the main meaning in this lesson.
sections[].tip: ～たところ ≠ ～た時に! ～た時に is neutral (when I...). ～たところ implies a result that you found out or experienced through the action — often with a moment of surprise.
Distinguish: ～たところ (result/discovery) vs. ～たところだ (just now). The key is the sentence pattern: ～たところ + new fact = result. ～たところだ at the end of the sentence = point in time.
sections[].examples[].de: When I asked the teacher, he said the test is next week.
When I took the medicine, my fever went down right away.
When I looked into it, the information turned out to be wrong.
I'm just about to head out. (About to)
I'm in the middle of eating right now. (In the middle of it)
I've only just this moment got home. (Just now)

en.title: ～ものの・とはいえ
en.subtitle: Granted... but — limitations and contradictions
en.intro: This lesson covers two concessive expressions that both mean "although" or "it's true that... but". ～ものの concedes something and then adds a limiting or contradictory reality. ～とはいえ goes one step further and says: "Even if you say/claim that, reality is different." Both are typical N2 grammar points and often appear in argumentative texts.
sections[].heading: ～ものの — Granted... but / Although... still
～とはいえ — Even though it's said that... / Nevertheless
sections[].text: ～ものの expresses that while something is true, the result or reality turns out differently than expected. It concedes the first fact but qualifies it in the second part. The construction is: Verb (普通形) + ものの, い-Adj + ものの, な-Adj + な/である + ものの, Noun + である + ものの. The second half of the sentence contains a negative surprise, a problem or a limitation.

～とはいえ is made up of と (quotation), は (topic) and いえ (say; a classical form of 言う). Literally: "Even if one says (that)..." It concedes a general statement, assumption or claim, but points out that reality isn't that simple. The construction is: Clause (普通形) + とはいえ or Noun + とはいえ.
sections[].tip: ～ものの often expresses frustration or disappointment: "I tried so hard, but still..." It is more formal than ～けど and is often used in written texts.
～とはいえ is more elegant and analytical than ～ものの. It is often used to concede a widely held opinion and then add a more nuanced view.
sections[].examples[].de: Although I've studied Japanese for three years, I still can't speak it well.
I bought a new computer, but I don't know how to use it.
I got the qualification, but I can't find a job.
It may be spring, but the cold days are still continuing.
Children though they may be, they should still mind their manners.
Even if it's safe, you must never let your guard down.

en.title: ～わけにはいかない
en.subtitle: That just won't do — moral duty and social norms
en.intro: The expression ～わけにはいかない means "I can't just..." or "it won't do to..." and expresses that something cannot be done for moral, social or situational reasons — even if you might want to or be able to. It's not about physical inability but about a sense of duty, social norms or the circumstances. An essential N2 expression.
sections[].heading: ～わけにはいかない — I can't just...
～ないわけにはいかない — I have to... (double negative)
sections[].text: わけ means "reason, sense", and ～わけにはいかない literally means "there is no reason why I could do that" — in other words, the circumstances don't allow it. It expresses that an action is not justifiable for moral, social or situational reasons. The construction is: Verb (辞書形) + わけにはいかない. It is often used for things you would like to do but can't out of a sense of responsibility.

The double-negative form ～ないわけにはいかない means "I have to do something" — the circumstances leave me no other choice. Literally: "It won't do not to do it." The construction is: Verb (ない-form) + わけにはいかない. It sounds stronger than ～なければならない because it stresses the necessity arising from the situation.
sections[].tip: ～わけにはいかない ≠ ～できない! できない = physical/technical inability. わけにはいかない = social/moral impossibility. "I could, but I mustn't / shouldn't."
The double negative sounds a bit clumsy in English, but it is perfectly natural in Japanese. It expresses a stronger obligation than a simple ～なければならない.
sections[].examples[].de: Even though I'm not feeling well, I can't just take today off.
Since I've been told the secret, I can't go telling other people.
When everyone is working so hard, I can't be the only one to go home.
Since I've been invited, I have to go.
Since my boss asked me, I can't not refuse... no wait, I can't refuse.
For the sake of my child's future, I have to work.

en.title: ～ざるを得ない
en.subtitle: I have no other choice — inevitability
en.intro: The expression ～ざるを得ない (ざるをえない) means "I cannot help but..." or "I have no choice but to..." and expresses that you have to do something even though you don't really want to. It's a formal way of saying: "The circumstances force me to." This expression uses the classical negative form ～ざる and sounds very refined.
sections[].heading: ～ざるを得ない — There's no choice but to...
Comparison: ざるを得ない vs. わけにはいかない vs. しかない
sections[].text: ～ざる is the classical Japanese negative form (like ～ない, but from Old Japanese). 得ない (えない) means "cannot". Together: "One cannot not do it" = "One has to do it." The construction is: Verb (ない-stem) + ざるを得ない. Exception: する → せざるを得ない (not しざる!). It expresses a reluctant necessity — you'd rather not, but the circumstances leave no choice.

All three express necessity, but with different nuances. ～ざるを得ない = "The circumstances force me" (reluctant, formal). ～ないわけにはいかない = "Social/moral duty doesn't allow otherwise." ～しかない = "There is no other option" (matter-of-fact, neutral). ～ざるを得ない is the most formal and expresses the strongest sense of reluctance.
sections[].tip: Watch out with する: the form is せざるを得ない, NOT しざるを得ない. This is one of the most common sources of mistakes in the N2 exam!
In the N2 exam, these three are often offered as answer choices. Pay attention to the context: reluctance → ざるを得ない, social duty → わけにはいかない, no alternative → しかない.
sections[].examples[].de: Now that the evidence is all there, there's no choice but to admit it.
Because of the budget, we had no choice but to change the plan.
I'm not feeling well, so I have no choice but to give up on taking part.
It's an order from my boss, so I have no choice but to obey. (Reluctant)
Since I've been invited, I have to attend. (Social duty)
There's no other way, so I'll just have to walk. (Matter-of-fact)

en.title: ～かねる・かねない
en.subtitle: Not even with the best will — and: it could happen
en.intro: The expressions ～かねる and ～かねない look similar but have completely different meanings. ～かねる means "I'm afraid I can't..." (polite refusal), while ～かねない means "it could very well happen that..." (negative possibility). Both are important N2 points and are often confused in the exam — which is exactly why it's important to learn them together.
sections[].heading: ～かねる — I'm afraid I can't... (polite refusal)
～かねない — It could very well happen that... (warning)
sections[].text: In this context, かねる (兼ねる) means "to be unable" and is used as a polite, indirect refusal. It expresses: "I'd like to, but unfortunately I can't." The construction is: Verb (ます-stem) + かねる. This expression is extremely common in business Japanese and comes across as much more polite than a direct ～できません.

～かねない is the negative of かねる and literally means "it's not that it can't happen" — in other words, there is a risk that something negative will happen. The construction is: Verb (ます-stem) + かねない. It is used almost exclusively for negative, undesirable possibilities and serves as a warning.
sections[].tip: ～かねます is the standard polite form in customer service and business. Where an English speaker would say "I'm afraid that's not possible", a Japanese speaker says ～かねます.
Memory aid: かねる = "can't" (polite). かねない = "may well" (warning). The negative completely reverses the meaning — a typical N2 pitfall!
sections[].examples[].de: I'm afraid I'm unable to comment on that matter.
I'm afraid we are unable to accommodate your request.
I'm afraid I can't agree under these conditions.
If you push yourself that hard, you could collapse.
If this problem is left as it is, it could lead to a serious accident.
Careless remarks could lead to misunderstandings.

en.title: ～っぽい・がち・気味
en.subtitle: Tendencies, inclinations, a touch of...
en.intro: This lesson covers three suffixes that all express some kind of tendency or inclination, but with different nuances. ～っぽい means "-ish, -like" and expresses an impression. ～がち means "tending to, often" and describes an undesirable tendency. ～気味 means "a touch of, slightly" and describes a mild state. All three are N2 classics.
sections[].heading: ～っぽい — -ish / -like / Seems like...
～がち — Tending to / Often (undesirable)
～気味 — A touch of / Slightly / Somewhat
sections[].text: ～っぽい attaches to nouns, verbs (ます-stem) or adjective stems and expresses that something gives the impression or appearance of something — even if it may not actually be that. The construction is: Noun/Verb stem/Adj stem + っぽい. It is conjugated like an い-adjective (っぽくない, っぽかった). It can be neutral or slightly negative.

～がち expresses that someone or something has an undesirable tendency — something happens more often than you'd like. The construction is: Verb (ます-stem) + がち or Noun + がち. ～がち is used like a な-adjective (がちな, がちに). It almost always has a negative connotation.

～気味 (ぎみ) expresses that a state is present slightly, to some degree — not fully developed, but noticeable. The construction is: Verb (ます-stem) + 気味 or Noun + 気味. ～気味 is treated like a な-adjective or a noun. It is often used for physical conditions and general tendencies.
sections[].tip: っぽい with colors = "-ish" (whitish, bluish). With people = often negative (childish, forgetful, hot-tempered). With materials = "looks like" (安っぽい = looks cheap).
～がち always describes something undesirable. You don't say 「成功しがち」 (tends to succeed) — that would be unnatural. It is always about problematic tendencies.
Comparison: っぽい = impression/appearance (seems like X). がち = frequent negative tendency (tends to X). 気味 = mild state (somewhat X, a touch of X).
sections[].examples[].de: He has a short temper. (Tends to get angry)
This color is whitish. (Looks white)
I've become forgetful lately.
He tends to be late.
In winter, people tend to catch colds.
He's often away from home, so it's hard to see him.
I've been putting on a bit of weight lately.
I have a touch of a cold, so I'm going to bed early.
This project is running a bit behind schedule.

en.title: ～に限って・に限り
en.subtitle: Of all times! — limits and irony
en.intro: The expression ～に限って has two different uses: the first means "only, limited to" (a formal restriction), and the second expresses irony or astonishment: "Of all X..." Both meanings are relevant for N2 and are used in different contexts.
sections[].heading: ～に限り / に限って① — Only / Limited to
～に限って② — Of all... (irony)
sections[].text: 限る (かぎる) means "to limit, to restrict". In the first meaning, ～に限り/に限って expresses a formal restriction or limit. The construction is: Noun + に限り/に限って. This use is typical of rules, offers, announcements and official notices.

In the second meaning, ～に限って expresses irony, surprise or annoyance: "Of all situations, in this one..." or "Just when you don't need it..." It describes situations where Murphy's Law strikes — exactly what shouldn't happen does happen. The construction is: Noun + に限って.
sections[].tip: ～に限り is more formal than ～だけ and is used especially in promotions, regulations and official announcements.
The ironic meaning of ～に限って describes the feeling: "It always happens exactly when it's worst!" In the exam, pay attention to the context to tell the two meanings apart.
sections[].examples[].de: Today only: 20% off all items.
There is a special discount for members only.
Only one entry per person.
It always rains on the very day I don't have an umbrella.
It's precisely when you're in a hurry that the train is late.
My child, of all people, would never do such a thing. (A typical parent's remark)

en.title: ～向け・向き
en.subtitle: For whom? For what? — target audience and suitability
en.intro: The expressions ～向け (むけ) and ～向き (むき) both describe who or what something is intended or suitable for, but with different nuances. ～向け means "designed for / aimed specifically at" (a deliberate target group), while ～向き means "suitable for / well suited to" (natural suitability). Both are important in everyday life and in the N2 exam.
sections[].heading: ～向け — Specifically for... / Aimed at...
～向き — Suitable for / Well suited to
sections[].text: 向ける (むける) means "to point toward, to direct at". ～向け expresses that something was deliberately designed for a specific target group. It's an active choice by the manufacturer, author or provider. The construction is: Noun + 向け(の). Typical contexts are: products, books, courses, TV programs, websites.

向く (むく) means "to face, to suit". ～向き expresses that something is naturally suitable for someone or something — not necessarily designed that way on purpose, but simply a good fit. The construction is: Noun + 向き(の). It describes a natural suitability or fit.
sections[].tip: ～向け always implies a deliberate choice: someone made this product/offer specifically for this target group.
Difference: 子供向けの本 = a book written specifically for children. 子供向きの本 = a book that happens to be suitable for children as well. 向け = deliberately designed. 向き = naturally suitable.
sections[].examples[].de: This textbook is designed for beginners.
Anime made for children is popular.
I signed up for a Japanese course for foreigners.
This job is suited to meticulous people.
This spicy dish isn't suitable for children.
South-facing rooms are bright and warm.

en.title: ～末に・あげく
en.subtitle: After a long struggle — results after effort
en.intro: This lesson covers two expressions that both mean "after a long..." or "as a result of...", but with different nuances. ～末に describes a result after long deliberation or effort (neutral to positive). ～あげく describes a result after long effort that is disappointing or negative. The difference in connotation is crucial for the N2 exam.
sections[].heading: ～末に / 末の — At the end of / After a long...
～あげく(に) — After all that... and then (negative)
sections[].text: 末 (すえ) means "end, close". ～末に expresses that a result comes about after a long phase of effort, deliberation or struggle. It is neutral to positive — the result can be good or bad, but the effort is respected. The construction is: Verb (た-form) + 末に or Noun + の末に.

あげく (挙げ句) literally means "the final result" and expresses that after a long, arduous phase a disappointing or negative result comes about. The nuance is: "You tried so hard, and in the end it still went wrong." The construction is: Verb (た-form) + あげく(に) or Noun + の + あげく(に).
sections[].tip: ～末に is often combined with words like ようやく (finally) and ついに (at last), which reinforce the sense of relief after a long effort.
Remember: ～末に = result after effort (can be neutral/positive). ～あげく = result after effort (almost always negative/disappointing). In the exam, pay attention to the mood of the sentence!
sections[].examples[].de: After long discussions, an agreement was finally reached.
After agonizing over it, I decided to change jobs.
After much trial and error, I finally found a solution.
After going back and forth endlessly, I ended up buying nothing.
After hours of discussion, no conclusion was reached.
After a quarrel, the two of them ended up breaking up.

en.title: たい, ほしい, できる
en.subtitle: Wishes and abilities
en.intro: "I want to eat sushi!", "I'd like a coffee", "I can speak Japanese" — these three kinds of expressions cover a huge part of everyday life. Japanese has its own grammatical constructions for wishes and abilities, and they work quite differently from English "want", "would like" and "can". Especially important: in Japanese you only talk directly about your own wishes — putting other people's wishes into words is culturally delicate.
sections[].heading: たい — "I want to (do something)"
ほしい — "I'd like (a thing)"
てほしい — "I want someone to..."
できる — "I can"
sections[].text: たい attaches to the verb stem (ます-stem) and expresses your own wish to carry out an action. Once formed, the word behaves like an い-adjective — which means you can conjugate it: たくない (don't want to), たかった (wanted to), たくなかった (didn't want to). Also note: the object can be marked with either を or が — が puts more emphasis on the wish.

While たい is for actions (wanting to eat, wanting to go), ほしい expresses that you want to have a concrete object. It's an い-adjective, and the desired object is marked with が (not with を!). Like たい, ほしい mainly applies to your own wishes.

If you want someone else to do something, you combine the て-form with ほしい. The person you expect it from is marked with に. This construction is somewhat more direct than a request and expresses a genuine wish — it's softer than a command, but stronger than a mere question.

できる means "can / to be possible" and is extremely versatile. There are two main uses: with a noun + が (naming an ability directly) or with verb + ことが (expressing an action as something you "can" do). できる itself is a る-verb and conjugates completely normally: できます (polite), できない (can't), できた (could).
sections[].tip: Important cultural note: you only use たい for your own wishes or in direct questions to the person you're talking to. For the wishes of third persons you say たがっている (he/she shows signs of wanting to...) or rephrase with ようだ/らしい. Saying "He wants..." directly is considered presumptuous, because you can't look inside other people's heads.
As with たい: don't use ほしい to describe what OTHER people want. For third persons you say ほしがっている (he/she shows signs of wanting...). "He wants a car" = 彼は車をほしがっている, not 彼は車がほしい.

Besides ことができる there's also the potential form (食べる → 食べられる, 読む → 読める). It's shorter and used more often in everyday speech — it's covered in detail in lesson 35. To start with, できる is the safest way.
sections[].examples[].de: I want to eat.
I'd like to go to Japan. (polite)
What would you like to drink?
I want a new car.
What would you like?
I wish I'd had (more) time.
I want you to come.
I'd like the teacher to explain it.
I want you to be quiet.
I can speak Japanese. (noun + が + できる)
I can swim. (verb + こと + が + できる)
I can't cook.

en.title: ～にしたがって
en.subtitle: Following the flow — parallel change and compliance
en.intro: The expression ～にしたがって (に従って) has two main meanings: "the more... the more..." (parallel change, similar to ～につれて) and "in accordance with / according to" (following a rule or instruction). Both meanings derive from the verb 従う (したがう, "to follow, to obey") and are relevant for the N2 exam.
sections[].heading: ～にしたがって① — The more... the more... (parallel change)
～にしたがって② / に従い — In accordance with / Following (instructions)
sections[].text: In the first meaning, ～にしたがって describes a parallel, gradual change: when X changes, Y changes in proportion. The construction is: Verb (辞書形) + にしたがって. This meaning is very similar to ～につれて and ～に伴って, but にしたがって puts more emphasis on "following" — Y follows the change in X as a natural course of events.

In the second meaning, ～にしたがって expresses that you follow a rule, instruction, regulation or person. It means "according to, in accordance with, following". The construction is: Noun + にしたがって/に従い. The more formal variant ～に従い is preferred in official texts.
sections[].tip: にしたがって, につれて and に伴って overlap in the meaning "the more... the more...". With gradual changes, all three are often interchangeable.
The two meanings are easy to tell apart: if a verb comes before it (変わる, 進む) → parallel change. If a noun comes before it (指示, ルール, 命令) → following an instruction/rule.
sections[].examples[].de: The higher the altitude, the lower the temperature.
As urbanization advances, green spaces are shrinking.
As my Japanese improved, I also came to understand Japanese culture more deeply.
Please take the medicine as instructed by your doctor.
Please act in accordance with the rules.
Please follow the signs.

en.title: 質問のことば
en.subtitle: Question words — 何・誰・どこ・いつ・どう・なぜ
en.intro: Asking questions is the fastest way to learn a language — and in Japanese, question words are refreshingly simple. Unlike in English, you don't have to rearrange the word order: the question word simply slides into the spot of the information you're looking for, and か goes at the end of the sentence. In this lesson you'll learn the most important question words and see how flexibly they can be used. Don't be shy about asking lots of questions — Japanese people are happy about every question asked in Japanese!
sections[].heading: 何・誰・どこ・いつ — What, Who, Where, When
どう・なぜ/どうして — How and Why
いくら・いくつ — How much / How many
sections[].text: The four basic questions cover most everyday situations. 何 (なに/なん) asks about things ("what?"), 誰 (だれ) about people ("who?"), どこ about places ("where/where to?") and いつ about points in time ("when?"). Note: 何 becomes なん before certain sounds (e.g. 何ですか = なんですか), while before particles it often stays なに (何を = なにを). The question word goes exactly where the answer would normally be in the sentence.

どう asks about the manner ("how?") or about an opinion/assessment. なぜ and どうして both ask for the reason ("why?"), with どうして sounding somewhat softer and more conversational, while なぜ feels more written or formal. In everyday life you also often hear なんで, which is even more casual. The answer to a why-question typically contains から (because) at the end of the sentence.

いくら asks about price ("how much does it cost?") and is one of the most useful words when shopping. いくつ asks about quantity ("how many?") or about age (for children). Both words are indispensable in everyday life. For more specific quantities, counters are used: 何人 (なんにん, how many people), 何個 (なんこ, how many pieces), 何枚 (なんまい, how many flat things).
sections[].tip: いつ doesn't take に when it's used as a question word: いつ行きますか (When are you going?) — but the answer often needs に: 三時に行きます.
どう vs どうやって: どう asks about "how" in general (state/opinion), どうやって asks about the concrete method (how exactly do you do it?).
いくつですか can also mean "How old are you?" — but only with small children. With adults, it's more polite to ask: おいくつですか or 何歳ですか (なんさいですか).
sections[].examples[].de: What is this?
Who came?
Where is the restroom?
How do you find Japanese?
Why were you late?
Why are you studying Japanese?
How much is this?
How many apples are there?
How many of you are going?

en.title: いる & ある
en.subtitle: 存在動詞 — Verbs of existence
en.intro: Where English gets by with a single "there is", Japanese strictly distinguishes between living and non-living things. いる is for everything that can move of its own accord — people, animals, insects. ある is for everything else — books, buildings, ideas, appointments. This concept feels unfamiliar at first but quickly becomes second nature. These two verbs are among the most frequent words in Japanese, so it's worth internalizing them thoroughly.
sections[].heading: いる — For living beings
ある — For objects and abstract things
Negation and common patterns
sections[].text: いる (polite: います) expresses the existence or location of animate beings — people, animals, fish, insects. The basic structure is: place に + living being が + います (at place X there is Y) or living being は + place に + います (Y is at place X). The negative is いません, the past いました.

ある (polite: あります) is for inanimate things — objects, buildings, plants, abstract concepts and also appointments or events. The structure is identical to いる; only the verb changes: place に + thing が + あります. The negative is ありません, the past ありました. Important: plants use ある too, even though they're "alive" — they don't move on their own.

Negation works regularly for both verbs: いません / ありません (polite) or いない / ない (casual). A particularly useful pattern is the question 〜はありますか (do you have...?), which you need all the time when shopping. The combination with も (also/even) is important too: 何もない (there's nothing), 誰もいない (nobody is there).
sections[].tip: Robots and ghosts too: characters that are thought of as having a life of their own often take いる — e.g. ロボットがいる. When in doubt: can it move by itself? → いる.
ある is also used for events: パーティーがある (there's a party), 会議がある (there's a meeting). Even though people are involved, the event itself is inanimate.
Memory aid: question word + も + negative = total negation. 何も (nothing), 誰も (nobody), どこにも (nowhere). This works with all question words!
sections[].examples[].de: There's a cat in the garden.
Tanaka is in the classroom.
Do you have any siblings? (Literally: Are there siblings?)
There's a book on the desk.
The convenience store is over there.
There's a test tomorrow.
There's nothing in the fridge.
There's nobody in the room.
Excuse me, do you have size S?

en.title: 数え方の基本
en.subtitle: Counters — つ・人・個・枚・本・杯
en.intro: Japanese doesn't just count "one, two, three" — you almost always need a counter (助数詞, じょすうし) that matches the shape or kind of the thing being counted. Flat things are counted differently from round ones, long things differently from small ones. That sounds overwhelming at first, but don't panic: with the universal つ-counter and a handful of other counters you'll get along fine in everyday life. Japanese people themselves often use the つ-counter when they don't know which specific counter fits.
sections[].heading: The つ-counter — Your life preserver
人・個・枚 — People, pieces, flat things
本・杯 — Long things and drinks
sections[].text: The つ-counter (ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ...) uses the old native Japanese numbers and works as a universal counter for almost everything — especially when you don't know the specific counter. It goes from ひとつ (1) to とお (10); beyond that you switch to specific counters or simply use the Sino-Japanese numbers. The forms sound unfamiliar at first, because they're completely different from いち, に, さん.

人 (にん/り) counts people — but careful: 一人 (ひとり) and 二人 (ふたり) are irregular; from three on it becomes regular (三人 = さんにん). 個 (こ) counts small, compact, round things like eggs, apples, candies. 枚 (まい) counts flat, thin things like paper, plates, T-shirts, tickets, pizzas. Together with つ, these three counters already cover a large part of everyday life.

本 (ほん/ぼん/ぽん) counts long, thin things — pens, bottles, trees, umbrellas, movies, phone calls and even train lines. The pronunciation changes: いっぽん, にほん, さんぼん, よんほん... 杯 (はい/ばい/ぱい) counts containers with contents — cups, glasses, bowls. Here too the pronunciation changes: いっぱい, にはい, さんばい. To ask about the number, you put 何 (なん) in front of the counter: 何本 (なんぼん), 何杯 (なんばい), 何人 (なんにん).
sections[].tip: Memorize the sequence: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, とお. From 11 on there's no つ-form anymore — then you use specific counters.
With 個 there are sound changes: いっこ (1), ろっこ (6), はっこ (8), じゅっこ (10). These so-called "促音変化" (sound doubling) occur with many counters.
If you forget the right counter, just use the つ-counter or the bare number — you'll still be understood. Perfection comes with time!
sections[].examples[].de: Three apples, please.
I have just one question.
I bought two pieces of cake.
The three of us went out to eat.
I bought six eggs.
Two tickets, please.
I have three pens.
I drank a cup of coffee.
How many people are coming?

en.title: 時間の表現
en.subtitle: Time expressions — 前に・後で・時・てから・ごろ・まで・から・間
en.intro: Time plays a central role in every language, and Japanese has an elegant system for expressing relationships in time. In this lesson you'll learn the most important time words and particles — from "before" through "after" and "only then" all the way to "while". With these building blocks you can tell what you did when, what you're planning next and what your daily routine looks like. The good news: most of the forms follow clear, logical patterns.
sections[].heading: 前に・後で・てから — Before, after and only then
時・ごろ — Point in time and approximate time
から・まで・間 — From, until, while
sections[].text: 前に (まえに) means "before" and is attached either to a verb in the dictionary form (辞書形) or to a noun + の. 後で (あとで) means "after" and follows the た-form of a verb or a noun + の. ～てから also means "after", but puts more emphasis on the order: first A, then B. These three patterns are indispensable for describing sequences in time. Note: 前に can also mean "in front of" in a spatial sense (建物の前に = in front of the building).

時 (とき) means "when" and is attached to verbs, adjectives or noun + の: 子供の時 (when I was a child), 暇な時 (when I'm free), 食べる時 (when I eat). ごろ means "around/about" with clock times and points in time: 三時ごろ (around three). Don't confuse ごろ with ぐらい — ごろ is for points in time, ぐらい for durations and amounts.

から marks the starting point of a time span ("from/since"), まで the end point ("until"). Together they form a pair: 九時から五時まで (from 9 to 5). 間 (あいだ) means "while" or "during the time span" and is often combined with に (間に = during [a period], at some point within it). Without に, 間 emphasizes the entire duration: 夏休みの間 (throughout the whole summer vacation).
sections[].tip: 前に takes the dictionary form (辞書形), not the ます-form: 食べる前に (correct), 食べます前に (wrong). 後で takes the た-form: 食べた後で. ～てから often sounds more like "and only then".
時 is extremely versatile — past before 時 (食べた時 = when I ate) and present before 時 (食べる時 = when I eat / before I eat). The tense before 時 affects the meaning!
から can also mean "because" (reason), not just "from" (time). Context makes it clear: 時間がないから (because I don't have time) vs 三時から (from three o'clock).
sections[].examples[].de: Before I go to bed, I brush my teeth.
After I eat, I drink coffee.
After I get home, then I do my homework.
Before class, I prepare.
When I was in Japan, I ate ramen every day.
I get up around seven.
When I'm free, I watch movies.
I work from Monday to Friday.
Until what time is class?
While I was sleeping, it snowed.

en.title: もう & まだ
en.subtitle: Already, still, not yet, no longer
en.intro: Two little words, four big meanings — もう and まだ are words you need from day one. "Have you eaten yet?" "No, not yet." "Are you still studying?" "No, not anymore." Sentences like these are everywhere in daily life, and the nice thing is: the logic behind もう and まだ is crystal clear once you understand them as a system. It's always about whether an expected change of state has already happened — or not yet.
sections[].heading: もう + past — "Already done"
まだ — "Still" and "not yet"
もう + negative — "No longer"
sections[].text: もう combined with a positive past form means "already". It signals that an expected action has been completed. The question もう〜ましたか (Have you already...?) is one of the most common everyday questions of all. To the question もう食べましたか you answer either はい、もう食べました (Yes, already) or いいえ、まだです (No, not yet).

まだ + positive form means "still" — a state continues that will end at some point. まだ + negative form (or simply まだです) means "not yet" — something expected hasn't happened yet. まだです is the standard short answer to もう〜ましたか questions and extremely common in daily life.

もう + negative form means "no longer / not anymore" — a state that used to exist is now over. This is the fourth and last combination of the system. Put together, it forms an elegant square: もう+positive = already; まだ+positive = still; まだ+negative = not yet; もう+negative = no longer. This system is perfectly symmetrical and logical.
sections[].tip: もう can also mean "soon / any moment" when combined with present/future: もう行きます (I'm leaving now), もうすぐ来ます (He'll be here any minute). Here もう expresses an imminent change.
まだ + ている = a state continues (まだ寝ている = is still sleeping). まだ + ていない = an expected action is still pending (まだ寝ていない = hasn't fallen asleep yet).
The four-way system at a glance: もう＋肯定 = already ✓ | まだ＋肯定 = still ↔ | まだ＋否定 = not yet ✗→ | もう＋否定 = no longer ←✗. Learn this pattern as a unit — it comes up on every JLPT!
sections[].examples[].de: Have you done your homework yet?
Yes, I already did.
I've already had lunch.
It's still raining.
I haven't eaten yet.
Is the report not ready yet?
I don't drink alcohol anymore.
I'm not a child anymore.
That shop doesn't exist anymore.

en.title: 比較の基本
en.subtitle: Comparisons — より・ほう・一番
en.intro: Comparing is one of the most basic things we do in a language: what's bigger, what tastes better, who's faster? In Japanese, comparisons work differently from English — there are no comparative or superlative forms like "bigger" or "biggest". Instead you use constructions with より (than), ほう (side/alternative) and 一番 (number one). Sounds unfamiliar, but it's ultimately simpler than the English system with its irregular forms.
sections[].heading: AはBより〜 — A is [more] than B
AのほうがBより〜 — Emphasized comparisons
一番 & どちらが〜 — Superlative and comparison questions
sections[].text: The basic structure of a comparison is A は B より + adjective + です. It means: "A is [adjective]-er than B." The adjective stays in its basic form — no "-er" needed! より literally means something like "seen from B" or "compared with B". The order is flexible, but A は B より is the most common arrangement.

When you want to emphasize which side stands out in the comparison, you use A のほうが B より + adjective. ほう means "side" or "alternative" and makes the comparison more explicit. This form is especially common in answers to comparison questions. You can also leave out the より part when the thing being compared is clear from context: Aのほうが好きです (I like A better).

一番 (いちばん) means "the most / number one" and is placed directly before the adjective to express the superlative: 一番 + adjective. For comparison questions between two things, you use どちらが〜ですか (Which of the two is...?). With three or more things, you ask with どれが一番〜ですか or 何が一番〜ですか.
sections[].tip: In Japanese the adjective NEVER changes: 大きい stays 大きい, whether in its basic form or in a comparison. Only the context (より) shows that a comparison is being made.
ほう is often used in recommendations: こっちのほうがいいですよ (This one is better!). Very useful when shopping and making decisions.
一番 can also be used to mean "favorite": 一番好きな食べ物は何ですか (What's your favorite food?). And: で marks the scope of the superlative — クラスで一番 (the most in the class), 世界で一番 (the most in the world).
sections[].examples[].de: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.
I like summer better than winter.
Japanese is harder than English.
The train is faster than the bus.
This one is cheaper.
I prefer tea (to the other one).
The highest mountain in Japan is Mt. Fuji.
Which do you like better, coffee or tea?
What was the most delicious?

en.title: あげる・もらう・くれる 入門
en.subtitle: Giving & Receiving — Perspective Matters
en.intro: In English you have "give" and "get", and that's it. Japanese, on the other hand, has three basic verbs for giving and receiving, and the choice depends on who gives, who receives and from whose perspective the story is told. That sounds confusing at first, but there's a beautiful system behind it that weaves respect and social relationships into the language. Let's start with the basics — the more polite variants come in later lessons.
sections[].heading: あげる — I give (away from me)
くれる — Someone gives to me (toward me)
もらう — I receive (I get)
sections[].text: あげる means "to give" and is used when the speaker (or someone in the speaker's group) gives something to another person. The direction is away from the speaker. The basic structure is: Giver は Recipient に Object を あげる. あげる can also be used when a third person gives something to another third person — as long as it isn't directed "to me".

くれる also means "to give", but the direction is reversed: someone gives something to the speaker (or the speaker's in-group). The movement goes toward the speaker. くれる always carries a nuance of gratitude — the speaker sees the gift as a kind gesture. The structure is: Giver が/は (私に) Object を くれる. The 私に is often left out because くれる already makes it clear.

もらう means "to get/receive" and is used from the recipient's perspective. The structure is: Recipient は Giver に/から Object を もらう. Unlike くれる (where the focus is on the giver), もらう puts the recipient at the center. もらう also carries a nuance of gratitude. You mark the source with に or から.
sections[].tip: Important: NEVER say 私にあげる for "someone gives ME something" — for that you need くれる. あげる always goes away from the speaker!
くれる always expresses gratitude. 〜てくれる (someone does something for me) is one of the most common and important patterns in Japanese — it shows that you appreciate what the other person did.
Simple memory aid: あげる = ↑ away from me, くれる = ↓ toward me, もらう = ← I take it in. Think of the arrow and you'll always pick the right one!
sections[].examples[].de: I gave my friend a book.
My mother gave my little sister some cake.
What are you going to give Tanaka?
My friend gave me a book.
The teacher was kind enough to explain it (to me) carefully.
Who gave this to me?
I got a book from my friend.
What did you get for your birthday?
I got a bonus from the company.

en.title: ～ましょう・～ませんか
en.subtitle: Suggestions & invitations — doing something together
en.intro: How do you suggest doing something together in Japanese? How do you politely invite someone? And how do you offer help? In this lesson you'll learn three closely related forms that are all built on the ます-form. The difference between them lies in the nuance: from a casual call to action, to a polite invitation, to a considerate offer of help. All three forms are extremely common in everyday life and on the JLPT.
sections[].heading: ～ましょう — "Let's...!"
～ませんか — "Wouldn't you like to...?"
～ましょうか — "Shall I...?"
sections[].text: ～ましょう is formed by replacing ます with ましょう. It expresses a suggestion or shared intention — "Let's do X!" The speaker assumes the other person will join in. It's energetic, positive and a bit more direct than ～ませんか. You use it when you're fairly sure the other person agrees.

～ませんか is formed by replacing ます with ませんか. Literally it's a negative question: "Won't you do it?" But in practice it's a polite invitation: "Wouldn't you like to...? Would you be up for...?" It's more reserved than ましょう and leaves the other person free to decline. That's why it's the preferred form when inviting someone you don't know very well.

～ましょうか (ましょう + か) has two meanings: (1) offer of help: "Shall I do X for you?" — here the speaker kindly offers help. (2) joint decision: "Shall we do X?" — here the speaker seeks agreement on a shared plan. The meaning comes from context.
sections[].tip: ましょう sounds decisive — like "Let's go!" If you want to invite more politely and cautiously, use ませんか.
ませんか is THE form for invitations and making plans. It comes up constantly in the JLPT listening section!
The difference in a nutshell: ましょう = "Let's go!" (decision), ませんか = "How about it?" (invitation), ましょうか = "Shall I / Shall we?" (offer/question). All three are polite but fit different situations.
sections[].examples[].de: Let's eat together!
Let's watch a movie!
Let's head home soon.
Wouldn't you like to have some tea together?
Shall we go to karaoke next time?
Shall we watch a movie this weekend?
Shall I carry your bags?
Shall I open the window?
What time shall we meet?

en.title: ～ながら・～たり～たりする
en.subtitle: At the same time & in turn — multiple actions
en.intro: Sometimes you do two things at the same time, sometimes you do this and that in turn. Japanese has elegant structures for both situations: ながら for simultaneous actions and たり〜たりする for a loose list of activities. Both forms are extremely useful in everyday life and are expected from N5 on. Whenever you want to describe what your day looks like or what you get up to in your free time, you'll need these forms all the time.
sections[].heading: ～ながら — Two things at once
～たり～たりする — Doing this and that
ながら vs たり〜たりする — The difference
sections[].text: ～ながら expresses that two actions happen at the same time — like "while" in English. The formation is simple: verb ます-stem + ながら + main action. Important: the main action (= the more important one) comes at the end of the sentence, and the secondary action (= the one you do on the side) comes before ながら. Both actions must be carried out by the same subject.

～たり～たりする lists several actions loosely, without claiming to be complete — like "doing things like X and Y". Formation: verb た-form + り for each activity, and at the end comes する (します). You usually list two or three activities, but a single たり-form is also possible (then it means "doing something like X"). The form also works with adjectives and nouns.

Both forms describe multiple actions, but in fundamentally different ways: ながら = two things at the same time (listening to music AND studying, simultaneously). たり〜たりする = several things in turn or as a list (reading, watching TV, going for a walk — not necessarily at the same time). With ながら the subject must be the same; with たり not necessarily, as long as there's an overarching theme.
sections[].tip: The secondary action before ながら is the LESS important activity. 歌いながら料理する = I cook (main thing) and sing while doing it (on the side). The order matters!
Don't forget the する at the end! 読んだり見たり... → 読んだり見たりします。The する carries the tense (します, しました, したい etc.).
Memory aid: ながら = at the same time (multitasking), たり = one after another or loosely listed (a list). If you want to say "among other things", go with たり!
sections[].examples[].de: I study while listening to music.
Please don't talk on the phone while walking.
I eat while watching TV.
On weekends I do things like reading books and watching movies.
In Japan I did things like eating sushi and bathing in hot springs.
The weather is sometimes hot, sometimes cold.
I read the newspaper while drinking coffee. (at the same time)
On my days off I do things like shopping and cleaning. (in turn)
I had fun doing things like taking walks and taking photos.

en.title: から, ので, けど, のに
en.subtitle: Connecting sentences like a pro
en.intro: Single sentences are good — but only once you can connect them does your Japanese sound truly natural and fluent. In Japanese, the linking words usually come between the two parts of the sentence (not at the start of the clause like English "because"). Here you'll learn the four most important connectors for reasons and contrasts — and their subtle but important nuances.
sections[].heading: から — "Because" (direct and personal)
ので — "Because" (gentle and objective)
けど / けれど — "But / Although"
のに — "Although" (with frustration or regret)
sections[].text: から is the most direct way to give a reason. It comes after the reason clause (in the plain form or ます-form) and leads into the consequence. から comes across as neutral to slightly assertive — the speaker stands behind their reasoning. It fits most everyday situations and is the standard for all kinds of reasons.

ので expresses the same reason but sounds softer and more polite. It implies that the connection is objectively understandable to the listener — you're not explaining your personal opinion but a situation anyone can follow. Important: ので is always preceded by the plain form. With な-adjectives and nouns, だ becomes な (静かなので, 学生なので).

けど (casual) or けれど(も) (more formal) connects two sentences with a contrast. What many people don't know: けど is also often used as a soft transition without any real contrast — almost like "so..." or "by the way...". It cushions the second part and makes it less direct. This use is extremely widespread in Japanese.

のに expresses a contrast with disappointment, frustration or surprise. There's always an undertone of "and that's annoying / a shame / unfair!". Unlike けど, which is neutral, のに carries an emotional judgment. のに is preceded by the plain form; with な-adjectives だ becomes な, and with nouns as well.
sections[].tip: Rule of thumb: から sounds like "because I think..." (subjective, assertive), ので sounds like "since, as we all know..." (objective, reserved). In a work context and with older people, ので is the safer choice. In an email to your boss: better ので than から.

Quick comparison: けど = a neutral "but" (no judgment). のに = a frustrated "even though!" (always with an emotional undertone). Both can come at the end of a sentence with the second part left out: 「頑張ったのに…」= "Even though I tried so hard..." (the listener can fill in the rest).
sections[].examples[].de: It was hot, so I opened the window.
I have a test tomorrow, so I'm studying today.
I'm hungry, so let's eat something.
Since it's raining, I'll take an umbrella.
Since the train was delayed, I was late.
Since tomorrow is a day off, I'll take it easy.
Japanese is difficult, but it's fun.
I want to buy it, but I don't have any money.
Excuse me, do you have a moment? (が as a soft transition)
Even though I studied, I failed the test!
Even though he promised, he didn't come!
I went to all the trouble of making it, and nobody's eating it!

en.title: ～すぎる・～やすい・～にくい
en.subtitle: Too much, easy to, hard to — modifying verbs & adjectives
en.intro: How do you say "too expensive", "easy to understand" or "hard to read"? In Japanese you simply attach suffixes to the verb stem or adjective stem — no rephrasing needed. These three forms are incredibly practical and belong to the absolute basics. You'll need them every day: when shopping (高すぎる!), when studying (わかりやすい!), when eating (食べにくい...). In this lesson you'll get to know all three and avoid the typical beginner mistakes.
sections[].heading: ～すぎる — Too much / overdoing it
～やすい — Easy to do
～にくい — Hard to do
sections[].text: ～すぎる means "too much / too" and expresses that something goes beyond the appropriate amount. Formation: verb ます-stem + すぎる (食べすぎる = to eat too much) or い-adjective without い + すぎる (高すぎる = too expensive) or な-adjective + すぎる (静かすぎる = too quiet). すぎる itself behaves like a る-verb and can be conjugated: すぎます, すぎた, すぎない.

～やすい means "easy to" and describes an action that can be done without effort. The formation is simple: verb ます-stem + やすい. The result behaves like an い-adjective: わかりやすい (easy to understand), 使いやすい (easy to use, user-friendly), 読みやすい (easy to read). So you can use it in comparisons and negate it as usual: やすくない, やすかった.

～にくい is the opposite of やすい and means "hard to / difficult to". The formation is identical: verb ます-stem + にくい. にくい also behaves like an い-adjective. Important: にくい describes an objective difficulty — the thing itself is hard to do. When it's more about psychological discomfort (e.g. saying something embarrassing), you use づらい instead — but that only comes at higher levels.
sections[].tip: Common mistake: 高いすぎる (wrong!) — the い has to go! Correct: 高すぎる. With な-adjectives the な drops: 静か＋すぎる = 静かすぎる. And: いい/良い becomes よすぎる (not いすぎる).
やすい can also mean "to tend to": 風邪をひきやすい (you catch colds easily), 忘れやすい (you forget things easily). Context decides whether it's about ease or tendency.

The trio at a glance: すぎる = too much (excess), やすい = easy (simple / tending to), にくい = hard (objectively difficult). All three attach to the ます-stem: 食べ＋すぎる, 食べ＋やすい, 食べ＋にくい. Learn the stem once, use it three times!
sections[].examples[].de: I ate too much yesterday.
This bag is too expensive.
I drank too much last night and have a headache.
This room is too quiet. (な-adjective + すぎる)
This book is easy to read.
This dictionary is easy to use.
The teacher's explanation was easy to understand.
This kanji is hard to remember.
These shoes are hard to walk in.
Small writing is hard to read.

en.title: ～てください・～ないでください
en.subtitle: Requests & prohibitions — politely asking for an action
en.intro: With ～てください you politely ask someone to do something. With ～ないでください you ask someone not to do something. Both forms are part of the absolute N5 core and come up constantly in everyday life: in class, in announcements, in shops and on the JLPT.
sections[].heading: ～てください — "Please do ..."
～ないでください — "Please don't ..."
Request vs. prohibition
sections[].text: The form is built with て-form + ください. It's polite but direct. It's used for instructions, requests and notices. Compared with a bare imperative, ～てください sounds much softer and more suitable for everyday use.
For a negative request you use the ない-form + でください. The meaning is "Please don't ...". This form is very common in rules, notices and polite reminders.
Positive and negative form a pair: ～てください asks for an action, ～ないでください prevents one. At N5, what matters is that you can reliably recognize and produce both forms.
sections[].tip: ください almost always comes after the て-form. Learn common chunks directly as a unit: 待ってください, 見てください, 聞いてください.
Don't confuse them: ～ないでください is a polite request, not a strict prohibition. Stricter rules are often phrased with ～てはいけない or ～てはいけません.
Typical JLPT focus: the same verb once positive, once negative. So pay close attention to て-form vs. ない-form.
sections[].examples[].de: Please say it once more.
Please write your name here.
Please wait a moment.
Please don't take photos here.
Please don't worry.
Please don't talk during class.
Please open the window.
Please don't open the window.

en.title: ～たことがある
en.subtitle: Expressing experience — "I've ... before"
en.intro: With ～たことがある you talk about experiences: having done something before. The form is central to conversations about travel, food, hobbies and life events, and it clearly belongs to the beginner level.
sections[].heading: Formation and basic meaning
Specific event vs. experience
sections[].text: The form is built with verb in the た-form + ことがある. It doesn't mean "I have just done it now" but "I have had the experience". So it's about experiences in the past, not about a specific completed point in time.

A sentence with ～たことがある leaves the exact time open. If you want to say when something happened, you usually use a normal past form. This is an important difference for listening comprehension and for rewriting sentences.
sections[].tip: ～たことがある asks about experience, not habit. For habits you need other forms such as よく～ます or いつも～ます.
When an exact time like 昨日, 去年 or 三時に matters, the normal past form is often the better choice.
sections[].examples[].de: I've been to Japan before.
I've never eaten natto.
Have you ever seen Mt. Fuji?
I went to Kyoto last year.
I've been to Kyoto before.

en.title: ～んです・～のです
en.subtitle: Explaining and adding nuance — background, reason, feeling
en.intro: ～んです and ～のです are among the most important conversational forms in Japanese. They give a statement an explanatory, justifying or emotional coloring. Beginners run into this structure very early, but often only understand it systematically much later.
sections[].heading: What ～んです expresses
Formation
