sections[].text: With ～んです / ～のです you give a statement the character of an explanation, background information or justification. In casual speech you mostly hear ～んです; in more formal language also ～のです. In meaning the two are very close.
After verbs and い-adjectives you attach んです directly. After nouns and な-adjectives you need な + んです. This small difference comes up in exams.
sections[].tip: In questions, ～んですか often sounds less harsh than a bare question. It signals: "I'd like to understand the background."
Remember: nouns/な-adjectives need な. This is one of the most common beginner mistakes with this structure.
sections[].examples[].de: The thing is, I can't go today.
I'm studying Japanese, you see.
Why were you late?
I'm busy, you see.
The thing is, I'm a student.
It's handy, you see.

en.title: ～と思います・～つもりです
en.subtitle: Opinion and intention — thinking vs. planning
en.intro: With ～と思います you express an opinion or a guess. With ～つもりです you talk about a firm intention. Both patterns are indispensable for simple conversations about plans and assessments and should be kept clearly apart at the beginner level.
sections[].heading: ～と思います — "I think that ..."
～つもりです — "I intend to ..."
sections[].text: The structure is clause + と思います. You use it to express an opinion, an assessment or a cautious claim. ～と思います is especially important in polite communication because it makes statements sound less blunt.
The form verb in the dictionary form / ない-form + つもりです expresses a clear intention. It's stronger than a mere plan and shows that the speaker has already made up their mind.
sections[].tip: A complete clause comes before と思います. With nouns and な-adjectives, the plain style needs a だ: 静かだと思います.
Don't mix them up: ～と思います = opinion, ～つもりです = intention. These are two different communicative functions.
sections[].examples[].de: I think this book is interesting.
I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think Tanaka won't be here yet.
I plan to go to Japan next year.
I don't intend to drink any alcohol today.
I plan to study Japanese at university.

en.title: ～だけ・～しか～ない
en.subtitle: Limiting and excluding — two ways to say "only"
en.intro: Japanese has several ways to say "only". The most important ones for beginners are ～だけ and ～しか～ない. Both have a similar basic meaning, but the nuance differs: ～だけ is neutral, while ～しか～ない sounds stronger and rules out other possibilities.
sections[].heading: ～だけ — neutral limitation
～しか～ない — nothing but ...
sections[].text: ～だけ simply means "only, just". It describes a limitation without any strong emotional overtone. You attach だけ directly to nouns, pronouns or sometimes phrases.
With ～しか + negative form you say: "There's nothing but ...", "I have only ... and nothing else". This structure is stronger than だけ and often feels more restrictive.
sections[].tip: ～だけ is matter-of-fact and neutral. It often fits when you simply want to limit an amount, a time or a person.
しか is almost always followed by a negative. This exact combination is the core of the structure and is often specifically tested on the JLPT.
sections[].examples[].de: I only drink water.
Today I studied for only one hour.
Only I know.
I only have 1000 yen.
I can only speak Japanese.
I only take Sundays off.

en.title: ～のが好き・上手・下手
en.subtitle: Nominalized actions — what you like or are good at
en.intro: When an action itself becomes the topic, beginner Japanese often uses の. Especially common are the patterns ～のが好き, ～のが上手 and ～のが下手. With them you can talk about preferences and abilities without building complicated subordinate clauses.
sections[].heading: Nominalizing actions with の
～のは～です — defining or highlighting an action
sections[].text: With dictionary form verb + の you turn an action into something you can talk about. It's often followed by が, because this nominalized action becomes the subject of 好き, 上手 or 下手.
With verb + のは～です you set up an action as the topic and then make a statement about it. This is useful for definitions, contrasts and simple explanations.
sections[].tip: The pattern is very productive: verb + の + が + evaluation. It's one of the basic building blocks of natural beginner Japanese.
～のが好き and ～のは～です are related but not the same: が often marks what is being evaluated, は the topic of the whole sentence.
sections[].examples[].de: I like reading books.
He/She is good at cooking.
I'm bad at writing kanji.
My hobby is taking photos.
Studying Japanese is fun.
Getting up early is hard.

en.title: ～かもしれない・～ほうがいい
en.subtitle: Guesses and advice — uncertainty and recommendation
en.intro: From N4 on, you need to express not only facts but also probabilities and recommendations. That's exactly what ～かもしれない and ～ほうがいい are essential for: one makes statements cautious, the other gives advice.
sections[].heading: ～かもしれない — "maybe, possibly"
～ほうがいい / ～たほうがいい — giving advice
sections[].text: The structure clause + かもしれない expresses an uncertain guess. It's more cautious than でしょう and much more useful for everyday language at N4. Nouns and な-adjectives come directly before it, without だ: 雪かもしれない, 静かかもしれない.
With verb in the dictionary form + ほうがいい or, more commonly, verb in the た-form + ほうがいい you give advice: "you'd better ...". The た-variant is especially common in modern usage.
sections[].tip: かもしれない expresses uncertainty. It doesn't fit well when you want to sound very convinced. Then きっと or でしょう would be closer.
With the negative form you can also advise against something: 行かないほうがいい, 言わないほうがいい.
sections[].examples[].de: It might snow tomorrow.
Tanaka may have already gone home.
That shop might be famous.
You'd better go to bed early.
You should take this medicine.
You'd better not overdo it.

en.title: ～てみる・～ておく・～てある
en.subtitle: Trying out, preparing, resulting state
en.intro: These three て-form constructions are classic N4 patterns. They look similar but have different functions: ～てみる means trying something out, ～ておく means preparing or leaving something as it is, and ～てある describes a state that was created on purpose.
sections[].heading: ～てみる — trying something out
～ておく — doing in advance or leaving as is
～てある — a deliberately created state
sections[].text: With て-form + みる you say that you do something as a test. The original verb 見る loses its meaning "to see" here and becomes a helper form for experience or attempt.
The form て-form + おく often means "to do in advance", i.e. to prepare. But it can also mean deliberately leaving something in a certain state. In spoken language ておく is often contracted to とく.
With て-form + ある you describe a state that came about through a deliberate action. The subject is often the object of the original action. This clearly sets ～てある apart from ～ている.
sections[].tip: ～てみる is very productive: 着てみる, 使ってみる, 聞いてみる. It's always about an attempt or a test.
Preparation is the default meaning. When you hear or read a sense of "for later", ～ておく is often the right analysis.
～てある implies intent. For a natural description of a state without a focus on preparation, ～ている is often more suitable.
sections[].examples[].de: I'll try this cake.
Please try it once more.
I'd like to try living in Japan.
I'll book the hotel before the trip.
I'll leave it here because I'm going to read it later.
It's important, so please make a note of it.
A name is written on the desk.
The door has been opened and left open.
The materials for the meeting have already been prepared.

en.title: ～ていく・～てくる
en.subtitle: Change and direction — onward from now, up until now
en.intro: ～ていく and ～てくる combine an action with a perspective of movement or time. These structures are important for N4 because they express not only physical direction but also developments over time.
sections[].heading: Direction in space
Development over time
sections[].text: Literally, ～ていく can mean "do something and go away" and ～てくる "do something and come here". This concrete meaning of movement is the easiest way in.
Very important at N4 is the metaphorical meaning: ～ていく describes a change going forward from now, ～てくる a development that has built up until now.
sections[].tip: With ～てくる the link to the speaker is strong: something moves toward me / up to this point. With ～ていく something moves away from the speaker.
N4 exam question: Has the change already taken place up to now? Then it's often ～てくる. Does it continue from now on? Then it's often ～ていく.
sections[].examples[].de: I'll go buy a drink at the convenience store and come back.
My friend went home ahead of me.
From now on I'll keep studying Japanese more.
It has gradually gotten colder.
The number of people will keep increasing.

en.title: ～ないまでも / ～なりとも
en.subtitle: At least that – settling for less
en.intro: Both expressions lower expectations: the ideal is out of reach, but there should at least be a minimum. ないまでも explicitly names the unattained ideal; なりとも attaches to a small amount.
sections[].heading: ないまでも — if not X, then at least Y
なりとも — even if it's only a little
sections[].text: Verb (ない-form) + までも, followed by the minimum, often with せめて or 少なくとも. Typical: ～とは言わないまでも.
Quantity expression (少し, 多少, 一目, わずか) + なりとも. Polite and written, often in requests, wishes and job ads.
sections[].tip: Does the sentence name the ideal (満点, 毎日) and then the minimum? ないまでも. Is the focus only on a small amount (少し, 多少)? なりとも – in everyday speech simply でも.
sections[].examples[].de: I won't say a perfect score, but I'd at least like to get eighty points.
Even if you won't help, at least don't get in the way.
I hope I can be of help, even if only a little.
I hope you recover, even if only a single day sooner.

en.title: ～ならいざしらず / ～ならまだしも
en.subtitle: Granting exceptions and drawing lines
en.intro: Both patterns contrast two cases. The first is set aside or only just accepted; the second is judged critically. The judgment should be clear from the context.
sections[].heading: ならいざしらず — maybe for A, but not for B
ならまだしも — A would still be acceptable
sections[].text: Noun + ならいざしらず. The speaker explicitly sets the first case aside and stresses that their judgment applies to the second. There is often a contrast such as 昔 versus 今 or 初心者 versus 経験者.
A noun or a nominalized situation + ならまだしも. The first case is still within an acceptable limit; the second goes beyond it. The meaning is not just a neutral condition.
sections[].tip: ならまだしも fits especially well when there is a recognizable limit of tolerance. ならいざしらず takes a different case out of the statement.
sections[].examples[].de: It may have been different in the old days, but now you can easily get in touch with people overseas.
For a beginner it would be understandable, but it's a problem when experienced people don't know this procedure.
One day would be one thing, but no reply for a whole week is worrying.
As a joke it would be one thing, but if you mean it seriously, that's a problem.

en.title: ～ったらない / ～極まりない
en.subtitle: Taking feelings and judgments to the extreme
en.intro: Both expressions mean "extremely". ったらない sounds spoken and expresses your own feeling; 極まりない is stiff written language and evaluates a behavior or situation.
sections[].heading: ったらない — indescribably (spoken)
極まりない — extremely (written, evaluative)
sections[].text: い-adj + ったらない; with nouns ending in ～さ: ～といったらない. Often used for your own feelings such as fear, embarrassment, loneliness or anger.
な-adj stem + 極まりない / 極まる. Typical with 失礼, 危険, 不愉快, 無責任. Sounds official or indignant and suits criticism of a behavior.
sections[].tip: An い-adjective and your own feeling in conversation? ったらない. A な-adjective and a critical judgment in a formal tone? 極まりない.
sections[].examples[].de: Nights alone are unbearably lonely.
The frustration I felt back then was indescribable.
Using a smartphone while driving is extremely dangerous.
Breaking a promise without even getting in touch is extremely rude.

en.title: ～こととて / ～手前
en.subtitle: Giving reasons to ask for leniency or to save face
en.intro: Both expressions give a reason with other people in mind. こととて asks for understanding for a mistake; 手前 explains why you feel compelled to do something for the sake of your own reputation.
sections[].heading: こととて — since, after all … (asking for leniency)
手前 — out of concern for your own standing
sections[].text: Verb / Noun + の + こととて. Old-fashioned and polite, especially in apologies: the reason is meant to make the mistake understandable.
Verb (た-form / dictionary form) / Noun + の + 手前. You have said something or are standing in front of others, so you can't back out. It is usually followed by ～わけにはいかない or ～しかない.
sections[].tip: Are you apologizing for something that happened? こととて. Are you explaining why you have to do something to save face? 手前.
sections[].examples[].de: As it was my first time, I wasn't able to do it well – I'm very sorry.
Because it was all so sudden, my reply was delayed.
Having promised in front of everyone, I can't back out now.
In front of their subordinates, a boss can't afford to show weakness.

en.title: いかんせん / ～いかんでは
en.subtitle: Two expressions with 如何（いかん）
en.intro: Both expressions go back to classical 如何 ("how"), but they do completely different jobs: いかんせん laments an obstacle, ～いかんでは makes a result depend on something.
sections[].heading: いかんせん — unfortunately, nothing can be done
～いかんでは — depending on …
sections[].text: At the start of a sentence, usually after a が／けれど clause with the positive part: you would like to, but the obstacle is stronger.
Noun (+ の) + いかんでは / いかんによっては. The outcome depends on the factor named; counterpart: ～いかんによらず ("regardless of").
sections[].tip: Does the expression come at the start of the sentence and lament an obstacle? いかんせん. Does it follow a noun and name a condition? いかんでは.
sections[].examples[].de: I'd like to go, but unfortunately I don't have the money.
The idea is interesting. Unfortunately, it's hard to put into practice.
Depending on the exam results, having to repeat a year is also possible.
Depending on the weather, the game may be called off.

en.title: ～が早いか / ～たとたん
en.subtitle: Barely done – and the next thing happens
en.intro: Both expressions link two events that happen almost simultaneously. たとたん is everyday language and often stresses surprise; が早いか belongs to written language and stresses the speed of a deliberate action.
sections[].heading: たとたん — at the very moment (N3)
が早いか — no sooner... than (N1)
sections[].text: Verb (た-form) + とたん(に). The second event is usually unexpected and not controlled by the speaker. Very common in conversation.
Verb (dictionary form / た-form) + が早いか. Someone acts lightning-fast after the first event. Typical of narrative texts; the second part is not a request or an intention.
sections[].tip: Is the second event a surprise that happens to you (めまいがした)? Then たとたん. Does someone act deliberately and immediately (飛び出した)? Then が早いか fits – or や否や just as well.
sections[].examples[].de: The moment I opened the door, the cat jumped out.
The moment I stood up, I felt dizzy.
No sooner had he hung up than he rushed out of the room.
No sooner had the child been given the toy than it started opening the box.

en.title: ～にして初めて / ～て初めて
en.subtitle: When an experience truly brings understanding
en.intro: In the right contexts, both patterns mean "only then". The connecting form shows whether the prerequisite is an action or a particular point in time or state.
sections[].heading: て初めて — only after something happens
にして初めて — only at this stage
sections[].text: Verb in the て-form + 初めて. The experience makes possible an insight or change that wasn't possible before. This is different from 初めて日本に行く: there it simply means going to Japan for the first time.

Noun + にして初めて. Emphatic and typical of written language: only at this age, in this situation or with this much experience does something become possible. The form presents the prerequisite as especially significant.
sections[].tip: A verb before the gap? 暮らして初めて. An age presented as a highlighted threshold? 四十歳にして初めて.
sections[].examples[].de: It was only when I lived on my own that I realized how much work housework is.
It was only after hearing the explanation that I noticed the mistake.
It was only at forty that I finally had a shop of my own.
Some judgments only become possible with many years of experience.

en.title: ～にかこつけて / ～にかまけて
en.subtitle: Pretext or complete absorption?
en.intro: Both expressions explain a behavior by pointing to some other circumstance. What matters is whether someone uses that circumstance as a pretext, or is so taken up by it that other things are left undone.
sections[].heading: にかこつけて — using something as a pretext
にかまけて — completely taken up by something
sections[].text: Noun + にかこつけて. The stated reason is put forward in order to pursue a different intention. The speaker usually views this critically. A neutral occasion is more likely expressed with をきっかけに.
Noun + にかまけて. Work, pleasure or some other activity takes someone over completely. A neglected duty often follows. Unlike にかこつけて, there doesn't have to be a pretext involved.
sections[].tip: Check yourself: is 忙しい just an excuse? Then にかこつけて. Is someone genuinely consumed by work? Then にかまけて.
sections[].examples[].de: He used a business trip as an excuse to go and see a friend.
I used being busy as an excuse to put off replying.
I was so caught up in my work that I never made time with my family a priority.
I was so busy playing that I forgot about my homework.

en.title: ～ものを / ～ではあるまいし
en.subtitle: Recognizing regret and reproach
en.intro: These patterns carry the speaker's attitude. If you only translate the facts, it's easy to miss the regret, criticism or lecturing tone. They are rarely the best choice for neutral requests.
sections[].heading: ものを — it could have turned out differently
ではあるまいし — after all, it's not …
sections[].text: Verb or adjective in the plain form + ものを. Often a condition comes first: had someone acted differently, a better outcome would have been possible. The second part can be left unsaid.

Noun + ではあるまいし. The case that is ruled out serves as the reason for criticism or a demand. 子供ではあるまいし can easily sound condescending. When working together politely, it is better to say things directly and objectively.
sections[].tip: ものを often looks back with regret at a missed opportunity. ではあるまいし draws a critical comparison in the here and now.
sections[].examples[].de: If you had come to me sooner, I could have helped you.
I should have taken my umbrella, but I left it behind.
You're not a child, so tidy up after yourself.
It's not as if it's an exam; you don't need to be so nervous.

en.title: ～がてら / ～かたがた / ～ともなく
en.subtitle: Side purpose, formal occasion, or no intention at all
en.intro: Not every incidental action works the same way. がてら combines purposes, かたがた names a formal occasion, and ともなく describes an action without any clear intention.
sections[].heading: がてら — making use of the opportunity
かたがた — on this occasion, also
ともなく — without any clear intention
sections[].text: Noun or ます-stem + がてら. One action is combined with a second, often when you go out somewhere. Unlike ながら, it's often about two purposes of the same outing, not about exact simultaneity.
Noun + かたがた. Formal, especially with お礼・お詫び・ご挨拶 and a visit. Don't attach it to just any verb.
Dictionary form + ともなく, especially with 見る・聞く・考える. A perception happens without any aim. This is not an additional purpose of a planned visit.
sections[].tip: Two deliberately combined purposes → がてら. A formal reason for a visit → かたがた. Aimless perception → ともなく.
sections[].examples[].de: I took a walk and bought some bread while I was at it.
I saw my friend off to the station and did some shopping on the way.
I have come to thank you and to pay my respects at the same time.
I visited my teacher, partly to give them a report.
I was gazing absently out of the window.
The conversation I had been half listening to suddenly caught my interest.

en.title: ～きらいがある / ～がち
en.subtitle: Describing tendencies – neutral or critical?
en.intro: Both expressions say that something happens often or that someone tends to do something. がち is everyday language and tends to describe states; きらいがある judges an undesirable trait from a distance.
sections[].heading: がち — happens often (N3)
きらいがある — has the (bad) habit of (N1)
sections[].text: Verb (ます-stem) / Noun + がち. Common with things you can't fully control: 病気がち, 遅れがち, 曇りがち. Usually slightly negative, but not judgmental.
Verb (dictionary form) / Noun + の + きらいがある. Describes a character trait or attitude that the speaker criticizes. Only for people, groups and their behavior.
sections[].tip: A clock or the weather can't have a きらいがある – use がち for those. If you're passing judgment on a person's behavior, reach for きらいがある.
sections[].examples[].de: In winter, people tend not to get enough exercise.
This clock has been running slow a lot lately.
He has a habit of not listening to people all the way to the end.
Japanese meetings tend to put off reaching a conclusion.

en.title: ～ずにはおかない / ～ずにはすまない
en.subtitle: Certain effect or unavoidable obligation
en.intro: The similar form hides an important difference: either an effect is certain to occur, or an action is unavoidable out of responsibility. Both use the negative verb stem; する becomes せず.
sections[].heading: ずにはおかない — is bound to cause
ずにはすまない — there's no getting around it
sections[].text: ない-form without ない + ずにはおかない. The speaker expects a strong, unavoidable effect or expresses a firm resolve. Verbs like 感動させる and 驚かせる are especially typical.
An apology, explanation or other necessary response cannot be avoided under the circumstances. The variant ないではすまない has the same basic meaning. It is often about social or moral responsibility.
sections[].tip: Test: a story moves its readers → 感動させずにはおかない. You have to apologize for a mistake → 謝らずにはすまない.
sections[].examples[].de: This film is bound to move everyone who sees it.
Her remarks will no doubt spark a debate.
Since I caused trouble for other people, there's no getting out of apologizing.
A change this big can't go unexplained.
